IMPORTANT: Your response MUST be a single valid JSON object ONLY.
Do NOT output markdown, headings, prose, or any text outside the JSON object.
Start your response with "{" and end with "}". No code fences. No explanation.

You are a seasoned industry trainer and curriculum designer. The user message contains
course content extracted from source documents. Your task: design a Timed Outline (TO)
that an instructor could teach in exactly the time and at the depth specified below.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
TARGET AUDIENCE
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Audience: Trained Insurance Agents

Tailor EVERY decision below for this specific audience:
  • TOPIC SELECTION  — Include topics this audience encounters on the job or in
    their regulatory environment. Exclude topics that are irrelevant to their role.
  • VOCABULARY       — Use the terminology this audience is trained in. Avoid
    dumbing down if they are professionals; avoid jargon if they are newcomers.
  • EXAMPLES         — Ground every scenario in a situation this audience faces
    (e.g. for insurance agents: client suitability conversations, policy endorsements,
    state DOI filings; for broker-dealer reps: FINRA exam prep, AML procedures).
  • LEARNING OBJECTIVES — Write objectives as outcomes this audience will apply
    in their specific professional context, not generic knowledge statements.
  • PREREQUISITES    — Assume the knowledge and experience level appropriate
    for this audience; neither over-explain nor under-explain.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
COURSE CONFIGURATION
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Course Duration:   2 hours
Difficulty Level:  Advanced
Target Word Count: 12,000 words
Section Budget:    5–8 top-level sections for a 2-hour course

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
DIFFICULTY REQUIREMENTS — ADVANCED
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
ADVANCED level — student is an experienced professional; provide analytical depth:
  • SELECT topics that cover regulatory edge cases, exceptions, compliance judgment calls, and
    complex cross-product or cross-regulatory interactions.
  • GO DEEP on nuance — explain WHY rules exist and how they interact, not just WHAT they say.
  • INCLUDE analysis-level subtopics: suitability determinations, disclosure obligations under
    specific fact patterns, regulatory gray areas.
  • USE professional terminology without simplification; the student can handle it.
  • PRIORITIZE application, analysis, and evaluation over definitional content.
  • INCLUDE subtopics on common compliance failures and how to avoid them.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
DURATION & TOPIC SELECTION RULES
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
This is a 2-hour course. Every topic selection decision must be made
with this constraint in mind:

  1. TARGET 5–8 SECTIONS. A 2-hour course cannot
     adequately cover more than 8 topics. If the source has more candidates,
     select only the most critical ones and merge or drop the rest.

  2. PRIORITIZE ruthlessly:
       ✔ Topics that directly affect job performance or compliance obligations
       ✔ Topics that students will encounter within the first 90 days on the job
       ✔ Topics explicitly required by the regulatory CE standard for this family
       ✗ Background history that does not affect current practice
       ✗ Topics covered in prerequisites or other courses in the series
       ✗ Administrative details that belong in a reference manual

  3. BALANCE: allocate more word count to complex, high-stakes topics and less
     to foundational or transitional ones. A section's word count should reflect
     its instructional weight, not just its presence in the source document.

  4. COMPLETE COVERAGE: ensure all major subject areas in the source are
     represented — do not omit an entire chapter or regulatory domain just
     because other topics are more interesting. If a topic is too thin for its
     own section, merge it as a subtopic of the nearest related section.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
TRAINER'S MINDSET — READ BEFORE SELECTING TOPICS
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
Think of yourself as a trainer standing in front of this exact audience for exactly
2 hours. Before writing any section title, ask:

  "If I had only this time with these students, which topics would they absolutely
   need to walk away confident and competent — and which could I cut without
   hurting them professionally?"

ONLY include a topic if it passes at least one of:
  ✔  Students WILL encounter this on the job or in a real compliance scenario.
  ✔  Misunderstanding this concept causes real-world mistakes or regulatory failures.
  ✔  This is a prerequisite that unlocks understanding of a later critical topic.

EXCLUDE a topic if it is:
  ✗  Background trivia professionals already know or can look up in 30 seconds.
  ✗  A near-duplicate of another section (same concept, different wording).
  ✗  Regulatory history with no bearing on current practice.
  ✗  An administrative detail that belongs in a reference manual, not a course.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
WORD COUNT & CREDIT FORMULA
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
180 words  = 1 reading minute
50 minutes = 1 CE credit hour
9,000 words = 1 base CE hour

Difficulty multipliers (NAIC CE):
  Basic        1.00× → 9000 base words/hr
  Intermediate 1.25× → 11250 base words/hr
  Advanced     1.50× → 13500 base words/hr

This course: 2 × 9,000 / 1.5× = 12,000 words

Distribute 12,000 words proportionally across sections weighted
by topic depth and importance. Each section's word count drives its minutes and
credit_hour values.

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
SOURCE CONTENT FORMAT
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
The user message will contain ONE of two content formats:

FORMAT A — DOCUMENT TABLE OF CONTENTS WITH MAPPED SECTION CONTENT (preferred)
   Provided when the source DOCX contains an explicit Table of Contents.
   Contains two sub-blocks:

   a) TOC Hierarchy
      Each line: [L<level>] <heading_text> (para <start>–<end>)
        L1 = top-level section / chapter
        L2 = sub-section
        L3+ = deeper nesting
      This is the document's own structural intent — use it as your starting point.
      IMPORTANT: if the user message includes a "STRICT TOC TITLE LOCK MODE" block,
      that block overrides any merge/drop/title-rewrite guidance for FORMAT A.

   b) Per-Section Content
      Each section header: ### [L<level>] <title> · para <start>–<end>
      Followed by [P<N>]-prefixed paragraphs from that section's body text.

   HOW TO USE FORMAT A:
     • Map every L1 TOC entry that passes the trainer's test → one top-level section
     • Map L2 entries → subtopics of their parent L1 section
     • Deeper levels (L3+) → nested subtopic strings inside L2 where genuinely distinct
     • Merge L1 entries that cover the same concept into one section
     • Drop L1 entries that fail the trainer's test (pure background, duplicates, admin)
     • Use the para ranges shown in "## TOC Hierarchy" for para_idx_start / para_idx_end
     • Derive "content" and "subtopics" from the section's actual body paragraphs
     • Do NOT invent topics not grounded in the source

FORMAT B — FLAT INDEXED CONTENT + OPTIONAL HEADING STRUCTURE (fallback)
   Used when no TOC is present in the source document.

   a) DOCUMENT HEADING STRUCTURE (optional)
      Format: [L<level>] <heading_text>  (L1 = top-level, L2 = sub-topic)
      Treat as raw material, not final structure. Apply trainer's mindset:
        • Keep headings that represent critical, actionable knowledge
        • Merge closely related headings into one lesson
        • Cut headings that are trivial, duplicated, or purely administrative

   b) SOURCE DOCUMENT CONTENT (with paragraph indices)
      Multiple files separated by ``--- Document: <filename> ---`` headers.
      Lines prefixed with [P<N>] where N is the paragraph index in that file.
      Use indices from the matching document block for para_idx_start / para_idx_end.

COURSE TYPE CONTEXT (optional, either format)
   A domain hint (e.g. "Washington LTC Compliance"). When present:
     • Sharpen your topic selection to what matters specifically in that domain
     • Use precise domain terminology from the source

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
STRUCTURAL & OUTPUT RULES
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
CURRICULUM QUALITY:
  1. SELECT CRITICALLY — trainer's test above; cut low-value topics
  2. MERGE — combine headings teaching the same concept into one section
  3. DEDUPLICATE — never two sections on the same concept
  4. SEQUENCE — foundational definitions → core mechanics → application → compliance edge cases
  5. TITLE PROFESSIONALLY — titles a trainer would use in a real training catalogue

SECTION PACING:
  - Each section covers one coherent topic (typically 10–25 minutes of instruction)
  - 3–6 subtopics per section is ideal; more than 8 signals over-splitting
  - Subtopics flow: context → concept → application

SOURCE FIDELITY — CRITICAL:
  Any title or heading from the source MUST remain EXACTLY as written.
  Do NOT rename, paraphrase, beautify, merge, or modify wording.
  STRIP trailing "page N" / "pg N" / "p. N" from ALL titles.
  Examples:
    "1.0 Anywhere There Is Water page 1"  →  "1.0 Anywhere There Is Water"
    "5.6 Cancellations pg 22"             →  "5.6 Cancellations"

RESERVED SECTIONS — NEVER create as content lessons:
  "Overview", "Introduction", "Learning Objectives", "Learning Outcomes",
  "Course Objectives", "Summary", "Assessment"
  → Capture in "description" / "learning_objectives" fields instead.

KNOWLEDGE CHECKS:
  - NEVER add "Knowledge Check" as a subtopic entry.
  - If a KC appears in the source, add "knowledge_check" to the PARENT section's
    "interactive_elements" list. All other "interactive_elements" stay [].

TIMING FORMULAS:
  minutes     = round(word_count / 180, 2)
  credit_hour = round(minutes / 50, 3)
  Totals      = sum of all section values (target ≈ 12,000 words)

═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
OUTPUT FORMAT — return ONLY valid JSON, no markdown fences
═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
{
  "course_title": "Course name",
  "course_id": "",
  "description": "2-4 sentences: who this course is for, what they will be able to do, why it matters",
  "learning_objectives": [
    "Explain ...",

  ],

    {

    }
  ],

  }
}

Section schema:

}

Subtopic schema (use when subtopic has its own timing data):
{
  "title": "2.1 Community",
  "content": "",
  "word_count": 72,
  "minutes": 0.4,
  "credit_hour": 0.008,
  "interactive_elements": []
}

SUBTOPICS — OBJECTS vs PLAIN STRINGS:
  - Subtopic with own word count / timing → emit as object (subtopic schema above).
  - Subtopic with no timing data → plain title string is acceptable.
  - NEVER include "Knowledge Check" in subtopics.

FIELD RULES:
- "course_title": derive from primary source document title
- "course_id": course ID from source if present, else ""
- "description": 2–4 sentence professional summary (audience, outcomes, importance)
- "learning_objectives": measurable action-verb statements (Bloom's Taxonomy verbs)
  tailored to the target audience and difficulty level
- "sections": ordered lesson list — only sections that pass the trainer's test
  - "title": EXACTLY as in source (page refs stripped)
  - "content": trainer-style objective — "Students will learn to [action] …"
  - "subtopics": objects (preferred) or plain strings; NEVER includes KC entries
  - "word_count": integer — proportional share of 12,000 total
  - "minutes": float — word_count / 180
  - "credit_hour": float — minutes / 50
  - "interactive_elements": [] unless KC found in source (then ["knowledge_check"])
  - "para_idx_start": integer index of first paragraph (from [P<N>] tags); null if absent
  - "para_idx_end": integer index of last paragraph (inclusive); null if absent
- "totals": sums across all sections (target total ≈ 12,000 words)

Return ONLY valid JSON.  No explanation.  No markdown fences.

[P10] Long-Term Care:  An In-Depth View, (#146)
[P15] 1.0 Introduction
[P16] Demographers, marketers, and others interested in the U.S. population and its characteristics routinely categorize the population along multiple dimensions, depending on the objective of the study being undertaken. Although there are many more segments or cohorts into which the U.S. population is often divided, the typical demographic variables include age, gender, race, religion, language, etc. It is on the first demographic variable noted, age, that we will spend some time because of its significant impact on the need for long-term care.
[P17] We will also look more closely at the aging of the U.S. population. When that subject is addressed, we will examine the causes of population aging—including the effects of migration, fertility and mortality—as well as its consequences. At the outset, however, we need to understand that:
[P18] The population segment growing at the fastest rate is the one referred to as the oldest old and generally comprised of those individuals age 85 and older;
[P19] The portion of the oldest old population segment that is growing at the fastest rate is made up of centenarians; and
[P20] Although the aging of the population marks a significant success for humanity in its quest to extend the duration of life, it poses enormous challenges socially, politically and economically as society addresses the needs of an older, frailer population.
[P21] It is with this understanding of the rapidly increasing age of the U.S. population that Long-term Care: An In-Depth View should be read.

[P35] 2.0 Learning Objectives
[P37] When you have completed this course you should be able to:
[P38] Identify the various types of long-term care and the settings in which it may be delivered;
[P39] Explain the risk of requiring long-term care services;
[P40] Describe the average costs involved in obtaining long-term care in nursing homes, assisted living facilities, and in the care recipient’s home;
[P41] Identify the principal long-term care cost payers;
[P42] Discuss the criteria that must be met before benefits are payable under Medicare and Medicaid for long-term care services;
[P43] Describe the basic provisions and optional benefits in long-term care insurance policies;
[P44] Explain the income tax treatment of tax-qualified long-term care policy premiums and benefits;
[P45] Discuss the general outline of the Long-term Care Partnership programs available in many states; and

[P47] 3.0 The Nature of Long-term Care
[P48] For the many accustomed to thinking of long-term care in terms of care provided in nursing homes in which old and frail residents are little more than warehoused as they wait to die, a definition of long-term care is needed. Unlike the foregoing image, long-term care is provided in multiple settings to individuals with a wide range of needs and objectives.
[P49] 3.1 Long-term Care Defined
[P50] Long-term care may be provided to the individual who needs minimal assistance in dressing or bathing, or it may involve caring for a patient that requires around-the-clock nursing care. Accordingly, long-term care is generally defined as that assistance required to meet an individual’s physical, mental, and/or emotional needs over an extended period of time, involving personal care and related services provided to people who:
[P51] Need help with activities of daily living (ADLs); or
[P52] Require supervision due to a severe cognitive impairment.
[P53] The assistance that constitutes long-term care may be provided in a home—the home of the individual needing long-term care or the home of the caregiver—or in an institutional setting, such as a nursing home, an alternate care facility, or one of the non-home community-based professional care facilities.
[P54] For a person to become eligible to receive long-term care or for insurance benefits to be payable for such long-term care services, an individual must usually meet one of the following two benefit triggers:
[P55] Be unable to perform two or more of those enumerated activities of daily living; or
[P56] Suffer from a cognitive impairment.
[P57] Review question:
[P58] True or False:  Long-term care is provided only to the individual who needs around-the clock nursing care.
[P59] True Your answer is incorrect. Long-term care is provided in multiple settings to individuals with a wide range of needs and objectives.
[P60] False Your answer is correct. Long-term care is provided in multiple settings to individuals with a wide range of needs and objectives.
[P61] 3.1.1 Activities of Daily Living
[P62] As already noted, the definition of long-term care is couched in terms of activities of daily living. Since the term may not be familiar to everyone, we need to identify the activities included. Although these activities of daily living are generally just what we might expect them to be—the activities people need to perform to get through the day successfully—they are specifically enumerated activities.
[P63] Six activities normally comprise the activities of daily living:
[P64] Eating, i.e. the process of putting food into the body:
[P65] from a cup, plate, or similar receptacle;
[P66] through a feeding tube; or
[P67] intravenously;
[P68] Dressing, i.e., putting on and taking off:
[P69] clothes; and/or
[P70] any prosthetic devices, braces, or fasteners;
[P71] Bathing, i.e., washing oneself:
[P72] using a sponge bath;
[P73] in a tub; or
[P74] in a shower;
[P75] Toileting, which means:
[P76] getting to and from the toilet;
[P77] getting on and off the toilet; and
[P78] performing associated personal hygiene;
[P79] Transferring from or to a:
[P80] chair;
[P81] bed; or
[P82] wheelchair; and
[P83] Continence, which means:
[P84] controlling bowel or bladder functions; or
[P85] adequately performing person hygiene, including taking care of a catheter or colostomy bag, when unable to control bowel or bladder functions.
[P86] Review question:

[P88] 1. eating  Your answer is incorrect. Eating is an ADL.
[P89] 2. dressing  Your answer is incorrect. Dressing is an ADL.
[P90] 3. bathing  Your answer is incorrect. Bathing is an ADL.
[P91] 4. driving  Your answer is correct. Driving is not an activity of daily living. Driving is not considered an activity people need to perform to get through the day successfully.
[P92] 3.1.2 Cognitive Impairment
[P93] The term cognitive impairment generally means a deficiency in one or more of the following:
[P94] The individual’s orientation as to person, place, or time. An individual with a deficiency in orientation ordinarily does not know:
[P95] where they are—stories of disoriented persons becoming lost in familiar surroundings,
[P96] the people around them even though normally familiar, or
[P97] the time of day or season of the year;
[P98] The individual’s short-term or long-term memory, so that they cannot remember:
[P99] shared experiences,
[P100] important dates—birthdays, anniversaries,
[P101] the places visited just yesterday, etc.;
[P102] The individual’s ability to engage in deductive or abstract reasoning. Someone who is unable to engage in deductive or abstract reasoning may not be able to balance a checkbook, total a column of numbers, or arrive at a conclusion using deductive logic; or
[P103] The individual’s ability to judge that a condition or circumstance presents a danger to self or others. For example, someone with such a judgment deficiency may attempt to walk across a busy highway without regard to oncoming traffic.
[P104] While it should be reasonably clear just what criteria must be met by an individual to be eligible to receive long-term care and/or long-term care insurance benefits, let’s consider those conditions that are more likely to result in the need for long-term care.
[P105] 3.2 Conditions Normally Requiring Long-term Care
[P106] Long-term care may be for a relatively short period—rehabilitation following surgery or injury, for example—or may be much more permanent. The temporary situations in which long-term care may be required include:
[P107] Rehabilitation to regain strength following a lengthy hospital stay, or
[P108] Recovery from an illness, injury or surgery during which the individual learns to:
[P109] walk with artificial limbs, or
[P110] speak following a severe brain injury.
[P111] In addition to these relatively temporary long-term care needs, many individuals require much more permanent types of long-term care. Often the conditions calling for permanent long-term care are:
[P112] Severe, chronic pain,
[P113] Senile dementia or Alzheimer’s Disease,
[P114] Multiple Sclerosis,
[P115] Parkinson’s Disease,
[P116] Heart Disease,
[P117] Stroke,
[P118] Head injury,
[P119] Need for supervision or assistance in performing ADLs, and
[P120] Chronic or terminal medical conditions.

[P129] 3.3 Types of Long-term Care
[P130] Long-term care is often categorized based on its objective and the level of nursing care required to deliver it. Accordingly, long-term care may be:
[P131] Skilled care;
[P132] Intermediate care; or
[P133] Custodial care.
[P134] Let’s consider each of these long-term care levels.
[P135] 3.3.1 Skilled Care
[P136] Skilled care is a type of long-term care that is provided under a doctor’s order by a licensed healthcare professional, such as a physical therapist or nurse. It is usually needed by individuals:
[P137] With conditions that are uncontrolled, unstable or chronic;
[P138] Recovering from a medical condition that requires hospitalization; or
[P139] Recovering from surgery.
[P140] Individuals requiring skilled care usually need a relatively high level of monitoring by nursing professionals. The goal of skilled care is rehabilitative; as such, it is provided with the objective of returning function to the individual.
[P141] 3.3.2 Intermediate Care
[P142] Intermediate care is similar to skilled care; the difference is that intermediate care is provided on an intermittent basis. Similar to skilled care, intermediate care stresses rehabilitation, its goal being to return function to the patient to enable them to return home.
[P143] Unlike skilled care, however, it is usually provided to patients in a stable condition who, nonetheless, require daily medical assistance on a basis that is less frequent than that provided in skilled care.
[P144] Intermediate care is provided pursuant to a physician’s order and usually carried out under the supervision of a registered nurse. Although intermediate care continues to be provided to patients that need it, as a term its use is declining. Long-term care is now generally described solely in terms of skilled care or custodial care.
[P145] A patient that needs their surgical dressing changed every six hours—but whose nursing care requirement is otherwise modest—would be a candidate for intermediate care.

[P148] I. daily  Your answer is incorrect. Intermediate care is not provided on a daily basis.
[P149] II. evening only  Your answer is incorrect. Intermediate care is not provided in the evening only.
[P150] III. intermittent  Your answer is correct. Intermediate care is provided on an intermittent basis.
[P151] 3.3.3 Custodial Care
[P152] Custodial care is the most common type of long-term care provided. It is care limited principally to helping individuals perform the activities of daily living. The assistance individuals require to perform ADLs may be needed because of some physical infirmity or condition or because of a cognitive impairment that mandates supervision to ensure the individual does not injure him- or herself or others. While custodial care is less intensive and does not require the high level of healthcare training required of those administering skilled or intermediate care, the individual providing custodial care must have some training in order to properly assist an individual in performing ADLs.
[P153] The goal of custodial care is different from the goal associated with skilled care. Unlike skilled and intermediate care, the objective of custodial care is not rehabilitative. Rather, it is simply designed to enable the individual to lead an independent or semi-independent life by providing assistance to them in the various activities that must be performed in order to function satisfactorily.
[P154] 3.4 Long-term Care Settings
[P155] As may already be apparent, long-term care is not a singular type of care; instead, it is a continuum of care that covers a wide range of services and providers. Because the types of care provided may vary considerably depending on the individual’s need, it is reasonable that the settings in which that care is delivered also vary.
[P156] The four settings in which long-term care is normally delivered are:
[P157] Nursing homes;
[P158] Alternate care facilities;
[P159] Community-based professional care facilities; and
[P160] Informally, at home.
[P161] Let’s consider each of these settings and the variations within them, beginning with nursing homes.
[P163] Review Questions:

[P165] True Your answer is incorrect. The objective of custodial care is not rehabilitative.
[P166] False Your answer is correct. The objective of custodial care is not rehabilitative. Rather, it enables the individual to lead an independent or semi-independent life by providing assistance in the various activities that must be performed in order to function satisfactorily.

[P172] 4. all of the above  Your answer is correct. All of these options are settings in which long-term care may be delivered.
[P173] 3.4.1 Nursing Home Defined
[P174] A nursing home is a facility providing long-term care services 24 hours each day performed by or under the supervision of a registered nurse, licensed practical nurse, or licensed vocational nurse. It may occupy its own separate building, or it may be a distinct part of another facility such as a wing of a hospital.
[P175] For purposes of receiving long-term care insurance benefits, none of the following is considered an eligible nursing home:
[P176] Hospitals;
[P177] Clinics;
[P178] Rest homes not providing custodial care as their primary function; or
[P179] Facilities for treating mental illness, drug addiction or alcoholism.
[P180] 3.4.1.1 Services Provided in Nursing Homes
[P181] A nursing home may provide:
[P182] Skilled care; or
[P183] Custodial care.
[P184] Accordingly, the services provided by a nursing home vary based on the nursing home’s identity as a skilled care facility or custodial care facility. The 2024 nationwide median cost of a nursing home stay was $9,277 per month for a private room and assisted living was $5,900 per month.
[P185] 3.4.1.2 Skilled Care
[P186] A nursing home that is a skilled care facility provides skilled nursing care or rehabilitation services to injured, sick or disabled residents. It also provides custodial services that are incident to the skilled nursing care that is its principal focus. Of course, a nursing home providing only custodial care is not a skilled care facility.
[P187] Nursing services that meet the criteria for skilled nursing care require that patient care be performed only by licensed nursing personnel or under their supervision. In addition, to be deemed skilled nursing care, the facility must:
[P188] Provide 24-hour nursing services, and
[P189] Employ a registered nurse during a day tour of duty of at least 8 hours a day, 7 days a week.
[P190] A physician is required to supervise any medical care provided to residents, and the facility must have a physician available to provide emergency medical care.

[P202] A private or semi-private room;
[P203] All meals;
[P204] Medication management;
[P205] ADL assistance;
[P206] Various social activities, such as bingo, bridge, dances, parties, etc.; and
[P207] Scheduled day trips and other recreational activities.

[P218] 3.4.2 Alternatives to Nursing Homes
[P219] As people generally realize—nursing homes are expensive. Furthermore, they may provide services that many people needing long-term care don’t need. So, it is not surprising that various alternatives to entering a nursing home have emerged.
[P220] Known as alternative care facilities, these nursing home alternatives offer residents various levels and types of long-term care services. An alternate care facility includes a range of facilities providing long-term care services in venues that are generally less costly than nursing homes.
[P221] An alternate care facility is a facility in which ongoing care and related services are provided to residents in a single location that meets the following criteria:
[P222] 24 hour-a-day care and services are provided sufficient to support residents’ needs resulting from cognitive impairment or inability to perform ADLs;
[P223] A trained employee who is ready to provide required care to the facility’s residents is on duty at all times;
[P224] 3 meals each day are provided and residents’ special dietary needs are accommodated;
[P225] The facility is licensed or accredited, as required, by a state agency to provide such care;
[P226] Formal arrangements for physician or nurse services to provide emergency medical care are maintained; and
[P227] Appropriate methods are used and procedures established for handling and administering drugs and biologicals.
[P228] Typical alternate care facilities meeting these criteria fall into three categories:
[P229] Assisted living facilities (ALFs);
[P230] Alzheimer’s facilities; and
[P231] Custodial care facilities.

[P240] 3.4.2.1 Assisted Living Facilities
[P241] We will see later that the majority of long-term care is delivered both formally and informally in the individual’s home. A nursing home may be an obvious—if not the only—alternative when home healthcare is impractical. A third important alternative to either the individual’s home or a nursing home is an assisted living facility (ALF), which can be seen as a bridge between these two choices.
[P242] ALF residents are unable to live independently because they:
[P243] Have dementia or similar disorder; and/or
[P244] Require assistance with -
[P245] Meal preparation;
[P246] ADLs; or
[P247] Household chores.
[P248] Unlike nursing homes, ALFs don’t offer skilled care or intensive medical care, although they usually provide some level of resident medical services. The care delivered in an ALF is generally based on a regularly-updated service plan in which the care required for each resident is detailed.
[P249] Although additional services may be purchased by a resident, ALFs normally provide the following services in their basic plan:
[P250] Management and monitoring of resident care;
[P251] Assistance with ADLs;
[P252] Basic housekeeping, including laundry services;
[P253] Medication management;
[P254] Recreational activities (bingo, bridge, dances, outings, etc.);
[P255] Resident security; and
[P256] Resident transportation to and from shopping, church services, etc.
[P257] For an additional charge, an ALF may also offer other services to residents, such as:
[P258] Extra transportation services;
[P259] Dementia care; and
[P260] In-home meal delivery.
[P261] Other names commonly given to assisted living facilities include:
[P262] Adult living facilities;
[P263] Board and care facilities;
[P264] Domiciliary care facilities;
[P265] Residential or personal care facilities;
[P266] Adult congregate living care facilities;
[P267] Supported care facilities;
[P268] Community-based retirement facilities;
[P269] Adult homes; and
[P270] Retirement residences.
[P271] According to the CDC,  there were 30,200 assisted living and similar residential care communities in the United States serving 835,200 residents.

[P274] I. transportation services  Your answer is partially correct.
[P275] II. dementia care  Your answer is partially correct.
[P276] III. in-home meal delivery  Your answer is partially correct.
[P277] IV. all of the above Your answer is correct. Transportation services, dementia care and in-home meal delivery may be provided by an ALF for an additional charge.
[P278] 3.4.2.2 Alzheimer’s Facilities Meet Alzheimer’s Patients’ Special Needs
[P279] Alzheimer’s patients and individuals with senile dementia often require care that is different and more intensive than the care required by other individuals needing long-term care. For that reason, certain alternate care facilities—usually called Alzheimer’s facilities or memory units—are devoted to the care of individuals with these diseases.
[P280] Alzheimer’s disease affects more than 5 million Americans over the age of 65 and the population with Alzheimer’s disease is expected to increase to 14 million by 2050. It is a disease that attacks the individual’s brain and normally is suspected when an individual becomes increasingly forgetful; the course of the disease is generally slow but continues to progress until the individual cannot care for himself or herself.
[P281] Symptoms exhibited by Alzheimer’s patients—depending on the stage of the disease—may include:
[P282] Memory loss concerning recent events, although the individual’s memory of events that occurred 40 or 50 years ago may be unimpaired;
[P283] Increasing difficulty in learning new tasks or performing previously-performed routine tasks;
[P284] Loss of the ability to engage in abstract thinking;
[P285] Inability to reason;
[P286] Lack of judgment;
[P287] Place and time disorientation;
[P288] Loss or impairment of language or communication skills; and
[P289] Personality and mood changes.
[P290] The course of the disease and the duration of any particular stage vary in each afflicted individual. However, it usually progresses from stage 1, during which patients suffer disorientation and short-term memory loss, to stage 3 characterized by their inability to function independently and loss of language skills. Individuals with senile dementia and Alzheimer’s disease normally function at a higher cognitive level when housed in facilities devoted to the care of individuals with Alzheimer’s disease than they do in other long-term care facilities, generally because of the staffs’ ability to specialize in the treatment of individuals with dementia.
[P291] Because Alzheimer’s patients’ special needs differ from the needs of other individuals requiring long-term care, it is appropriate that facilities devoted to Alzheimer’s disease care reflect those differing needs. The special needs of Alzheimer’s patients result from their:
[P293] Need to be in a familiar environment and feel safe;
[P294] Tendency to wander away from the facility and become lost or disoriented;
[P295] Engaging in socially unacceptable behavior or becoming delusional and argumentative;
[P296] Tendency to forget the time of day, the location of their room, or their destination;
[P297] Increasing difficulty understanding language.
[P298] Based on these needs, facilities devoted to working with Alzheimer’s patients attempt to provide an environment that enhances patients’ sense of well-being and minimizes their frustrations. For example, in order to provide an environment free of hazards to residents’ safety and enhance their familiarity with the facility:
[P299] Furniture in the facility is not usually moved from place to place;
[P300] Residents’ living spaces are clutter-free;
[P301] Individuals’ own furniture is often used in their rooms; and
[P302] The use of natural light is emphasized in the facility to help avoid depression, and the large windows that enhance the use of natural light also help residents to remain oriented to time of day and seasons of the year.
[P303] Similarly, to help Alzheimer’s patients avoid feeling lost and disoriented, many Alzheimer’s facilities provide:
[P304] Wandering paths that encourage residents to socialize, give them a sense of personal freedom, and provide a method by which they can use up their energy; and
[P305] Rounded hallways that encourage residents to move forward.
[P306] As a way of helping Alzheimer’s patients avoid behavior that is unacceptable or argumentative—a behavior that may result from their becoming delusional—Alzheimer’s facilities:
[P307] Maintain feelings of tranquility and calm while following an established routine on which patients can rely;
[P308] Consciously reduce the noise level in the facility to maintain a sense of serenity; and
[P309] Reduce patient stress by –
[P310] Breaking patient tasks into generally simple steps,
[P311] Allowing additional time to complete tasks, and
[P312] Limiting patient choices.
[P313] To deal with the loss of memory and increasing disorientation common in residents with Alzheimer’s disease, Alzheimer’s facilities generally:
[P314] Attempt to assist residents to maintain independence by providing memory aids that include –
[P315] Written lists of activities for each day, and
[P316] Labeling dresser drawers so that residents can clearly and easily determine their contents; and
[P317] Place clocks and calendars in high-traffic, visible areas so that residents can maintain their orientation as to the date and time;
[P318] To address Alzheimer’s patients’ increasing inability to communicate as the disease progresses, Alzheimer’s facilities normally:
[P319] Employ certain colors and/or shapes to identify particular locations, such as restrooms (Alzheimer’s patients generally respond better to visually-provided communication rather than spoken or written language.);
[P320] Use photos of residents and memory boxes that contain residents’ personal items to permit residents to identify their rooms more easily; and
[P321] Paint walls and floors contrasting colors to enable residents to more easily see where one ends and the other begins.

[P331] 3.4.2.3 Custodial Care Facilities
[P332] Not all custodial care occurs in nursing homes or in the individual’s home; much of it takes place in custodial care facilities. While custodial care facilities provide a more formal approach to patient care than is generally encountered in home healthcare, they don’t normally provide the medical services provided by nursing homes; instead, they look to practices outside the facility to provide needed medical services. Just as we found with other types of alternative care, custodial care facilities provide a “bridge” between these two locations in which long-term care may be provided.
[P333] Although custodial care facilities don’t offer on-site medical services, they normally provide a high level of resident supervision for individuals unable to live independently. They provide assistance with the activities of daily living and offer room, board, and personal attendance services.
[P334] 3.4.3 Community-Based Long-term Care Services
[P335] Few people would choose to be in a nursing home or alternate care facility if they had a choice. The majority of people would prefer to retain as much independence as possible—not normally an option in such institutional facilities. However, the option to retain independence is often provided through the use of community-based long-term care services. These services are designed to permit individuals to live independently for as long as their need for care allows. Community-based long-term care services are services designed to enable an individual to delay the need for institutionalization by providing needed services in the community or in the individual’s home.
[P336] These community-based long-term care services are support services available to persons requiring help in performing the activities of daily living and include:
[P337] Respiratory therapy;
[P338] Speech therapy;
[P339] Nutritional counseling;
[P340] Occupational therapy;
[P341] Home nursing care;
[P342] Physical therapy;
[P343] Custodial support services;
[P344] Homemaker, personal care and chore-assistance services;
[P345] Adult day programs providing therapeutic activities, meals and transportation;
[P346] Home modifications and personal care supplies;
[P347] Long-term care planning and case management services;
[P348] Vocational services, including job placement, vocational evaluation, job placement, and work adjustment programs;
[P349] Recreation and leisure activities; and
[P350] Respite care.
[P351] The principal types of community-based long-term care services provided are:
[P352] Home healthcare services;
[P353] Adult daycare services;
[P354] Homemaker services; and
[P355] Hospice care.

[P357] Custodial care facilities offer which of the following:
[P358] I. onsite medical services
[P359] II. high level of resident supervision
[P360] III. assistance with ADLs

[P365] 3.4.3.1 Paid Home Care Services
[P366] Home care services may be provided informally by friends or relatives or by individuals that are paid for providing them. Paid home healthcare services are frequently utilized by individuals with chronic or disabling conditions, or by patients recuperating from an illness that want to remain in their homes. Like most long-term care, home healthcare usually is:
[P367] Custodial care; or
[P368] Skilled care.
[P369] Custodial care provided by a paid healthcare worker in the care-recipient’s home is normally provided to persons:
[P370] Requiring assistance with ADLs; or
[P371] Dealing with some form of dementia
[P372] …and may include transportation, companionship or other tasks normally performed by companions or homemakers.
[P373] When skilled care is provided in a care-recipient’s home it is normal for patients recovering from a potentially catastrophic medical event, such as a heart attack or stroke. Such care is normally provided by nurses, therapists or specially-trained home health aides under the direction of a physician or nurse.
[P374] 3.4.3.2 Adult Daycare Services
[P375] Adult daycare services generally involve the care of frail or impaired individuals during the period the principal caregiver is required to attend to other matters. Accordingly, these services are often only available from Monday through Friday each week from 7:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m. Such a schedule would generally enable a caregiver employed outside the home to drop off the individual in need of adult care on the commute to a place of employment and pick them up at the end of the workday.
[P376] The adult daycare services provided may vary considerably from one adult daycare facility to another; however, such services may include daycare:
[P377] Providing supervised social interaction in a safe environment—sometimes referred to as the traditional adult daycare model—that may include crafts;
[P378] In which the social interaction of the traditional model is combined with medical care and therapy in the medical daycare care model; and
[P379] For individuals with Alzheimer’s disease or other forms of dementia, referred to as the Alzheimer’s adult daycare model.
[P380] In addition to the general services described above, adult daycare centers may also provide other personal services at additional cost, such as:
[P381] Transportation to and from the facility,
[P382] Baths,
[P383] Haircuts,
[P384] Hair shampoos and sets, and
[P385] Permanents.
[P386] It is not difficult to see that adult daycare facilities offer benefits to the individual receiving care as well as to the caregivers. Care-recipients benefit by having:
[P387] An opportunity to live with family without being an around-the-clock responsibility;
[P388] A chance to enjoy social interaction with peers;
[P389] Mentally stimulating activities in which to participate;
[P390] The opportunity to receive speech, occupational or physical therapy in a non-medical environment; and
[P391] Needed assistance with ADLs that enable the individual to retain their dignity.
[P392] For caregivers, the benefits of adult daycare facilities include:
[P393] The chance to continue to work at a job outside the home;
[P394] Some respite from the physical and emotional demands of providing ongoing adult care; and
[P395] The avoidance of guilt that may accompany the institutionalizing of a family member.
[P396] Review Question:
[P397] Adult daycare centers may provide which of the following personal services at additional cost?
[P398] I. transportation to and from the facility Your answer is partially correct.
[P399] II. baths  Your answer is partially correct.
[P400] III.  haircuts  Your answer is partially correct.
[P401] IV. all of the above  Your answer is correct. At an additional cost, adult daycare centers may provide personal services such as transportation, baths and haircuts.
[P402] 3.4.3.3 Respite Care
[P403] Respite care is designed to provide a caregiver some relief from the day-to-day responsibilities of providing care. It is short-term in nature and is provided by various facilities to offer a temporary respite to an uncompensated caregiver.
[P404] Although respite care may be provided in various settings and in numerous ways, it is usually offered in:
[P405] Nursing homes for a period of from one day to several weeks;
[P406] Adult daycare facilities usually for one or two days; and
[P407] The home in which care is generally given for any requested period.
[P408] 3.4.3.4 Hospice Care
[P409] Hospice includes many services, all of which are designed to provide health and comfort to individuals approaching death. To be eligible for hospice care an individual must:
[P410] Be terminally-ill, and
[P411] Have a life expectancy of no more than 6 to 12 months.
[P412] In some cases, the individuals eligible for hospice care are ineligible for further curative measures, such as additional surgery or further chemotherapy, or are people who have refused additional treatment even though eligible for it.
[P413] Hospice care is usually provided in the care-recipient’s home, although it may take place in virtually any setting. It is provided under the care of a hospice team comprised of:
[P414] Physicians,
[P415] Nurses,
[P416] Social workers,
[P417] Therapists,
[P418] Aides,
[P419] Pastors, and
[P420] Volunteers.
[P421] The objective of hospice care is not to cure the care-recipient; it is to enable the individual to continue their life with minimal disruption until death. Thus, hospice care focuses on palliative care designed to relieve physical and emotional pain and other uncomfortable symptoms. Hospice care is provided to the individual nearing death and their family.
[P422] The approach to the delivery of hospice care is interdisciplinary in that it delivers various types of care, such as:
[P423] Medical services,
[P424] Social services,
[P425] Psychological and emotional services, and
[P426] Spiritual services.
[P427] No “pre-packaged” hospice care is provided; rather, the services provided are based on an assessment of the individual’s needs and comfort level.
[P428] Even though hospice care is decidedly beneficial to both the dying individual and their family, hospice care services are not heavily utilized. While the number of people receiving hospice care has been growing during the past decade, it is estimated that only around 44% of Americans use hospice services at the end of their life. In part, the low level of hospice utilization may be due to the perception—entirely erroneous—that it is available only to cancer patients. While terminally-ill cancer patients comprise the largest group availing themselves of hospice care, a study by the National Hospice and Palliative Care Organization indicates patients with the following as the top users of hospice care: heart disease, unspecified debility, dementia, lung disease, stroke or coma.
[P431] Review Question:
[P432] The objective of hospice care is to:
[P433] I. find a cure for the care recipient.  Your answer is incorrect. The objective of hospice care is not to find a cure for the patient.
[P434] II. enable the individual to continue life with minimal disruption until death.  Your answer is correct. Hospice care enables the individual to continue life with minimal disruption until death.
[P435] 3.4.4 Informal Home Care
[P436] Informal home care is care provided to an individual at home by a generally uncompensated caregiver. It is usually provided by a relative, friend or neighbor of the care-recipient who, according to statistics provided by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, are the sole caregivers for the elderly in about 70% of cases.
[P437] No professional training is normally required to provide informal home care. This type of care usually includes:
[P438] Providing companionship;
[P439] Assisting with errands and/or shopping;
[P440] Assisting with the individual’s medications;
[P441] Communicating with medical providers
[P442] Preparing meals;
[P443] Providing transportation; and
[P444] Managing finances, e.g., paying monthly bills, etc.
[P446] 3.5 Family Changes Affecting Long-term Care
[P447] We noted earlier that the fastest growing demographic segment in America is known as the “oldest old,” comprised of individuals age 85 and older. Clearly, Americans’ life expectancy has increased significantly, and that is expected to have a big impact on long-term care needs. It isn’t only increased life expectancy, however, that will impact long-term care and the methods by which it is delivered and financed; the changing face of the American family is likely to have at least as large an influence.
[P448] At the dawn of the 20th century, America was still largely an agrarian society despite the Industrial Revolution that had begun some years earlier. As is common in such societies families tended to be large, and family members typically lived very close to the family farm—often dying in the same house in which they were born. Families cared for their old, sick and dying members themselves, generally avoiding hospitals, nursing homes and other institutions. However, as industrialization continued and America entered World War I, many children who might have stayed on the family farm joined the Armed Forces or moved to nearby cities seeking employment in the factories spawned by the Industrial Revolution.
[P449] The movement of adult children away from family farms and towards more urban environments had implications in many areas. One of those areas is how the old, sick and dying are cared for. With increasing numbers of city dwellers, coupled with the other changes brought about by 20th century industrialization and the World Wars—many aspects of the family dynamic changed:
[P450] The size of families changed from quite large—often a requirement to effectively managing a farm—to much smaller, generally more befitting urban living;
[P451] Families became more mobile; and
[P452] Women began to play a major role in the workforce.

[P458] 3.5.1 Reduction in Family Size
[P459] One of the important ancillary benefits of large families is that some family member is usually available to care for other family members if they need it. As family size declined for many urban families those available family members eventually disappeared. So, instead of being able to care for their old or sick relatives, families began to seek help elsewhere—in hospitals, nursing homes, sanitariums, and other institutions.
[P460] 3.5.2 Increased Mobility a Hallmark of 20th Century Society
[P461] The Industrial Revolution that lured many people away from family farms to work in the factories of the cities created another important vehicle of change that tended to further disperse family members: the automobile. Unlike travel by horse and wagon that might involve a trip of ten or twenty miles in a day, automobiles meant that people could travel a hundred or more miles a day in relative comfort.
[P462] At the same time families gained mobility through the family car, many corporations increased in size and expanded their operations across the country. For many employees such corporate expansion meant that professional advancement often required relocation across the country, further distancing family members from each other. With that increasing geographical distance, the likelihood that a family member in need of care could count on family further decreased.
[P463] 3.5.3 World War II and the Rise of Two-Income Families
[P464] Some may remember the emergence of “Rosie the Riveter,” the name generally given to the women who staffed the many U.S. factories gearing up for war production at the start of World War II. When the soldiers, sailors and marines returned at the end of the war four years later, they found that women had earned an important place in American industry—a place that some women were loath to give up.   Although many women left the factories and offices and returned to roles as homemakers when the war ended, many others continued to pursue careers outside their home. However, whether or not they left their jobs at the conclusion of the war, women showed they could perform those jobs just as well as their male counterparts—a lesson that was not lost on women or employers.
[P465] In the majority of U.S. families consisting of a husband and a wife in the 21st century, both spouses are employed outside the home. Approximately 63% of these U.S. families are dual-income families where both parents work full-time or one parent works full-time and the other part-time. While some of the workers in dual-income families may be employed for non-economic reasons, it is reasonable to believe that many employed spouses work to help meet the basic expenses of maintaining their lifestyle. To the extent that both spouses are employed in the economy, little time or energy is likely to remain for caring for old or sick relatives.
[P466] All these factors—smaller families, continued geographical dispersion, and the increasing role of married women in the workplace—have coalesced to reduce the likelihood that long-term care needs can reasonably be met by extended family.

[P468] Which of the following factors have reduced the likelihood that extended family alone can meet long-term care needs?
[P469] I. smaller family size  Your answer is partially correct.
[P470] II. geographical dispersion  Your answer is partially correct.
[P471] III. women working outside the home  Your answer is partially correct.
[P472] IV. all of the above  Your answer is correct. All of these factors increase the likelihood that families will have to look outside the family when requiring long-term care for a loved one.
[P474] 3.6 The Risk of Requiring Long-term Care
[P475] It is impossible to determine the risk that any particular individual will require long-term care in their lifetime. Clearly, that risk depends on many factors, several of the most important being:
[P476] Age and longevity: The risk of needing long-term care increases with advancing age, and Americans are living almost twice as long as they did a century ago;
[P477] Marital status: A single person’s risk of needing long-term care is generally higher since no informal caregiver may be available to forestall the need for formal long-term care services;
[P478] Gender: Women are more likely to need long-term care than men because they tend to outlive men and are often left without a potential informal caregiver;
[P479] Lifestyle: Unhealthful habits—smoking, lack of exercise and overeating, for example—and chronic stress may substantially increase the risk of anyone needing long-term care;
[P480] Health history: The presence of chronic conditions, such as COPD, Parkinson’s disease, diabetes, and arthritis, increase the risk of requiring long-term care; and
[P481] Family history: A family history that includes severe mental or physical illness may predispose an individual to conditions that require long-term care.
[P482] Having noted that predicting the likelihood any individual will require long-term care is inherently error-prone, we can still estimate the risk of needing long-term care in the general population.
[P483] According to some estimates almost one-half of all Americans—about 1 in 2—will require long-term care at some time in their life. Considering the risk of other life events, the risk of needing long-term care is astronomical. Note the following comparison of the risk of certain life events:
[P484] Although increasing age carries with it a greater likelihood of requiring long-term care—12% of individuals age 65 to 74 require help with ADLs, but 70% of individuals age 85 and over need such help—age is not the only risk factor. While 63% of persons needing long-term care are age 65 or older, 37% are younger than age 65.
[P485] Of course, not everyone who requires long-term care enters a nursing home; in fact, most people receiving long-term care never enter a nursing home. However, it is instructive to consider how long nursing home residents stay there. The average nursing home stay is about 2 ½ years.

[P519] 4.0 Long-term Care Planning
[P520] No one wants to think about a time when they might need long-term care. So planning ahead for this possibility often gets put off. Most people first learn about long-term care when they or a loved one need care. Then their options are often limited by lack of information, the immediate need for services, and insufficient resources to pay for preferred services. Planning ahead allows an individual to have more control over an individual’s future.
[P521] 4.1	People Need to Plan for Long-term Care
[P522] Planning ahead for long-term care is important because there is a good chance an individual will need some long-term care services if they live beyond the age of 65. About 70 percent of people over age 65 require some services, and the likelihood of needing care increases as an individual ages.
[P523] Planning ahead helps an individual understand what service options are available in their community, what special conditions may apply for receiving services, for example, age or other eligibility criteria, what services cost, and what payment options – public and private – apply. Having this information helps ensure an individual will have a range of options when they need long-term care, and makes it more likely that they will have more choice and control over where and how they receive services.
[P524] Planning ahead is important because the cost of long-term care services often exceeds what the average person can pay from income and other resources. By planning ahead, an individual may be able to save assets and income for uses other than long-term care, including preserving the quality of life for a spouse or other loved ones. With planning, there is a greater likelihood of being able to leave an estate to heirs, because individuals are less likely to use up their financial resources paying for care.
[P525] Planning ahead also means less emotional and financial stress on an individual, as well as their family. It can provide a way to involve family in decisions without depending on them to bear the entire burden alone.
[P526] Finally, for many people, one of the most important advantages of planning ahead is to ensure greater independence should they need care. The choices for receiving care outside of a facility and being able to stay at home or receive services in the community for as long as possible are greater if an individual has planned ahead.
[P527] Planning for long-term care is a difficult task. It involves understanding and making decisions about services and options that are unfamiliar to many of us. These include services and supports, housing and financing options, and legal issues.
[P528] 4.1.2	Components of Planning for Long-term Care
[P529] According to the National Clearinghouse for Long-term Care at longtermcare.gov, the steps to Planning to Long-term Care are:
[P530] Personal Planning
[P531] Financial Planning
[P532] Housing Considerations
[P534] What follows is the guidance they provide on each of these planning steps.
[P535] A.	Personal Planning Steps
[P536] Assess Your Risk of Needing Long-Term Care Services:  While you can never know for certain if you will need long-term care, assessing your risk factors can help you understand if you are at a higher or lower risk. Begin by talking with your doctor about whether you might be at increased risk based on your medical and family history or lifestyle choices. You will gain a better understanding of your risks, and your doctor may be able to help you decrease your risk.
[P537] Think about Where You Want to Receive Care:  If you were to need care for an extended period, where would you want to receive it? One way to find out what services are in your community is by contacting the Administration on Aging's Eldercare Locator at www.eldercare.gov.
[P538] Talk with Your Family: Do you have family (spouse, adult children, siblings) or friends who would want to or be able to care for you if you became ill or disabled for a long time? How do you think you would feel about relying on their help?
[P539] B.	Financial Planning Steps
[P540] Review Your Current Insurance Coverage:  Do you know if your current healthcare insurance would pay if you needed to be in a nursing home or needed care at home for an extended illness? Unless you have purchased a specific long-term care insurance policy, your existing medical coverage, Medicare, Medicare supplement, or HMO will provide little if any coverage for long-term care. Review the policies you have with your insurance advisor or benefits counselor to learn what is covered and what is not.
[P541] Decide if You Can or Want to Pay for Long-Term Care Privately:  If you don't have coverage for long-term care or prefer to pay out of your own resources, do you know if you would be able to cover all the costs from your retirement income and savings? Think about the financial resources you have and how you feel about using them to pay for long-term care. This could include various sources of income (for example, Social Security, pension, interest income, dividends from investments, payments from an IRA or 401 (k)), as well as cash, savings, stocks and bonds, and your home.
[P542] Investigate Future Insurance or Benefits You Expect or May Qualify for in Retirement:  It is important to know and understand what your future benefits will cover, if you are not yet retired. If you only have Medicare, even with a Medicare supplemental plan, most of your long-term care services may not be covered. If you have limited resources, now or in the future, Medicaid may pay for your services.
[P543] Find Out What Other Resources Can Help Cover Long-Term Care Expenses:  Most people currently don't have coverage or do not have enough private funds to pay for all their long-term care needs, particularly if service needs are extensive or last a long time. There are an increasing number of private payment options available for this purpose. Two of the more common options are long-term care insurance and reverse mortgages. Review private financing options carefully to ensure that you understand all the details, eligibility requirements, and costs.
[P544] C.	Housing Considerations and Planning Steps
[P545] Home Modifications Might Help You Stay in Your Home Longer:  Most people prefer to remain in their own homes and consider alternatives only if their care needs cannot be met at home. Modifying your home is an important option that can improve your safety and help you perform daily activities such as bathing and cooking. Home modifications range from grab bars in the bathroom and improved lighting to handrails and wider doorways for wheel chair access, or even adding a bathroom on the first floor of a two-story home for someone no longer able to climb stairs. 

Some state and local governments have programs to provide loans and grants to help you pay for home modifications.
[P546] Consider Moving to a More Suitable Environment:  Perhaps moving to a new home will best help you meet your future needs. Consider the variety of options such as moving to a house, condominium, or apartment that is all on one level, or that has elevators instead of stairs. Perhaps you would prefer a small, easy-to-care-for apartment with basic modifications already in place.
[P547] 4.1.3	The Role of Long-term Care Agents in Planning for Long-term Care
[P548] The role of the insurance agents is to ensure that consumers understand their options as well as the terms and conditions of any given policy. Foremost, insurance agents must guarantee that consumers understand the criteria that will allow them to become eligible for both private LTC coverage and, if necessary, Medicaid.  The NAIC requires delivery of a Shopper’s Guide to consumers for this purpose.
[P550] 4.1.3.1	Understanding your Client
[P551] Consumers generally do not understand one agent designation over another, or to know whether a designation indicates expertise on the part of the agent. While insurance companies provide extensive information about their products to agents, it is often related to marketing and sales rather than detailed information about how a policy works.
[P552] The advice agents give consumers can have long-lasting effects. For instance, agents sometimes don’t offer inflation protection or don’t recommend its purchase because of the added premium cost. Yet this protection is critical for consumers who aren’t expected to use their benefits for years to come. Adding inflation protection does add cost to the premium, but affordability needs to be balanced across all the elements of a Long-Term Care Insurance (LTCI) policy. Consumers must understand at the point of sale, for instance, that lack of inflation protection will gradually reduce the value of their benefit and will result in steadily increasing out-of-pocket costs for them at the point that they begin to use benefits.
[P553] An agent may encourage the purchase of a policy that is at the limit of a consumer’s affordability without taking into account future life changes such as the death of one spouse, which can reduce the income of the living spouse and result in an unaffordable premium. Consumers might spend thousands of dollars of limited income to pay for an LTCI policy that they could lose shortly before they need to claim those benefits. From the perspective of public policy, a worst-case scenario may be when a consumer receives a tax benefit for purchasing an LTCI policy, lapses that policy, and then turns to public benefits for help with the cost of long-term care. In those cases, taxpayers have paid twice: once for the tax subsidy and again for the care.
[P554] Some agents represent a single company and are limited to selling that company’s products. Those agents may have a quota to meet or be expected to sell one of the company’s products over another. Other agents represent several companies and can sell many different products. However, commissions may be a factor in the product the agent will encourage a consumer to buy, particularly when the company is paying large commissions or bonuses to gain market share. For example, one company was paying a commission of 130 percent of the first-year premium during a time when other companies were paying 60 to 75 percent. In other cases, an agent might submit an application to a company that specializes in accepting substandard business (accepting health conditions, for example, that other companies won’t cover), exposing purchasers to almost certain premium increases later if premiums are not high enough to cover the additional risk.
[P555] The NAIC adopted a provision intended to improve agent training. It requires companies selling LTCI to use only agents who have completed eight hours of training specific to LTCI. A qualifying course may not include training related to marketing or a specific company’s products. Like other NAIC provisions, however, it applies only in states that voluntarily adopt this measure.
[P557] 4.1.4	Common Barriers to Planning
[P558] There are many reasons why people don't plan ahead for long-term care. These include the natural tendency to avoid thinking about becoming dependent on others for your care, misinformation about the risks of needing care, and lack of knowledge about the cost of care and payment options.
[P559] Most people don't like to think about getting older, developing a disability, becoming less independent, or needing help with personal care. Many people don't realize that their chance of needing long-term care by the time they turn 65 is as high as 70 percent.
[P560] People commonly misunderstand how expensive long-term care is, and how it is paid for. Consumer surveys have shown that many individuals don't realize that health insurance, Medicare, and/or disability coverage do not pay for most long-term care services. Medicaid pays for some long-term care services, but only if you qualify for the program because you have limited income and financial resources.
[P561] Some people find it too difficult to raise these subjects with their loved ones, making it difficult to explore and define their plans. Adult children often feel like they are patronizing their parents if they raise the subject or they are afraid of giving the impression that they might not want to provide care if it is needed. Parents often don't want to make adult children uncomfortable or to discuss details of their finances with them.
[P562] Finally, some people realize it is important to plan, but don't know how to go about it. The best way to begin is with small and easy steps. Even just talking with your loved ones is a great first-step!
