[P587] 5.0 Long-term Care Costs and Payers
[P588] As discussed in the preceding chapter long-term care may involve little more than supervision of an individual—common under some adult daycare models—or it may require the intensive hands-on nursing provided in skilled care facilities. In light of those substantial differences, it should not be surprising that the costs of long-term care vary widely based on several factors, including the:
[P589] Venue in which the long-term care is delivered;
[P590] Type of care provided; and
[P591] Region of the country.
[P592] Because of these variations, we will look at the range of costs for long-term care provided:
[P593] In nursing homes;
[P594] In assisted living facilities; and
[P595] At home.
[P596] Let’s begin with an examination of the 2024 U.S. nursing home costs.
[P597] 5.1 Nursing Home Costs
[P598] We noted earlier that many people see “long-term care” as synonymous with “nursing home.” Although that view is clearly inaccurate and too restrictive, nursing homes, nonetheless, provide long-term care for many people. Nursing homes generally involve the highest level of long-term care as well as the greatest expense.
[P599] Review Question:
[P600] The cost of long-term care can vary based on which of the following factors?
[P601] I. venue in which the LTC is delivered  Your answer is only partially correct.
[P602] II. region of the country  Your answer is only partially correct.
[P603] III. age of the recipient  Your answer is incorrect. The age of the recipient is not a factor in the cost of LTC.
[P604] IV. both I & II Your answer is correct. Both the venue in which the LTC is delivered and the region of the country are factors in the cost of LTC.
[P606] 5.1.1 Private Room Costs
[P607] The median cost in the U.S. for long-term care received in a nursing home in 2024 was $350 per day, or $127,750 annually, when the resident was housed in a private room.
[P608] To get some sense of the inflation rate applicable to private-room nursing home care, that country-wide average rate represents a 9% increase over the previous year.
[P609] Very significant regional cost differences were found as well. The highest state-wide average private-room nursing home care cost in 2024 was found to be in Alaska where the average daily room rate was $999 or $364,453 annually. The lowest rates were recorded in Texas ($233 per day or $85,045 annually).
[P610] 5.1.2 Semi-Private Room Costs
[P611] In 2024, the national median daily rate in a nursing home for a semi-private room was $305, or $111,325 annually. The percentage cost increases over the prior year affecting the national median semi-private nursing home room rate in the U.S. was 7%.
[P612] Similar regional variations were found with respect to median semi-private room rates, and the highest and lowest rates were found in Alaska and Texas, respectively. In 2024, Alaska’s median semi-private nursing home rate was $999 per day—$364,453 annually.  Texas’s median semi-private nursing home rate was $233 per day—$85,045  annually.
[P613] It may be reasonable to expect some variation in the quality of care provided and/or the attractiveness of nursing homes included in the survey from which average nursing home rates were taken since these factors were not considered. The criteria for nursing homes included in the survey were that the nursing home must:
[P614] Be licensed;
[P615] Provide skilled and custodial care; and
[P616] Offer a private pay rate for long-term custodial care, not the Medicare or Medicaid reimbursement rate.
[P617] 5.2 Assisted Living Facilities Provide Care at Lower Cost than Nursing Homes
[P618] While nursing homes deliver long-term care at various levels, including skilled care, many people needing long-term care can be adequately cared for at facilities that are considerably less expensive. For individuals who require assistance in day-to-day living but who don’t need the higher level of skilled nursing care found in nursing homes, an assisted living facility may be entirely appropriate.
[P619] As we noted earlier, assisted living facilities provide a bridge between care provided in the recipient’s or caregiver’s home and nursing home care. While not offering skilled care or intensive medical care, they normally make some level of resident medical services available and deliver long-term care based on a detailed and updated service plan for each resident.
[P620] 5.2.1 Assisted Living Facility Costs
[P621] Over 835,000 Americans received long-term care in approximately 30,000 assisted living facilities in the United States. The average number of beds in these facilities is 28. Around 53 percent of residents are age 85 and older, while 40 percent of residents are between ages 65 and 84.
[P622] The 2024 national median cost for a private room and private bath in an assisted living facility was $5,900 per month, or $70,800 annually. As we saw in the case of nursing home costs, the variation in assisted living facility costs is significant, ranging from a low of $4,350 per month in South Dakota to $11,311 per month in Hawaii.
[P623] The 2024 national median for assisted living facility costs at $5,900 monthly represents an increase of 10% over the previous year.
[P624] Just as quality of care and amenities offered in nursing homes are likely to vary—presumably reflecting the variation in costs—they are likely to vary as well in the case of assisted living facilities. However, every surveyed ALF met the following criteria:
[P625] It was licensed according to its state’s licensure standards;
[P626] It provided personal care assistance; and
[P627] It had a private pay rate.
[P628] In addition to the monthly rate, some ALFs charge residents a one-time lump-sum entrance fee. Depending on arrangements, some or all of such entrance fee may be refunded when the resident permanently leaves the facility. In addition to these fees, some ALFs may also charge fees for delivering meals to a resident’s quarters and for other services.
[P629] Review Question:
[P630] Over _____ Americans receive long-term care in approximately _________ assisted living facilities in the United States.
[P631] I. 1,000,000; 50,000  Your answer is incorrect. Over one million Americans do not receive long-term care in approximately 50,000 assisted living facilities in the United States.
[P632] II. 500,000; 80,000  Your answer is incorrect. Over 500,000 Americans do not receive long-term care in approximately 80,000 assisted living facilities in the United States.
[P634] III. 835,000; 30,000  Your answer is correct. Over 835,000 Americans receive long-term care services in approximately 30,000 assisted living facilities in the United States.
[P635] 5.2.2 Assisted Living Facility Dementia Care Costs
[P636] Many assisted living facilities also provide dementia care to residents. Approximately half of those ALFs charge additional fees for providing such care. The median additional fees for dementia care provided in ALFs in 2024 are $1,260 per month. But this figure is quite variable.
[P637] 5.3 Home Care may involve Skilled or Custodial Care
[P638] Although we might intuitively expect that long-term care received at home would be of a less medically-skilled nature, such is not always true. In fact, paid home care may involve:
[P639] End-of-life care;
[P640] Skilled care; or
[P641] Custodial care.
[P642] Some recipients of home care may have been diagnosed with a terminal illness and simply wish to live out the remainder of their life as comfortably as possible and in the environment most familiar to them. While such end-of-life care may not rise to the level of hospice, it is palliative in nature and has characteristics of skilled and custodial care.
[P643] When skilled care is delivered in the care-recipient’s home, it is normally required as a means to rehabilitate the individual after a period of hospitalization following a heart attack, stroke, or major surgery. In such cases, skilled care is usually provided by nurses, therapists or home health aides working under a physician’s or nurse’s direction.
[P644] Custodial care received at home is often most appropriate for individuals who are physically healthy but require assistance and supervision because they have Alzheimer’s disease or some other form of dementia. Such care delivered in the individual’s home permits them to age in place surrounded by furniture and other objects that are most familiar. Typically, this custodial care includes:
[P645] Companionship;
[P646] Transportation; and
[P647] Assistance with the activities of daily living.
[P648] Review Question:
[P649] Paid home care may involve:
[P650] I. end of life care  Your answer is only partially correct.
[P651] II. skilled care  Your answer is only partially correct.
[P652] III. custodial care  Your answer is only partially correct.
[P653] IV.  all of the above  Your answer is correct. Paid home care may involve end of life care, skilled care and custodial care.
[P654] 5.3.1 Home Care Costs Vary Based on Services Provided and Region
[P655] The survey found that home care costs varied substantially depending on the services provided—whether the care required home health aide services or homemaker/companion services—and the region in which they were delivered. The national median hourly rate for home care in 2024 was:
[P656] $34 per hour for a home health aide (non-Medicare certified); and
[P657] $33 per hour for a homemaker/companion.
[P658] Inflation affected home care services as well as other long-term care services and resulted in a 10% increase in the hourly cost for a homemaker/companion and a 3% increase in the hourly cost of a home health aide over the prior year.
[P659] 5.4 Long-term Care Cost Payers
[P660] It doesn’t require too much calculation to arrive at the realization that paying for any extended period of long-term care can have a devastating economic effect on the individual requiring the care and their family. Often, long-term care results in impoverishment as assets are exhausted.
[P661] Several long-term care funding sources may be available, including:
[P662] Medicare;
[P663] Medicaid;
[P664] Personal assets; and
[P665] Insurance.
[P666] Let’s examine each of these sources of payment for long-term care services.
[P667] 5.4.1 Medicare as a Long-term Care Cost Payer
[P668] There is a perception shared by many people that Medicare pays for most long-term care services, particularly when they are required by individuals age 65 or older. With certain exceptions, that perception couldn’t be further from the truth. Based on statistics from the Center for Medicare and Medicaid Services, Medicare’s contribution to the national long-term care bill was as follows, based on the type of care provided:
[P669] Hospice care – 87%;
[P670] Home healthcare – 85%;
[P671] Short-term institution (skilled nursing home care following a 3-day hospital stay) – 83%; and
[P672] Nursing home care (custodial care) – 0%
[P673] Medicare is a federal program designed to provide health insurance to certain individuals, including persons:
[P674] Age 65 or older;
[P675] Of any age suffering from permanent kidney failure; and
[P676] With certain disabilities.
[P677] Although Medicare has changed over the years since its creation in the 1960s to add prescription drug coverage (Medicare Part D) and to enable individuals to receive managed healthcare (Medicare Part C), the long-term care coverage for which certain individuals may be eligible is generally provided under traditional Medicare. Traditional Medicare consists of Medicare Part A and Medicare Part B that provide coverage as follows:
[P678] Medicare Part A provides hospital insurance; and
[P679] Medicare Part B provides insurance for certain other medical expenses.
[P680] Medicare provides limited coverage for certain types of long-term care meeting specific criteria. The types of long-term care coverage that may be covered include:
[P681] Care in a skilled nursing facility, provided certain conditions are met;
[P682] Certain home healthcare services; and
[P683] Hospice care.
[P686] Review Question:
[P687] True or False:  Medicare will pay 100% of nursing home care.
[P688] True Your answer is incorrect.
[P689] False Your answer is correct. Medicare will pay 100% of hospice care, but only pays for nursing home care if it is for the short term, following a three-day hospital stay.
[P690] 5.4.1.1 Medicare Covers Certain Long-term Care Services
[P691] The principal coverage offered by Medicare for long-term care services is provided by Medicare Part A. Medicare Part A provides coverage for:
[P692] Limited skilled nursing facility care;
[P693] Limited post-hospital home healthcare; and
[P694] Hospice care.
[P695] In addition, Medicare Part B provides benefits for certain home health services that are not directly related to hospital or skilled nursing facility stays.
[P696] Skilled nursing facility care: A Medicare beneficiary may qualify for skilled nursing facility benefits if all of the following conditions are met:
[P697] The individual’s condition requires daily skilled nursing or skilled rehabilitative services that can only be provided in a skilled nursing facility;
[P698] The individual has been in a hospital at least 3 consecutive days (not counting the day of discharge) before being admitted to the skilled nursing facility (but see exception in next paragraph);
[P699] The individual is admitted to the skilled nursing facility within a short time—usually within 30 days—following hospital discharge;
[P700] The individual’s skilled nursing facility care is for a condition that –
[P701] Was treated in the hospital, or
[P702] Arose while receiving care in the skilled nursing facility for a condition that was treated in the hospital; and
[P703] A medical professional certifies that the individual needs and receives skilled nursing or skilled rehabilitation services on a daily basis.
[P704] An exception to the 3-day prior hospitalization rule applies if there is no increase in cost to the program resulting from such exception and the acute nature of the benefit is not altered.
[P705] If a Medicare beneficiary meets the required criteria enumerated above, Medicare will provide benefits for skilled nursing facility care that includes:
[P706] Semi-private room (2 to 4 beds in a room) and board;
[P707] Skilled nursing and rehabilitative services; and
[P708] Other specified services and supplies.
[P709] The benefits provided for such long-term care during each spell of illness are as follows:
[P710] 100% of Medicare-approved charges for the first 20 days of covered services; and
[P711] 100% of Medicare-approved charges in excess of a daily coinsurance amount for the next 80 days of covered services.
[P712] No skilled nursing care facility costs incurred beyond 100 days during a spell of illness are covered by Medicare.
[P713] Post-hospital home healthcare: Medicare Part A pays benefits for a Medicare beneficiary’s required post-institutional skilled healthcare provided in the home for the treatment of an illness or injury. The benefits provided for such care are:
[P714] 100% of the Medicare-approved cost for 100 home health visits made on an intermittent basis by a participating home health agency during a home health spell of illness provided –
[P715] The care is post-institutional home health services;
[P716] The care includes intermittent skilled nursing care, physical therapy, or speech therapy;
[P717] The person is confined at home;
[P718] The person is under the care of a physician who determines the need for home healthcare and establishes a home health plan for the person;
[P719] The home health agency providing the services participates in Medicare; and
[P720] The services are provided on a visiting basis in the person’s home, or if it is necessary to use equipment that cannot be readily made available in the home, on an outpatient basis in a hospital, skilled nursing facility, or licensed rehabilitation center; and
[P721] 80% of the Medicare-approved cost for durable medical equipment, including-
[P722] Iron lungs;
[P723] Oxygen tents;
[P724] Hospital beds; and
[P725] Wheelchairs.
[P726] Medicare Part B also covers certain home health services that are not directly related to hospital or skilled nursing facility stays. Typically, these Part B-approved home health services are for chronic conditions and are different from the home healthcare services required for convalescent and rehabilitative care following a hospital stay that are covered under Part A. The costs covered under Medicare Part B home health services are:
[P727] 100% of the costs of part-time skilled care; and
[P728] 80% of the cost of durable medical equipment.
[P729] The home healthcare coverage provided under the Medicare Part B is unlimited in duration, but limited to part-time skilled care.
[P730] Hospice care: We noted earlier that hospice care is long-term care whose focus is on relieving the care recipient’s pain rather than attempting to cure the condition. It is an approach to treatment that recognizes the individual’s impending death. Hospice care is covered completely by Medicare and permits a hospice to provide appropriate custodial care including homemaker services and counseling.
[P731] For an individual to be covered by Medicare hospice benefits, they must:
[P732] Be eligible for hospital insurance benefits under Medicare Part A;
[P733] Be certified by a physician as terminally ill, with a life expectancy of 6 months or less; and
[P734] Waive all other Medicare coverage for hospice care other than the hospice care chosen.
[P735] When a terminally-ill Medicare beneficiary meets the eligibility criteria noted above, they may receive the following covered hospice services:
[P736] Nursing care;
[P737] Medical social services provided by a social worker;
[P738] Counseling with respect to the individual’s care and adjustment to approaching death;
[P739] Short-term inpatient care;
[P740] Medical appliances and supplies;
[P741] Home health aide and homemaker services;
[P742] Drugs for pain relief and symptom management; and
[P743] Various therapies—physical, occupational and speech—to control symptoms or permit the individual to maintain ADLs and basic function skills.
[P744] The hospice benefit period consists of two 90-day periods followed by an unlimited number of 60-day periods. At the beginning of each 60-day period, the care-recipient must be re-certified as terminally ill.

[P749] III. three months  Your answer is incorrect. For a person to be covered by Medicare  hospice benefits, they must be certified by a physician as terminally ill with a life expectancy of six months or less.
[P750] 5.4.2 Medicaid as a Long-term Care Cost Payer
[P751] Medicaid is a means-tested entitlement program for low-income individuals jointly financed by federal and state governments and administered by the states. It covers long-term care services for both elderly and non-elderly care-recipients in:
[P752] Institutional settings, such as nursing homes and intermediate care facilities;
[P753] Assisted living facilities;
[P754] Community-based settings, such as adult daycare facilities; and
[P755] Homes.
[P756] Spending on long-term care in the U.S. in 2021 topped $465 billion. Medicaid is the primary payer for long-term services and supports (LTSS), at $207 billion, 44% of the total LTSS spending. It is the primary long-term care funding source to pay for long-term care as care-recipients exhaust their existing assets. Its benefits vary from state to state due to each state’s defining the applicable Medicaid eligibility criteria and benefits. In spite of that variability, Medicaid pays the bulk of the overall U.S. long-term care costs. It is estimated that approximately 60% of nursing home residents rely on Medicaid to pay their long-term care costs.
[P757] Review Question:
[P758] ______ is the primary long-term care funding source to pay for long-term care as care-recipients exhaust their personal assets.
[P759] I. Medicare  Your answer is incorrect. Medicare is not the primary long-term care funding source to pay for long-term care as care recipients exhaust their personal assets.
[P760] II. Medicaid   Your answer is correct. Medicaid is the primary long-term care funding source to pay for long-term care as care recipients exhaust their personal assets.
[P761] 5.4.3 Long-term Care Costs from Personal Assets
[P762] Overall, a fairly substantial amount of long-term care costs are paid from the individual’s personal assets. Typically, however, individual assets provide the source for long-term care funding only until the individual has become impoverished and eligible for Medicaid’s long-term care benefits.
[P763] According to CMS statistics, out-of-pocket payments for long-term care were as follows:
[P764] Home healthcare – 11%;
[P765] Short-term institution – 7%; and
[P766] Nursing home care (custodial care) – 48%.
[P767] 5.4.4 Insurance Sources of Long-term Care Funding
[P768] Insurance as a source of payment of long-term care costs has generally played a minor role overall in providing long-term care funds. In general, sales of long-term care insurance policies have been disappointing. Although several reasons have emerged for the failure of individuals to purchase long-term care insurance, the most frequently stated reason is its high cost.
[P769] Certain limited insurance benefits for payment of long-term care costs are provided by Medicare supplement policies. The nature of the coverage provided to offset these long-term care costs depends on the Medicare supplement plan in force at the time services are provided.
[P770] Coverage provided under Medicare supplement plans is limited to skilled nursing care and home healthcare as follows:
[P771] Medicare supplement plans C, D, F, G and K through N provide benefits for the coinsurance payment due from the insured for skilled nursing care for days 21 through 100; and
[P772] Medicare supplement plans D and G provide an at-home recovery benefit, following an illness or injury provided the follow-up care is ordered by a physician.
[P773] None of the Medicare supplement policies offer coverage for the most prevalent type of long-term care: custodial care.
[P774] Based on recent statistics, private insurance pays for 8 percent of long-term care payments and support.
[P775] The bulk of long-term care costs are currently paid by Medicaid, the jointly-funded government program that provides healthcare funding for the indigent. The federal government and the government of the states are understandably interested in reducing the drain on their funds to pay long-term care costs, and the federal government has passed the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 and the Pension Protection Act of 2006, both of which contain provisions designed to move much of the long-term care payment burden from government shoulders to private insurers. We will consider this initiative later in the course when we examine state long-term care partnership programs.

[P779] II.  the high cost of LTC  Your answer is correct. The high cost of long-term care insurance prevents many people from purchasing it.
[P780] III.  most people can afford to pay out of pocket  Your answer is incorrect. The most frequently stated reason for the sluggish sales of LTC coverage is not that most people can afford to pay out of pocket.
[P781] 5.4.5	Long-term Care Financing
[P782] It's difficult to predict if or how much care an individual will need, whether an individual will have family or friends who can provide some or all of their care, and how much care may cost. However, it's reasonably easy to predict that if an individual needs extensive long-term care services or needs services over a long period of time, they will have to pay for some or all of it out of their personal finances. That's why an increasing number of people are using private financing options to help them pay for long-term care if and when they need it.
[P783] Private long-term care financing options include long-term care insurance, trusts, annuities, and reverse mortgages. Which option is best for an individual depends on many factors including age, health status, risk of needing long-term care, and personal financial situation. The following charts summarize how age and health status may affect eligibility for and choice of private financing options.
[P784] Some methods of paying for long-term care require undergoing health screening. Some options require that an individual be in relatively good health (not currently needing long-term care and not having a debilitating chronic condition such as Parkinson's disease that would almost certainly mean an individual would need long-term care eventually.) In contrast, some options are only available to an individual if they are in poor health.
[P785] The table below shows whether current health is a consideration in eligibility for each option listed.
[P786] Some private payment options are good choices for older people; while others make more sense for a younger person.
[P787] Let’s take a look at these alternate methods of paying for Long-Term Care.
[P788] Home Equity
[P789] Home equity is the difference between the appraised value of a home and what an individual owes on any mortgages. By the time an individual needs long-term care, they may have greatly reduced or paid off their home mortgage. The value of their home may also have risen beyond its original purchase price.
[P790] Choosing to tap home equity can be a big decision. The house may be an individual’s most valuable financial asset. There are many practical and financial factors to consider:
[P791] Should an individual sell their house or take out a home loan? It is important to balance health and safety issues with a desire for independence and a familiar setting.
[P792] If it makes sense to stay at home, what are the benefits and risks associated with different types of home loans?
[P793] How will using home equity affect eligibility for public programs, should they be needed?
[P794] Selling Your Home?
[P796] One of the most difficult decisions individuals may face as they age is whether it is time to leave their home and move to a more supportive setting such as an assisted living facility or nursing home.  Several factors should be considered as individuals decide whether staying at their own home makes sense. For many people, a house that was ideal 30 years ago may now be too difficult to handle alone. For suburban and rural elders, isolation can become a problem when driving is difficult. Deteriorating neighborhoods may also make an older person reluctant to go shopping or attend social activities. Getting good quality and reliable help, either from family caregivers or paid professionals, is another critical element.
[P797] Important Considerations:
[P798] If an individual sells their home, they will not be able to pass it on to their heirs.
[P799] The sale price may not be enough to pay for long-term care needs.
[P800] Market conditions will affect the selling price.
[P801] Individuals may have to pay taxes on the capital gains from the sale of the house, depending on the sale price relative to the original purchase price and other considerations. Consult your tax advisor for details.
[P802] C.	Sale–Leaseback Arrangement?
[P803] A Sale–Leaseback is an arrangement where an individual sells their home to an investor, typically at below market value, and then they remain in the home as a renter.  The individual essentially then rents their home from the investor on a long-term lease.  The individual no longer has to worry about maintenance of the home or paying taxes. They can use the proceeds from the home sale any way they like. The investor then takes over the property once the individual stops living there.
[P804] Important Considerations:
[P805] Because the investor takes over ownership of the property, even though an individual may continue to live there, their home will not stay in their family.
[P806] The individual potentially faces a high tax payment on the proceeds from selling the home.
[P807] The individual may not qualify for public assistance as a result of the income gained from the sale of their home.
[P808] D.	Taking Out a Home Loan
[P809] Tapping home equity typically involves taking out a loan that uses the home as the collateral to guarantee that an individual will repay the loan. There are several ways an individual can use the equity in their home to pay for long-term care:
[P810] Reverse mortgages
[P811] Conventional home equity loans
[P812] Home equity conversions
[P813] Reverse annuity mortgages
[P814] Lease backs
[P815] Home modification loans
[P816] There are usually significant upfront costs associated with any type of home loan. If an individual has an ongoing health problem, they need to decide if it is worth taking out a loan, since they may only be able to continue to live at home for a short time.
[P817] E.	Reverse Mortgage?
[P818] If an individual expects to live in their current home for several years, they should consider a reverse mortgage. A reverse mortgage is a special type of home equity loan. An individual receives cash against the value of their home without selling it. An individual chooses whether they want to receive a lump-sum payment, a monthly payment, or a line of credit. There are no restrictions on the use of reverse mortgage funds.
[P819] Reverse mortgages are available to homeowners age 62 and older. Unlike a traditional mortgage, with a reverse mortgage, an individual won't be required to make monthly payments. Instead, the amount owed, based on loan payouts and interest on the loan, accumulates over time.
[P820] An individual may continue to live in the home and retain title and ownership of it. The individual is also still responsible for taxes, hazard insurance, and home repairs.  They do not have to repay the loan as long as they continue to live in the home. The loan is repaid when the individual or the last borrower (such as the remaining spouse) dies, sells, or permanently moves out of the home. The funds from a reverse mortgage are non-taxable. They do not count toward income or affect Social Security or Medicare benefits or count as income for Medicaid benefits eligibility as long as the reverse mortgage payments received are spent within the month that they are received.
[P821] To qualify for a reverse mortgage:
[P822] All borrowers must be 62 or older.
[P823] There is no health requirement; health status is not a factor.
[P824] The home must be the individual’s primary residence.
[P825] Individuals must show that they have the financial resources to pay ongoing property charges, including real estate taxes and insurance.
[P826] Reverse mortgage funds must be used to pay off any existing mortgage or other debt against the home and to make required home repairs.  An individual can use any remaining funds for any purpose. There can be little or no outstanding balance on an individual’s current mortgage.
[P827] A reverse mortgage must be in first lien position, which makes it very difficult to borrow any more against the home once an individual obtains a reverse mortgage. Individuals can refinance a reverse mortgage if the house increases significantly in value.
[P828] All potential borrowers must first meet with a HUD-approved reverse mortgage counselor before they can start the loan process. These counselors can give you information to help decide whether a reverse mortgage is the right choice.
[P829] Individuals can use the funds received from a reverse mortgage to pay for a wide array of in-home and community services and other expenses, such as home repairs and transportation, which can make it safer and more comfortable for them to live at home. However, long-term care expenses may be greater than the amount obtained in the reverse mortgage. Individuals can also use the funds to purchase long-term care insurance. It may be hard for a married couple to purchase long-term care insurance or pay for long-term care costs for both people with the amount available from a reverse mortgage.
[P830] Heirs can keep the home by repaying the reverse mortgage. Heirs can also “keep the difference” if the home's sale price is greater than the reverse mortgage loan balance when it's time to repay the loan.
[P831] A reverse mortgage compares with a conventional mortgage as follows:
[P832] There are three types of reverse mortgages. These include:
[P833] Home Equity Conversion Mortgage (HECM) – This program is offered by the Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD) and is insured by the FHA. HECMs are the most popular reverse mortgages, representing about 90 percent of the market.
[P834] Fannie Mae Home Keeper Loan – Borrowers may receive more cash from these loans than with a HECM since the loan limit for these loans is higher.
[P835] Financial Freedom Cash Account Loans – These loans are designed for seniors who own expensive homes.
[P836] Most people get a reverse mortgage through a mortgage lender. Some credit unions and banks, along with state and local housing agencies, may also offer these loans.
[P837] The consumer protections attached to reverse mortgages include:
[P838] Borrower(s) continue to own the house and can never be forced to leave as long as they maintain the home, and make property tax and hazard insurance payments.
[P839] You must first meet with a government-approved reverse mortgage counselor before your loan application can be processed or you incur any costs.
[P840] Borrowers (or their heirs) will never owe more than value of the home at the time they sell the home or repay the loan, even if the value of their home declines.
[P841] For HECM loans, most upfront costs are regulated, and there are limits on the total fees and interest rates that can be charged.
[P842] F.	Home Modification Loans
[P843] Some government agencies and communities make low interest loans available for home modifications that help make your home a safer and more supportive living environment. While these loans are used specifically for home modifications and not to pay for long-term care costs, often a home modification can help someone with a physical limitation or disability to cope more effectively at home. Home modification loans may make it possible for you to stay in your own home instead of having to move to a care facility. Home modifications include things such as the installation of ramps or grab rails. The loan is repaid when you no longer live at your home.
[P844] Important Considerations:
[P845] Home modification loans are not available to everyone. They are designed for individuals with low or moderate incomes.
[P846] Each loan program will specify what home modifications can be made with the loan funds.
[P847] The loan payment is due if you move out of your home.
[P848] 5.4.6	Private Health Insurance or Health Maintenance Organization (HMO)
[P850] Most forms of health insurance (such as the private health insurance or Health Maintenance Organization (HMO) an individual may have on their own or through their employer) follow the same general rules as Medicare. If they do cover long-term care, it is typically only for skilled, short-term, medically necessary care. Like Medicare, the skilled nursing home stay must follow a recent hospitalization for the same or related condition. Coverage in a Skilled Nursing Facility is limited to 100 days. Home care is also limited to medically necessary, skilled care. Custodial or personal care is never covered. However, most people who need long-term care need custodial or personal care.
[P851] If an individual receives healthcare from an HMO, the plan may help pay for some of the co-pays or deductibles that Medicare would otherwise impose (for example, the per day cost for nursing home care for days 21 through 100), but they otherwise do not vary from Medicare's rules for what type of care is covered or for how long benefits are provided.
[P852] 5.4.7	Disability Insurance
[P853] Disability insurance is intended to replace some of the income of a working person who becomes disabled and can no longer work. Disability benefits do not cover either medical care or long-term care; they provide a partial salary replacement while the person is unable to work. Most disability insurance policies do not provide any benefits once an individual is over age 65 – exactly when an individual is more likely to need long-term care.
[P854] 5.5 Long-term Care Likely to be Affected by Health and Population Changes
[P855] We noted in our discussion of long-term care payers that the principal sources of payment for long-term care services are Medicare and Medicaid. Medicare generally provides benefits for individuals who are age 65 and over. This segment of the population has been growing fast. Here are the figures from the decennial censuses since Medicare became law:
[P856] Percent of Population Age 65 or Older
[P857] This trend is expected to accelerate as more baby boomers reach this age milestone.
[P859] Since long-term care services are required more frequently by older persons, this disproportionate growth suggests that the need for long-term care services and the funds needed to support those services will increase in the years ahead. The statistics also indicate that services will be more frequently used by women than men. You can see this if you visit most long-term care facilities.
[P860] 5.5.1 Obesity a Significant Health Issue for New Seniors
[P861] At the end of World War II, GIs returned home to pursue civilian careers and resume family life. That family life resumption included a jump in the birth rate of what was to become known as the Baby Boom generation. The Baby Boom generation includes those people born between 1946, the year after the war ended, and 1964. This generation represents a very large demographic bulge comprised of 76 million people some of whom—perhaps many of them—will need long-term care. To make the long-term care situation more challenging, this generation’s need for long-term care may be even greater due to its lifestyle.
[P862] According to the Centers for Disease Control, 32% of Americans have high blood pressure. This figure is higher in older individuals, exceeding half for age groups 55 and over. The CDC also says that 36.5% of all Americans are obese. Adults over 60 have a slightly higher rate of 37%. Middle aged individuals (40 to 59) have a higher rate yet at 40.2%. The United States has the highest incidence of obesity among developed nations—a distinction that has important implications for the long-term care industry and U.S. long-term care costs.
[P863] An article titled Obesity published by the Mayo Clinic identifies several health problems—many of which could lead to a need for long-term care—caused or exacerbated by obesity, including:
[P864] high blood pressure;
[P865] diabetes;
[P866] coronary artery disease;
[P867] heart attack;
[P868] stroke;
[P869] joint pain and stiffness caused by osteoarthritis;
[P870] cancer;
[P871] fatty liver disease, including cirrhosis;
[P872] gallbladder disease; and
[P873] gout.
[P874] As the Baby Boom generation ages, its use of long-term care services is expected to be disproportionately large even compared to its size, due principally to its general lack of fitness.

[P880] 5.5.2 U.S. Census Bureau Projects Disproportionate Older Population Growth
[P881] However, even if the Baby Boom generation did not present challenges associated with its lifestyle and reduced fitness level, its enormous size would present them. We can better envision the long-term care issues of an aging population by considering Census Bureau projections through 2050.
[P882] During the period from 2005 to 2050, the overall U.S. population growth is anticipated to be 42%. If we look behind the overall growth numbers, however, we can see that the older segments of the population are expected to grow at rates that may be staggering for the long-term care industry and the ability of Medicare and Medicaid to pay for its services. Specifically, the following growth rates are projected:
[P883] The population segment of individuals age 55 and older is expected to grow by 97%;
[P884] The population segment of individuals age 65 and older is expected to grow by 136%;
[P885] The population segment of individuals age 75 and older is expected to grow by 170%; and
[P886] The population segment of individuals age 85 and older is expected to grow by 307%.
[P887] If the U.S. Census Bureau projections are realized, the population segment most likely to need long-term care, comprised of people ages 85 and older, will grow from just over 5 million to almost 21 million. The combination of an increased number of old Americans with greater morbidity concerns is likely to tax the resources of the long-term care industry and society’s ability to pay for the care.

[P909] 6.0 Long-term Care Insurance
[P910] As we just noted in the last chapter long-term care insurance is one of the sources of payment for long-term care services. Despite its somewhat lackluster sales performance up to this point, recent legislation is likely to make long-term care insurance more attractive and its sales more robust. Before we examine that legislation and look at the reasons why it is likely to be seen as more attractive, let's consider the insurance coverage itself.
[P911] 6.1	The Benefits of Long-term Care Insurance
[P912] There is a great deal of choice and flexibility in long-term care insurance policies. An individual can select a range of care options and benefits that allow an individual to get the services they need in the settings that suits them best. The cost of a long-term care insurance policy is based on the type and amount of services chosen to have covered, how old an individual is when they buy the policy, and any optional benefits they choose, such as Inflation Protection. If an individual is in poor health or already receiving long-term care services, they may not qualify for long-term care insurance, or they may only be able to buy a more limited amount of coverage, or buy coverage at a higher “non-standard” rate.
[P913] As we will discuss, long-term care insurance policies have a benefit period or lifetime benefit maximum, which is the total amount of time or total amount of dollars up to which benefits will be paid. Common benefit periods for long-term care policies are two, three, four, and five years, and lifetime or unlimited coverage. Other options between five years and lifetime/unlimited coverage are also available from many companies. Most policies translate these time periods into dollar amounts and do not actually limit the number of days for which they will pay for care – just the overall dollar amount that the policy will pay. There are fewer companies today willing to offer an unlimited/lifetime policy, although some have a “high coverage option”, such as a $1 million lifetime limit.
[P914] With long-term care insurance, an individual pays premiums in amounts they know in advance and can budget for, and the policy pays – up to its coverage limits – for the long-term care an individual needs when they need it. Typically, premiums are waived during the time an individual is receiving benefits.
[P915] 6.2	Potential Drawbacks
[P916] Like all insurance, long-term care policies have exclusions. These are listed in both the Outline of Coverage you receive before application, as well as in the policy after an individual has purchased coverage.  These exclusions often follow state regulations on what exclusions are allowed. Long-term care policies typically exclude the following (even if an individual meets all the other requirements of the policy):
[P917] Care or services provided by family member unless the family member is a regular employee of an organization that is providing the treatment, service or care; and the organization they work for receives the payment for the treatment, service or care; and the family members receives no compensation other than the normal compensation for employees in their job category;
[P918] Care or services for which no charge is made in the absence of insurance;
[P919] Care or services provided outside the United States of America, its territories or possessions. However, a growing number of policies now have an international care benefit that can provide care outside of the United States;
[P920] Care or services that result from war or act of war, whether declared or not;
[P921] Care or services that result from an attempt at suicide (while sane or insane) or an intentionally self-inflicted injury;
[P922] Care or services for alcoholism or drug addiction (except for an addiction to a prescription medication when administered in accordance with the advice of Your Physician);
[P923] Treatment provided in a government facility (unless otherwise required by law);
[P924] Services for which benefits are available under Medicare or other governmental program (except Medicaid), any state or federal workers' compensation, employer's liability or occupational disease law, or any motor vehicle no-fault law
[P925] Although most policies do not pay for care received from a family member, friend, or other individual who is not paid to provide your care, some policies provide a cash payment for each day that an individual receives care from anyone, even if it is a family member or friend. These policies cost more (about 25-40% more) but allow more flexibility in using benefit dollars.  Most policies provide training and support for family and friends who provide care.
[P926] Most policies require that the facility, agency or individual providing an individual’s care meet certain minimum standards with respect to quality, safety, and training. For example, a nursing home that is not licensed but operates in a state that requires licensure, would not be covered.  In states that do not require long-term care facilities or programs to be licensed, the insurance policy would typically describe the staffing, safety and other features that should be present to ensure that you receive appropriate and safe care.
[P927] Long-term care policies focus on paying for the types of services and providers that someone needs when they cannot perform their Activities of Daily Living on their own or when they have a Cognitive Impairment. They do not pay for care or services unrelated to these needs, such as hospital stays or prescription medications.
[P928] However, some policies may pay for prescription drugs provided while you are in a care facility (but not at home), and some policies pay for transportation costs to help you get to medical appointments when you are physically or cognitively impaired.
[P929] Some policies provide coverage for care related to everyday household needs such as housekeeping, laundry, meals, and managing medications, so-called “instrumental activities of daily living,” but only when you receive that help as part of the help you get from a paid care provider for assistance with Activities of Daily Living. So most policies do not pay for in-home help if all you need is help with services such as housekeeping, meals, laundry, and transportation.
[P930] Finally, long-term care policies do not pay for items provided solely for an individual’s comfort or convenience, for example a television in a nursing home room or a visit to the facility's hair care salon.
[P931] 6.3	To Buy or Not to Buy?
[P932] Long-term care insurance is particularly important for people who are middle class -- not rich enough to self-insure and not poor enough to qualify for Medicaid. Long-term care insurance is worth a look, particularly if there are assets to protect.
[P933] First, be aware of the costs of long-term care.
[P934] Waiting until you are 50 or older to purchase long-term care insurance may be recommended by various advocacy groups, although an injury or illness can happen at any time. Coverage is dependent upon current health status, and monthly rates are based upon an individual’s age when they apply.   Certainly, long-term care insurance is less expensive at younger ages. It may be unaffordable if you wait until late middle age.
[P935] The main determining factors in what long-term care insurance will cost are:
[P936] Age - The risk generally increases as you get older.
[P937] Marital Status - Single people are more likely to need care from a paid provider.
[P938] Gender - Women are at a higher risk than men, primarily because they tend to live longer.
[P939] Lifestyle - Poor diet and/or exercise habits can increase an individual’s risk.
[P940] Health and family history also impact an individual’s risk.
[P941] 6.4	Percent of Income Used to Buy Long-term Care Insurance
[P942] Generally, long-term care insurance premiums should consume no more than 7 percent of an individual's or couple's income according to The Shopper's Guide to Long-Term Care Insurance (National Association of Insurance Commissioners, Revised 2019). Be sure to consider present income and income in retirement. When premiums cause a relatively significant reduction in an individual's or couple's standard of living, long-term care insurance may not be an appropriate purchase, unless another strategy is created to support the premiums, for example, having premiums paid by family members.
[P943] Since an individual is responsible for paying their premiums to keep their insurance active, income should be sufficient to pay long-term care insurance premiums on a continuous basis. Using assets to support the premiums is not recommended unless the use meets the requirements of a special financial strategy. Such a strategy should be developed with the guidance of a financial advisor.
[P944] An individual’s income should guide you in determining the amount of coverage to purchase. For example, if nursing home care costs are $250 per day in an individual’s area and the customer can afford to pay $50 per day from their income, then they might purchase a policy for $200 per day, for a lower premium than the cost of a $250 per day policy. Under a Total Asset Protection plan, assets are fully protected when you apply for Medicaid Extended Coverage. However, an individual will be required to contribute income to the cost of their care.
[P945] 6.5	Suitability – Personal Worksheet
[P946] The NAIC model regulation specifies three specific disclosure forms that relate to:
[P947] The applicant’s Long-term Care Insurance Personal Worksheet;
[P948] A Things You Should Know Before You Buy Long-term Care Insurance disclosure form
[P949] A Potential Rate Increase Disclosure Form.
[P950] 6.6	Counseling
[P951] Care advisory services are long-term care assessment and planning services provided by a professional that are designed to:
[P952] Assess an individual’s need for long-term care;
[P953] Develop a long-term care services recommendation;
[P954] Coordinate the delivery of long-term care;
[P955] Monitor delivered long-term care services; and
[P956] Periodically re-assess long-term care needs.
[P957] These care advisory services are covered expenses under long-term care insurance policies. Depending on the policy design, the amount payable for such services may be subject to an annual maximum or may be borne entirely by the insurer.
[P958] 6.7	The Long-term Care Insurance Market
[P959] A 25-year study conducted for America's Health Insurance Plans (AHIP) by Lifeplans, Inc., titled "Who Buys Long-Term Care Insurance in 2015-2016" provides some insight into the Long-term Care Insurance Market.  In particular, the report compared buyers with non-buyers and with other Americans age 50 and over to better understand marketplace opportunities and barriers, contribute to the debate about public policy on LTC financing, and evaluate whether and how LTC insurance can help solve the increasingly complex puzzle of LTC financing.
[P961] In 2014, the total number of individuals with LTCI coverage was 7.2 million with total premiums of roughly $12 billion. This does not represent all people who have ever had policies—only those who still have them. Recent analysis shows that among Americans who are 65 years old and older, around 16 percent have LTC insurance.
[P963] Americans bought only about 60,000 stand-alone long-term care (LTC) insurance policies in 2018, down 13 percent from 2017. Only about 15 carriers were actively selling policies, and five of them accounted for more than three-quarters of the market, as measured by premiums. The average buyer of stand-alone policies was 56 years old, and the average annual premium for most policies hit $2,544. The average price for couples buying together was about $3,600.
[P964] (Source: https://www.ahip.org/who-buys-long-term-care-insurance/
[P965] 6.8	Market Segments by Type of Long-term Care Insurance Policies
[P966] According to an NAIC report, policies purchased by consumers today provide broader coverage.  Specifically:
[P967] The proportion of policies that cover both institutional care and home care grew from 37 percent in 1990 to 61 percent in 2005 and 95 percent in 2010. Virtually all policies sold by 2015, 99 percent, covered nursing home and home care. Data suggests that “nursing home only” policies or “institutional alternatives” only policies have virtually disappeared from the marketplace.
[P968] Between 2005 and 2015, the average daily home care benefit increased by 13% and the nursing home benefit increased by 12%.
[P969] Over three-quarters of policyholders chose some form of inflation protection in 2015, about the same as in 2005 and up from less than half in 2000.
[P970] LTC premiums have increased nearly 44 percent from 2005 to 2015.
[P971] Given that the policies purchased by consumers today provide broader coverage than they did in 1995, this means that consumers are receiving better value for their premium dollars today.

[P986] 6.14	Policy Improvements
[P987] In 2006, the NAIC adopted several revisions to the Long-term Care Model Act and Regulation, including provisions that increased access to care and allow insurance consumers more flexibility in managing the cost of their coverage. The amendments ensure that long-term care insurance policies would pay for services in facilities in other states, even if the facilities are licensed or registered in a different way from those in the state in which the policy was sold.
[P988] Carriers often require the long-term care facilities they reimburse to be licensed or registered to ensure the highest quality of care for their beneficiaries. This requirement has, at times, resulted in nonpayment to facilities in other states because they are not properly certified. The modification to the model act will allow carriers to protect their beneficiaries, without the unintended consequences.
[P989] The adopted amendments also will provide consumers with more options when new services or providers become available in the market and greater flexibility to reduce coverage in order to make premiums more affordable. These key improvements give consumers more control over their coverage.
[P991] 6.15 Two Methods of Delivering Benefits
[P992] Insurance generally tends to be inflexible with respect to the coverage it provides; long-term care insurance is somewhat different in that regard. Two basic approaches may be used in delivering long-term care insurance benefits. Those approaches involve a:
[P993] Very flexible "pool of money" approach; and
[P994] Less flexible specified daily benefit maximum and maximum benefit period.
[P995] Let's look somewhat more closely at these two approaches.
[P996] 6.15.1 A Pool of Money
[P997] When thinking about the “pool of money” approach to the delivery of long-term care insurance benefits, it might be more appropriate to look at it as a “bucket" of money from which the insured may take funds, as needed, to pay for covered long-term care services. To the extent they take more money from the bucket, the funds will be used up more quickly. Conversely, insofar as the insured takes less money from the bucket, the funds will last longer. Because the insured is directly impacted by the use of the funds in that bucket, they are more likely to be a savvy consumer of long-term care services.
[P998] Under a long-term care insurance policy using a pool of money approach, the insured is given two limits. They are limits that specify a:
[P999] Daily maximum amount; and
[P1000] Total lifetime benefit amount.
[P1001] The daily maximum amount is simply the maximum amount the insured may spend each day to purchase coverage services. The total lifetime benefit amount is the total amount in the bucket.
[P1002] Under this approach the insured may spend any amount of money each day on covered benefits up to the daily maximum amount. When they have spent an amount equal to the total lifetime benefit amount—the amount in the bucket—benefits end. So, if an insured elects to purchase covered services that cost $100 per day, their benefits will last twice as long as will the benefits available to an insured who purchases covered services that cost $200 per day.
[P1003] For example, suppose an insured purchased a long-term care insurance policy that delivers benefits under the pool of money approach and the policy specifies a daily maximum amount of $250 and a total lifetime benefit amount of $456,250. If the insured purchases long-term care services that cost exactly $250 daily, their benefit will continue for as long as long-term care services are needed but not more than five years. ($456,250  $250 = 1,825 days; 1,825 days  365 days = 5 years)
[P1004] However, suppose the same insured purchases the same policy but enters a long-term care facility that costs the insured $200 per day. Since this insured uses fewer of the dollars in the bucket each day, the bucket will contain cash for a longer period. In this case, the funds will last for six years and three months instead of being exhausted at the end of five years. ($456,250  $200 = 2,281 days; 2,281 days  365 days = 6.25 years)
[P1005] Review Question:
[P1006] Long-term care insurance policies using the pool of money approach give the insured two limits; these two limits specify a :
[P1007] I. daily maximum amount
[P1008] II. weekly maximum amount
[P1009] III. total lifetime benefit amount
[P1010] a. I and II  Your answer is only partially correct.
[P1011] b. I, II and III  Your answer is only partially correct.
[P1012] c. I and III only  Your answer is correct. The two limits given to those insured by LTC policies using the pool of money approach are the daily maximum amount and the total lifetime benefit amount.
[P1013] 6.15.2 Specified Daily Maximum & Maximum Benefit Period
[P1014] The other approach used in long-term care insurance policies specifies both a daily maximum amount and a maximum benefit period. Under this less-flexible approach, the maximum benefit period is simply the period specified in the policy regardless of whether the insured used the maximum daily benefit or some lesser amount.
[P1015] If we return to our earlier example, we can easily see the difference between these two approaches. Suppose that our insured had purchased a long-term care insurance policy that provides a $250 daily benefit and a five-year maximum benefit period. If the insured purchased long-term care services for $250 per day, they would have used $456,250 in benefits over the five-year maximum benefit period. ($250 x 365 = $91,250; $91,250 x 5 = $456,250) Clearly, in such a situation the insured is no better or worse off under one approach than under the other.
[P1016] However, if our insured purchased those long-term care services for $200 per day, the maximum benefit period would still be limited to five years. As a result, the benefit of our savvy insured’s thrift would inure to the insurer—whose total benefit payment would have been reduced to $365,000—rather than to the insured, assuming the policy provided a reimbursement benefit. ($200 x 365 = $73,000; $73,000 x 5 = $365,000).
[P1017] Long-term care insurance policies that specify both a daily benefit and a maximum benefit period may provide benefits on:
[P1018] A reimbursement basis; or
[P1019] An indemnity basis.
[P1020] 6.15.2.1 Reimbursement Basis Payments Limited to Actual Cost
[P1021] Long-term care insurance benefits paid on a reimbursement basis provide the insured with a daily benefit equal to the lesser of the:
[P1022] Maximum daily benefit; or
[P1023] Actual daily charges for covered care.
[P1024] Therefore, our thrifty insured whose long-term care insurance policy provided a maximum daily benefit of $250 but who spent only $200 for covered care would receive a benefit of $200. Since the policy provides a stated maximum benefit period, no further benefits would be paid under the policy after the benefit period specified in the policy ended. The $50 per day the insured saved by purchasing long-term care at a lower price would simply have reduced the insurer’s claim costs.
[P1025] Other insurance policies normally paid on a reimbursement basis include major medical health insurance policies.
[P1026] 6.15.2.2 Indemnity Basis Payments Not Based on Actual Cost
[P1027] Long-term care insurance policies whose benefits are paid on an indemnity basis work differently. Under an indemnity basis long-term care insurance policy, the benefit paid is equal to the benefit stated in the policy for every day the insured qualifies for long-term care, even if the actual cost of care is less than the stated benefit. Let's return again to our example.
[P1028] If our thrifty insured whose long-term care insurance policy provided a daily benefit of $250 but who spent only $200 for covered care owned a policy that paid benefits on an indemnity basis, they would have received a daily benefit of $250. That additional $50 each day could be used to for any purpose the insured wished.
[P1029] It should be obvious that insurance policies paying benefits on a reimbursement basis generally involve lower claims costs than otherwise identical insurance policies paying benefits on an indemnity basis. For that reason long-term care insurance policies whose benefits are paid on a reimbursement basis are normally somewhat less expensive than otherwise identical long-term care insurance policies that pay benefits on an indemnity basis.
[P1030] Insurance policies whose benefits are normally paid on an indemnity basis include:
[P1031] Disability income policies; and
[P1032] Daily hospital benefit policies.

A double indemnity basis long-term care insurance policy is not where the benefit paid is equal to the benefit stated in the policy for every day the insured qualifies for long-term care, even if the actual cost of care is less than the stated benefit.

[P1039] 6.16 Long-term Care Insurance Benefit Triggers
[P1040] Every insurance policy is designed to pay a benefit upon the occurrence of some event. In the case of a life insurance policy, that event is the death of the insured. In a disability insurance policy, it is the insured's disability. Each of these things—the insured’s death or disability—is a benefit trigger for those policies.
[P1041] Traditionally, in the case of a long-term care insurance policy, three possible conditions could apply that would be considered benefit triggers:
[P1042] The insured’s suffering a cognitive impairment;
[P1043] The insured's inability to perform a number of activities of daily living stated in the policy; or
[P1044] A physician’s determining that the insured’s receiving long-term care is a medical necessity.
[P1045] Generally, all long-term care insurance policies issued before 1997 contained these three benefit triggers.
[P1046] In 1996 the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act—more familiarly known as HIPAA—was passed. HIPAA created a category of long-term care insurance policies that were considered “tax qualified” and were, therefore, entitled to certain favorable income tax treatment. We will discuss this favorable tax treatment given to tax-qualified long-term care insurance policies in a later lesson.
[P1047] More importantly for our immediate purposes is that HIPAA defined a tax-qualified long-term care insurance policy. That definition appears in §7702B(b) of the Internal Revenue Code, whose salient provisions are shown in the following table:
[P1050] We can see that insurance benefits under a policy identified as a “tax-qualified” long-term care insurance policy are those payable only for care required by a chronically-ill individual. Such an individual is defined in terms of:
[P1051] The inability to perform at least 2 activities of daily living; or
[P1052] Requiring substantial supervisiondue to severe cognitive impairment.
[P1053] The traditional benefit trigger of medical necessity is not a benefit trigger in a tax-qualified long-term care insurance policy.

[P1056] I. The insured’s suffering a cognitive impairment;
[P1057] II. The insured's inability to perform a number of activities of daily living stated in the policy; or
[P1058] III. A physician’s determining that the insured’s receiving long-term care is a medical necessity.

In the case of long-term care insurance policies, benefit triggers might be: The insured’s suffering a cognitive impairment; inability to perform a number of ADLs stated in the policy; or a physician determining the insured’s receiving long-term care is a medical necessity.
[P1063] 6.16.1 Cognitive Impairment as a Benefit Trigger
[P1064] HIPAA retained cognitive impairment as a benefit trigger for tax qualified long-term care insurance policies, provided a licensed healthcare practitioner has certified that the insured requires substantial supervision because of it. The term cognitive impairment is normally used to refer to a condition that impairs the insured’s:
[P1065] Judgment, particularly in connection with their awareness of safety issues;
[P1066] Memory;
[P1067] Orientation with respect to people, time, or place; or
[P1068] Ability to reason deductively or abstractly.
[P1069] Severe cognitive impairment is often seen in individuals with Alzheimer's disease and other types of dementia, and may result in generally-inappropriate behavior and impaired judgment. Such inappropriate behavior may manifest itself in a lack of personal hygiene or in conduct that is assaultive or otherwise abusive. It is important to bear in mind that an insured diagnosed with a severe cognitive impairment that requires supervision does not need to be unable to perform any activities of daily living in order to be eligible for long-term care insurance benefits. Their needing supervision as a result of suffering from a severe cognitive impairment is sufficient.
[P1070] 6.16.2 Inability to Perform ADLs as a Benefit Trigger
[P1071] In addition to suffering from a severe cognitive impairment that requires substantial supervision, an insured under a tax qualified long-term care insurance policy may also qualify for benefits by being unable to perform two or more ADLs.
[P1072] As recited in IRC §7702B, a tax-qualified long-term care insurance policy must provide benefits for a chronically ill individual who is defined as an individual unable to perform at least two activities of daily living. Furthermore, a tax qualified long-term care insurance policy must include at least five of the following six activities of daily living:
[P1073] Eating,
[P1074] Toileting,
[P1075] Transferring,
[P1076] Bathing,
[P1077] Dressing, and
[P1078] Continence.

[P1082] I.  1; 60  Your answer is incorrect. A chronically ill individual has not been certified by a licensed healthcare practitioner as being unable to perform alone more than one activity of daily living for a period of more than 60 days due to a loss of functional capacity.

[P1085] 6.16.3 Medical Necessity as a Benefit Trigger
[P1086] It should be pointed out that not all long-term care insurance policies are tax qualified. Long-term care insurance policies that are nonqualified normally include medical necessity as a benefit trigger.
[P1087] Found generally in nonqualified long-term care insurance policies, medical necessity is a benefit trigger that enables an insured to receive long-term care insurance benefits when the need for such benefits is verified by a physician. A medical necessity benefit trigger permits an insured to qualify for long-term care insurance benefits even though they suffer no cognitive impairment and are able to perform the usual activities of daily living. It is generally because of the additional benefit trigger that agents sell and customers purchase nonqualified long-term care insurance policies despite their uncertain income tax treatment.
[P1088] 6.17 Long-term Care Insurance Policy Basic Provisions
[P1089] Long-term care insurance policies may vary substantially from insurer to insurer. In this section we will look at the basic policy provisions in these policies.
[P1090] 6.17.1 Long-term Care Policy Benefit Period
[P1091] The benefit period in a long-term care insurance policy is similar to the benefit period found in other types of insurance coverage such as disability income insurance. In general, it is the maximum period during which benefits may be payable for covered services for which the insured continues to be eligible.
[P1092] A distinction needs to be made with respect to the benefit period in policies employing a “pool of money" concept. In such policies, the maximum period during which benefits may be payable is somewhat flexible since the insured may increase the period during which benefits may be payable by decreasing the amount they spend on covered long-term care. In short, by reducing the amount of funds taken from the pool of money, they can increase the length of time the pool continues to hold available funds.
[P1093] Although any insurer may offer other long-term care insurance benefit period choices, the following benefit periods are commonly available:
[P1094] 2 years;
[P1095] 3 years;
[P1096] 4 years;
[P1097] 5 years;
[P1098] 6 years;
[P1099] 10 years; and
[P1100] Lifetime.
[P1101] At certain older issue ages, the longer benefit periods may not be available.
[P1102] 6.17.2 Long-term Care Policy Elimination Period
[P1103] Although certain differences apply, a long-term care insurance policy’s elimination period is similar to an elimination period found in a disability income insurance policy. An elimination period is the time period beginning when the insured becomes eligible to receive covered care and the time when long-term care insurance benefits begin. It is sometimes referred to as a “deductible” or a “waiting period.”
[P1104] In the case of a long-term care insurance policy (unlike a disability income insurance policy), the insured normally needs to satisfy the elimination period only once. Furthermore, the elimination period may normally be satisfied through consecutive or non-consecutive days of eligibility for covered benefits.
[P1105] For example, suppose an insured’s policy has an elimination period of 90 days. If the insured requires covered long-term-care services for 10 days and then no longer needs such services, they need only meet the remaining 80 days of the elimination period before benefits commence.
[P1106] In addition, some insurers provide shortened elimination periods—or no elimination period at all—when the long-term care provided to the insured is home care. Since long-term care services provided in an institutional setting are generally much more costly than such services provided at home, insurers normally encourage the use of home care where appropriate. Their methods of encouraging the use of home care include:
[P1107] Waiving the policy’s elimination period when covered home healthcare is received; and
[P1108] Counting days of home healthcare received towards meeting the elimination period applicable to the policy’s non-home care benefits.
[P1109] As in the case of benefit periods, an insurer may offer elimination periods that vary from those shown below. However, the usual choices of elimination periods include:
[P1110] 0 days;
[P1111] 15 days
[P1112] 20 days;
[P1113] 30 days;
[P1114] 60 days;
[P1115] 90 days;
[P1116] 100 days;
[P1117] 180 days; and
[P1118] 365 days.
[P1119] Some insurers offer older applicants—usually those who are age 80 or older—a minimum elimination period of 90 days as a way to manage their long-term care insurance claims. Although the choice of elimination period for any individual ought to consider their financial ability to self-insure a part of the risk, some age 65 and older applicants choose a 20-day or 100-day elimination period to coincide with Medicare’s skilled nursing care coverage.

[P1126] 6.17.3 Grace Periods for Premium Payment
[P1127] Insurers generally have a vested interest in keeping their policies in force. For that reason, they provide a period following the due-date of the premium during which the insured may pay the premium without penalty or lapse. Usually, that grace period is 30 days long. The effective grace period for qualified long-term care insurance policies, however, is longer.
[P1128] A qualified long-term care insurance policy must meet the requirements of IRC §7702B. One of those requirements relates to unintentional lapse, wherein a qualified long-term care insurance policy must meet the requirements of §8 of the NAIC model regulation. The portion of that section of the model regulation that impacts the grace period reads as follows:
[P1129] “Unintentional lapse. Each insurer offering long-term care insurance shall, as a protection against unintentional lapse, comply with the following:
[P1130] 1.
[P1131] c.   Lapse or termination for nonpayment of premium. No individual long-term care policy or certificate shall lapse or be terminated for nonpayment of premium unless the insurer, at least thirty days before the effective date of the lapse or termination, has given notice to the insured and to those persons designated pursuant to subdivision a, at the address provided by the insured for purposes of receiving notice of lapse or termination. Notice shall be given by first-class United States mail, postage prepaid, and notice may not be given until thirty days after a premium is due and unpaid. Notice shall be deemed to have been given as of five days after the date of mailing.”
[P1132] The effect of this requirement for notice to the insured at least 30 days before the effective date of lapse is to extend the 30 day grace period to 65 days. Typically, an insurer would mail the notice of its intent to lapse the policy for nonpayment of premiums at the end of the usual 30-day grace period. Five days after mailing that notice, the insurer can assume the notice has been received by the insured. Thirty days after the notice is deemed to have been received, the insurer may terminate the policy. We need simply to add each of these periods together to arrive at the 65-day requirement.
[P1133] 6.17.4 Long-term Care Policy Free Look Provision
[P1134] The free-look provision permits an applicant to return a newly-issued insurance policy to the insurer within a specified period and obtain a return of their entire premium. In the case of a life insurance policy that free-look period is normally 10 days, although it may be longer in certain states if the policy was issued as replacement.
[P1135] In qualified long-term care insurance policies the free-look period, within which the insured may return the policy for a refund of premiums, is 30 days. The free-look period begins when the policy is delivered to the insured.
[P1136] 6.17.5 Long-term Care Policy Renewability Provision
[P1137] Qualified long-term care insurance policies must contain a provision relating to the policies renewability. A qualified long-term care insurance policy must be either:
[P1138] Guaranteed renewable; or
[P1139] Noncancellable.
[P1140] A policy is guaranteed renewable if the insured has the right to continue the policy in force by timely payment of premiums, and the insurer may not cancel the coverage or change its terms unilaterally. In a guaranteed renewable policy, the insurer retains the right to increase premiums on a class basis.
[P1141] A policy is noncancellable if the insured has the right to continue the policy in force by timely payment of premiums, and the insurer may not:
[P1142] Cancel a coverage;
[P1143] Change the terms of the coverage unilaterally; or
[P1144] Increase the premiums.
[P1145] Because a guaranteed renewable provision enables an insurer to increase the premiums for all insureds in the same class if its claims experience justifies such an increase, guaranteed renewable long-term care insurance policies are generally less expensive than otherwise identical noncancellable long-term care insurance policies.
[P1146] The language in the NAIC model regulation concerning the required renewability provision for qualified long-term care insurance policies reads as follows:
[P1147] “4. Terms Under Which the Policy OR Certificate May Be Continued in Force or Discontinued.
[P1148] a. [For long-term care health insurance policies or certificates describe one of the following permissible policy renewability provisions:
[P1149] (1)  Policies and certificates that are guaranteed renewable shall contain the following statement:]

This means you have the right, subject to the terms of your policy [certificate], to continue this policy as long as you pay your premiums on time. [Company Name] cannot change any of the terms of your policy on its own, except that, in the future, IT MAY INCREASE THE PREMIUM YOU PAY.
[P1151] [Policies and certificates that are noncancellable shall contain the following statement:]

This means that you have the right, subject to the terms of your policy, to continue this policy as long as you pay your premiums on time. [Company Name] cannot change any of the terms of your policy on its own and cannot change the premium you currently pay. However, if your policy contains an inflation protection feature where you choose to increase your benefits, [Company Name] may increase your premium at that time for those additional benefits.”
