[P1158] 6.17.6 Long-term Care Policy Reinstatement Provision
[P1159] Reinstatement of a long-term care policy after lapse generally requires the insured to submit an application for reinstatement and provide evidence of insurability along with any required premium. If the policy is reinstated, it will normally cover only those losses due to injuries sustained or conditions that began after the date of reinstatement.
[P1160] However, when a qualified long-term care policy lapses due to nonpayment of premium at a time when the insured was cognitively impaired or suffering from a loss of functional capacity before expiration of the grace period, the insured must be permitted to reinstate the policy within five months following its termination. The requirements to reinstate the long-term care insurance policy are:
[P1161] Furnishing proof of cognitive impairment or loss of functional capacity on the date of termination; and
[P1162] Payment of all unpaid, overdue premiums.
[P1163] In such a case, policy coverage is treated as though the policy never lapsed. Accordingly, it will cover losses sustained between the date of lapse and date of reinstatement. The provision in the NAIC model regulation requiring such a reinstatement provision is as shown in the following text:
[P1164] “Unintentional lapse. Each insurer offering long-term care insurance shall, as a protection against unintentional lapse, comply with the following:
[P1165] 1.
[P1166] 2.   Reinstatement. a long-term care insurance policy or certificate shall include a provision that provides for reinstatement of coverage, in the event of lapse if the insurer is provided proof that the policyholder or certificate holder was cognitively impaired or had a loss of functional capacity before the grace period contained in the policy expired. This option shall be available to the insured if requested within five months after termination and shall allow for the collection of past-due premium, when appropriate. The standard of proof of cognitive impairment or loss of functional capacity shall not be more stringent than the benefit eligibility criteria on cognitive impairment or the loss of functional capacity contained in the policy and certificate.”
[P1167] Although the NAIC model regulation mandates reinstatement of a qualified long-term care insurance policy upon request in the case of cognitive impairment or loss of functional capacity within five months following lapse, an insurer may elect to provide such reinstatement over a longer period.

[P1173] 6.17.7 Non-Duplication of Long-term Care Insurance Benefits
[P1174] Insurers issue insurance policies containing non-duplication of benefits provisions in order to avoid the possibility that a claimant will profit from a claim. A qualified long-term care insurance policy must not pay or reimburse expenses that are incurred for services or items to the extent they are reimbursable under Medicare or would be reimbursable except for any deductible or applicable coinsurance. Long-term care insurance policies rely on a non-duplication of benefits provision to exclude treatment in a government facility or treatment for which benefits would be payable under:
[P1175] Medicare;
[P1176] Workers’ compensation or similar occupational disease law; or
[P1177] Other government programs.
[P1178] The language of the NAIC model regulation permitting the non-duplication of benefits provision is as follows:
[P1179] “Limitations and exclusions. A policy may not be delivered or issued for delivery in this state as long-term care insurance if the policy limits or excludes coverage by type of illness, treatment, medical condition, or accident, except as follows:
[P1181] e.   Treatment provided in a government facility, unless otherwise required by law, services for which benefits are available under Medicare or other governmental program, except Medicaid, any state or federal workers’ compensation, employer’s liability or occupational disease law, or any motor vehicle no-fault law, services provided by a member of the covered person’s immediate family, and services for which no charge is normally made in the absence of insurance;
[P1183] g.   In the case of a qualified long-term care insurance contract, expenses for services or items to the extent that the expenses are reimbursable under title XVIII of the Social Security Act or would be so reimbursable but for the application of a deductible or coinsurance amount;”
[P1184] 6.17.8 Long-term Care Policy Nonforfeiture Requirements
[P1185] IRC §7702B contains certain consumer protection provisions. One of those provisions, contained in §7702B(g)(4) shown below, relates to a qualified long-term care insurance policy’s nonforfeiture requirements.
[P1186] The Code provision requires that an insurer offer a nonforfeiture provision to the policyowner. Since a nonforfeiture provision increases both the insurer’s risk and the insured’s premium cost, it is an optional benefit the insured may accept or reject. The substance of the nonforfeiture provision will be explained when optional long-term care insurance policy benefits are addressed later in this chapter.

[P1188] 6.17.9 Coordination of Long-term Care Insurance Benefits
[P1189] Insurers routinely reserve the right to reduce the benefits payable under their long-term care insurance policies when they are also paying benefits for the same long-term care services under other long-term care insurance policies issued by them. This reduction of benefits is made under a policy provision normally called Other Coverage With Us, Coordination of Benefits, or other similar title. The reduction in benefits is made when the total benefits that would be paid by the insurer under all long-term care insurance policies issued by it for covered services would exceed the actual cost incurred by the insured for those services.
[P1190] For example, suppose an insured owned a long-term care insurance policy that paid a daily nursing home benefit of $100. A few years later, realizing that daily benefit would be inadequate to meet nursing home costs, the insured purchased an additional policy providing a daily nursing home benefit of $200. If the insured’s actual cost for subsequent covered nursing home care amounted to $250 per day, the insurer would only pay the actual costs ($250) rather than the combined policy benefits ($300).

[P1196] 6.17.10 Long-term Care Incontestability Requirements
[P1197] A contract is nothing more than an agreement enforceable at law. In other words, a party to a contract can bring a lawsuit and demand that the other party to the contract live up to the terms of the contract on which they agreed.
[P1198] Although contract law imposes many rights and obligations on parties to a contract, two basic tenets of contract law need to be borne in mind to better understand the incontestable clauses that are a normal part of insurance contracts. Those basic contract law principles are:
[P1199] Fraud in the formation of a contract renders the contract voidable by the innocent party to the contract; and
[P1200] Parties to a contract are not permitted immunity from the consequences of their own fraud.
[P1201] Fraud, in the case of a contract, involves intentional misrepresentation. Therefore, if John makes an intentional misstatement concerning the subject of his contract with Phil, Phil is free to declare the contract void and without effect. Suppose, for example, John told Phil that he would receive a new cell phone if he would contract for one year of telephone service provided by John’s company. Several months into the agreed-upon telephone service period, it becomes clear to Phil that John has misrepresented the contract and has no intention of providing the new cell phone. Since John has fraudulently misrepresented the agreement, Phil can unilaterally declare the contract without force or effect. In our example, the contract would remain in force if Phil had not exercised his right to void it.
[P1202] John cannot rely on the contract he fraudulently entered into with Phil to protect him from the consequences of his fraud. The immediate consequence of that fraud is the loss of revenue he would have received for the telephone service if the contract remained in force.
[P1203] An insurance policy is a contract between a policyowner and an insurer, and, for the most part, the usual rules concerning contracts apply to insurance policies. For example, there must be an offer, an acceptance and some type of consideration. In an insurance policy, that “consideration” is the policyowner’s premium payment.
[P1204] An incontestability provision significantly affects the normal contract rights of parties to an insurance contract with respect to the innocent party’s right to void it. In the case of a long-term care insurance policy, the right of an insurer to void the contract or deny an otherwise valid claim depends on:
[P1205] The duration of the policy; and
[P1206] The nature of the misrepresentation.
[P1207] If the policy has been in force for fewer than six months, the insurer may rescind the policy or deny an otherwise valid claim by showing that the misrepresentation is material to its acceptance of the risk.
[P1208] If the policy has been in force for at least six months but less than two years, the insurer may rescind the policy or deny an otherwise valid claim by showing that the misrepresentation:
[P1209] Is material to its acceptance of the risk; and
[P1210] Pertains to the condition for which the insured is seeking benefits.
[P1211] If the policy has been in force for at least two years, the insurer may contest the policy by showing the:
[P1212] Insured knowingly and intentionally misrepresented certain facts; and
[P1213] Misrepresented facts where relevant and related to the insured’s health.
[P1214] In the event an insurer has paid an otherwise valid claim and subsequently rescinds the policy, the claim payments are not recoverable by the insurer.

[P1255] 7.0 Long-term Care Insurance Policy Benefits
[P1256] Although all qualified long-term care insurance policies must meet the requirements of IRC §7702B, they may differ from each other in many ways, including the particular benefits that are basic to the contract (rather than being offered as optional benefits by rider). While realizing these differences exist, we will consider the basic benefits normally included in a long-term care insurance policy.
[P1257] The benefits that are normally part of a basic long-term care insurance policy include:
[P1258] Benefits for confinement in a nursing home;
[P1259] Benefits for alternative care facilities, such as an assisted living facility;
[P1260] Benefits for community-based services, such as –
[P1261] Respite care,
[P1262] Hospice,
[P1263] Adult daycare, and
[P1264] Paid home care;
[P1265] Benefits for care advisory services;
[P1266] Bed reservation benefits;
[P1267] Waiver of premium benefits; and
[P1268] Extended benefits in the event of lapse while the insured is confined in a nursing home.
[P1269] Although long-term care insurance policies provide benefits for a wide range of services, they typically will not cover the following:
[P1270] Physicians charges;
[P1271] Hospital charges;
[P1272] Laboratory charges;
[P1273] Charges for medications or medical supplies;
[P1274] Charges for transportation; or
[P1275] Charges for items of comfort or entertainment.
[P1276] 7.1 Nursing Home Confinement Benefits
[P1277] The covered charges for which benefits are normally paid for nursing home confinement under a long-term care insurance policy include the insured’s:
[P1278] Room;
[P1279] Board; and
[P1280] Care such as –
[P1281] Skilled or intermediate nursing care,
[P1282] Custodial care, and
[P1283] Hospice care.
[P1284] To qualify as a nursing home for which such benefits may be payable, the following criteria must normally be met:
[P1285] Nursing care provided is performed by a nurse or under a nurse’s supervision;
[P1286] The nursing home employs at least one full-time nurse; and
[P1287] A nurse is available 24 hours each day, either –
[P1288] On duty, or
[P1289] On call.

[P1296] 7.2 Alternate Care Facility Benefits
[P1297] The covered charges for which benefits are normally paid under a long-term care insurance policy for treatment while confined in an alternate care facility include the insured’s:
[P1298] Room;
[P1299] Board; and
[P1300] Care appropriate to the type of facility, which may be -
[P1301] An assisted living facility;
[P1302] An Alzheimer’s facility; or
[P1303] A custodial care facility.
[P1304] We noted earlier that to be an alternate care facility it must provide ongoing care and related services to residents in a single location meeting the following criteria:
[P1305] It provides 24 hour-a-day care and services to support residents’ needs resulting from cognitive impairment or inability to perform ADLs;
[P1306] A trained employee ready to provide required care to residents is on duty at all times;
[P1307] It provides 3 meals each day and accommodates special dietary needs;
[P1308] If required by the state, it is licensed or accredited to provide such care;
[P1309] It has formal arrangements for physician or nurse services to provide emergency medical care; and
[P1310] It has established procedures and employs appropriate methods for handling and administering drugs and biologicals.
[P1312] 7.3 Benefits Payable for Community-Based Long-term Care Services
[P1313] Community-based long-term care services are those required by an individual needing long-term care that enable them to avoid or delay confinement in a nursing home or alternate care facility to receive such services. These community-based services generally include:
[P1314] Respite care;
[P1315] Home care;
[P1316] Adult daycare; and
[P1317] Hospice.
[P1318] The benefits payable depend on the type of community-based care and services provided.
[P1319] 7.3.1 Respite Care Benefits
[P1320] Insurers have a vested interest in promoting informal, i.e., unpaid, home care for someone in need of long-term care over institutionalization or some other type of paid care. The reason for their vested interest is clear: it costs them far less in claims than institutionalization. Accordingly, insurers offer a respite care benefit and generally make it easy for an insured to obtain it.
[P1321] Respite care, as we noted earlier, is care provided to a long-term-care recipient that is designed to relieve an unpaid caregiver of the burden of caring for them. Benefits for respite care are normally provided up to a maximum amount or for a maximum duration, depending on policy design, and are often available even though the policy’s elimination period has not been met. The benefits paid are normally limited to the actual charges incurred for respite care in a nursing home or assisted-living facility.

[P1332] 7.3.2 Home Care Benefits
[P1333] Long-term care benefits payable for paid care an insured receives at home are generally equal to the expenses incurred, up to the limits in the policy schedule, for care and support services. These eligible services normally include:
[P1334] Nursing services;
[P1335] Services of therapists, such as –
[P1336] Physical therapists,
[P1337] Occupational therapists,
[P1338] Respiratory therapists, and
[P1339] Speech therapists;
[P1340] Home health aide services; and
[P1341] Homemaker services.
[P1342] In addition to these homecare benefits that are usually paid up to the long-term care maximum benefit, certain other expenses incident to receiving care at home may also be payable up to a lesser maximum amount. These additional covered expenses may include any of the following, depending on the policy’s design:
[P1343] Costs for durable medical equipment that is rented or purchased;
[P1344] Costs for modifications made to the care-recipient’s home—installation of handrails, for example—to facilitate their ability to live safely and independently at home;
[P1345] Costs for an emergency medical response system to enable care-recipient to summon assistance in the event of a medical emergency; and
[P1346] Costs of providing caregiver training to informal caregivers.

[P1352] 7.3.3 Adult Daycare Benefits
[P1353] Adult daycare benefits are normally paid under the basic long-term care benefits provision and are usually equal to the actual costs of adult daycare limited, of course, by any policy maximums. As noted earlier, the services provided in adult daycare may vary substantially depending on the individual’s need and the abilities of caregivers.
[P1354] Accordingly, adult daycare may involve:
[P1355] Supervised social interaction;
[P1356] Supervised social interaction combined with medical care and therapy; or
[P1357] Specialized care for individuals with Alzheimer’s disease or other forms of dementia.
[P1358] The costs incurred for adult daycare vary with the range of services provided.
[P1359] 7.3.4 Hospice Care Benefits
[P1360] Hospice care benefits are generally paid under the policy’s basic long-term care insurance benefit for care received at home or in a separate facility. Although most hospice care is received at home, it may also be provided in:
[P1361] A nursing home;
[P1362] An assisted living facility;
[P1363] An adult daycare facility; or
[P1364] A hospice care facility.
[P1365] In order to be eligible to receive hospice care an insured must generally be certified by a physician as having a life expectancy of less than six months or 12 months, depending on the design of the long-term care insurance policy.
[P1366] 7.4 Care Advisory Services Benefits
[P1367] Care advisory services are long-term care assessment and planning services provided by a professional that are designed to:
[P1368] Assess an individual’s need for long-term care;
[P1369] Develop a long-term care services recommendation;
[P1370] Coordinate the delivery of long-term care;
[P1371] Monitor delivered long-term care services; and
[P1372] Periodically re-assess long-term care needs.
[P1373] These care advisory services are covered expenses under long-term care insurance policies. Depending on the policy design, the amount payable for such services may be subject to an annual maximum or may be borne entirely by the insurer.

[P1379] 7.5 Waiver of Premium Benefit
[P1380] Waiver of premium is a long-term care insurance policy benefit under which the insurer waives the premium for the policy. Policy premiums are generally waived when the insured is receiving long-term care insurance benefits and the policy’s elimination period has been satisfied.
[P1381] The waiver of premium benefit normally begins to waive premiums as soon as the policy’s elimination period has been satisfied and ends when no further long-term care insurance benefits are payable.
[P1382] 7.6 Extension of Benefits in Event of Lapse
[P1383] When an insured is being cared for in a nursing home but has not begun to receive long-term care insurance benefits because the policy’s elimination period has not yet been satisfied, the waiver of premium benefit may not have begun to waive the insured’s premiums. In such a case, the premiums are due and payable; if the premiums are not paid within the grace period, the policy will lapse.
[P1384] Qualified long-term care insurance policies must include a provision that continues certain policy benefits in the case of lapse in such situations, provided the insured is continuously confined in a nursing home. The applicable policy provision provides that nursing home benefits will continue beyond the date of lapse until the earliest of the:
[P1385] Insured’s discharge from the nursing home;
[P1386] Date on which the policy's nursing home benefits are exhausted; and
[P1387] Insured’s death.
[P1388] This requirement is included in the NAIC model regulation and states:
[P1389] “Extension of benefits. Termination of long-term care insurance shall be without prejudice to any benefits payable for institutionalization if the institutionalization began while the long-term care insurance was in force and continues without interruption after termination. The extension of benefits beyond the period the long-term care insurance was in force may be limited to the duration of the benefit period, if any, or to payment of the maximum benefits and may be subject to any policy waiting period, and all other applicable provisions of the policy.”
[P1390] 7.7 Bed Reservation Benefit
[P1391] Obtaining a place in a nursing home or assisted-living facility sometimes requires an individual to wait several months or longer. So, it is important that someone confined in a nursing home or assisted living facility who leaves the institution for a temporary period—a brief stay in hospital, a trip to visit relatives, or for some other reason—be able to return.
[P1392] Because it is important that care-recipients be able to continue their required care in the same institution, long-term care insurance policies normally provide a bed reservation benefit. A typical bed reservation benefit in a long-term care insurance policy provides that benefits will continue for a limited period to the nursing home or assisted-living facility in which the insured was confined if the insured’s stay in the facility is interrupted for any reason. The duration of that limited period may be as long as 60 days each year.

[P1398] 7.8 Survivorship Benefit for Survivor of Insured Couple
[P1399] When one member of a couple owns long-term care insurance, it is not unusual for the other member also to own comparable coverage either under the same policy or under different policies issued by the same insurer. Insurers may offer a paid-up benefit for the survivor of such a couple, either as part of basic coverage or as an optional rider, upon the death of one of them.
[P1400] Under a common survivorship benefit, the surviving member of the couple would pay no further premiums for long-term care insurance. In order for the surviving member to have their policy deemed paid-up, several criteria must ordinarily be met:
[P1401] The policies must have been in force at least 10 years; and
[P1402] No long-term care insurance benefits were paid under the policy or policies for at least 10 consecutive years.
[P1403] 7.9 Basic Long-term Care Policy Exclusions and Limitations
[P1404] The NAIC model regulation, which is specifically referenced in IRC §7702B, prohibits long-term care insurance policies that exclude coverage on bases other than specified in the model regulation. According to the NAIC model regulation, a long-term care insurance policy may not limit or exclude coverage by type of illness, treatment, medical condition, or accident, with certain specified exceptions.
[P1405] The NAIC model regulation specifies the following for which a long-term care insurance policy may limit or exclude coverage:
[P1406] Preexisting conditions or diseases;
[P1407] Mental or nervous disorders;
[P1408] Alcoholism and drug addiction;
[P1409] Illness, treatment, or medical condition arising out of –
[P1410] Declared or undeclared war,
[P1411] Participation in a felony, riot, or insurrection,
[P1412] Service in the Armed Forces,
[P1413] Suicide, attempted suicide, or intentionally self-inflicted injury, or
[P1414] Aviation;
[P1415] Treatment provided in a government facility;
[P1416] Services for which benefits are available under –
[P1417] Medicare or government program, other than Medicaid, or
[P1418] any state or federal workers’ compensation, employer's liability or occupational disease law, or motor vehicle no-fault law;
[P1419] Services provided by a member of the covered person’s immediate family;
[P1420] Services for which no charge is normally made in the absence of insurance;
[P1421] Expenses for services or items available or paid under another long-term care insurance or health insurance policy; and
[P1422] In the case of a qualified long-term care insurance contract, expenses for services or items to the extent they are reimbursable under title XVIII of the Social Security Act or would be reimbursable but for the application of a deductible or coinsurance amount.

[P1429] 7.9.1 Preexisting Conditions Exclusions Limited Under Model Act
[P1430] Non-group long-term care insurance policies, although permitted to impose preexisting conditions exclusions, are restricted insofar as the:
[P1431] Definition of “preexisting condition"; and
[P1432] Period of time for which coverage for a preexisting condition may be excluded.
[P1433] The maximum preexisting exclusion under the NAIC model act is a 6 X 6 exclusion. Specifically, Section 6C of the NAIC model act requires that a non-group long-term care insurance policy that excludes coverage for preexisting conditions must not use a definition of “preexisting condition” that is more restrictive than
[P1434] medical advice or treatment recommended by, or received from, a provider of health-care services, within six months preceding the effective date of coverage
[P1435] It further stipulates that coverage for a preexisting condition may be excluded only if the loss or confinement begins within six months following the effective date of coverage.
[P1436] The NAIC model act language relating to long-term care insurance preexisting exclusions is shown below:
[P1437] Preexisting condition
[P1438] (1) No long-term care insurance policy or certificate other than a policy or certificate thereunder issued to a group as defined in Section 4E(1) shall use a definition of “preexisting condition” that is more restrictive than the following: Preexisting condition means a condition for which medical advice or treatment was recommended by, or received from a provider of healthcare services, within six (6) months preceding the effective date of coverage of an insured person.
[P1439] (2) No long-term care insurance policy or certificate other than a policy or certificate thereunder issued to a group as defined in Section 4E(1) may exclude coverage for a loss or confinement that is the result of a preexisting condition unless the loss or confinement begins within six (6) months following the effective date of coverage of an insured person.
[P1440] (3) The commissioner may extend the limitation periods set forth in Sections 6C(1) and (2) above as to specific age group categories in specific policy forms upon findings that the extension is in the best interest of the public.
[P1441] (4) The definition of “preexisting condition” does not prohibit an insurer from using an application form designed to elicit the complete health history of an applicant, and, on the basis of the answers on that application, from underwriting in accordance with that insurer’s established underwriting standards. Unless otherwise provided in the policy or certificate, a preexisting condition, regardless of whether it is disclosed on the application, need not be covered until the waiting period described in Section 6C(2) expires. No long-term care insurance policy or certificate may exclude or use waivers or riders of any kind to exclude, limit or reduce coverage or benefits for specifically named or described preexisting diseases or physical conditions beyond the waiting period described in Section 6C(2).
[P1442] 7.9.1.1 Replacement Cannot Extend Preexisting Conditions Limitations or Probationary Periods
[P1443] In some cases, replacement of an existing long-term care insurance policy with a new long-term care insurance policy may be appropriate. The NAIC model regulation addresses the treatment of preexisting conditions limitations and probationary periods in such replacement policies.
[P1444] If a long-term care insurance policy replaces an existing long-term care insurance policy, the replacing insurer must waive any time periods that apply to preexisting conditions and probationary periods in the new long-term care insurance policy for similar benefits to the extent those time periods were satisfied under the replaced policy. An example may serve to clarify.
[P1445] Suppose Brenda purchased a long-term care insurance policy containing a preexisting conditions exclusion that excluded care resulting from a specific condition for a period of six months. Four months later, Brenda replaced that policy with a new long-term care insurance policy containing a similar six-month preexisting conditions exclusion applicable to her condition. Since Brenda had already satisfied four months of that exclusion under the original policy, the new policy may only impose a maximum two-month preexisting conditions exclusion applicable to that condition.
[P1446] 7.9.2	 Continuation or conversion.
[P1448] The NAIC Model Regulation provides that group long-term care insurance provide covered individuals with a basis for continuation or conversion of coverage.
[P1450] "A basis for continuation of coverage" means a policy provision which maintains coverage under the existing group policy when such coverage would otherwise terminate and which is subject only to the continued timely payment of premium when due. Group policies that restrict the provision of benefits and services to, or contain incentives to use certain providers or facilities may provide continuation benefits that are substantially equivalent to the benefits of the existing group policy. The commissioner shall make a determination as to the substantial equivalency of benefits, and in doing so, shall take into consideration the differences between managed and nonmanaged plans, including provider system arrangements, service availability, benefit levels, and administrative complexity.
[P1452] "A basis for conversion of coverage" means a policy provision that an individual whose coverage under the group policy would otherwise terminate or has been terminated for any reason, including discontinuance of the group policy in its entirety or with respect to an insurance class, and who has been continuously insured under the group policy (and any group policy which it replaced), for at least six months immediately prior to termination, shall be entitled to the issuance of a converted policy by the insurer under whose group policy they are covered, without evidence of insurability.
[P1454] "Converted policy" means an individual policy of long-term care insurance providing benefits identical to or benefits determined by the commissioner to be substantially equivalent to or in excess of those provided under the group policy from which conversion is made. Where the group policy from which conversion is made restricts the provision of benefits and services to, or contains incentives to use, certain providers or facilities the commissioner, in making a determination as to the substantial equivalency of benefits, shall take into consideration the differences between managed and nonmanaged plans, including, but not limited to, provider system arrangements, service availability, benefit levels, and administrative complexity.  Written application for the converted policy must be made and the first premium due, if any, must be paid as directed by the insurer not later than thirty-one days after termination of coverage under the group policy. The converted policy must be issued effective on the day following the termination of coverage under the group policy, and must be renewable annually.
[P1456] Unless the group policy from which conversion is made replaced previous group coverage, the premium for the converted policy must be calculated on the basis of the insured’s age at inception of coverage under the group policy from which the conversion is made. Where the group policy from which conversion is made replaced previous group coverage, the premium for the converted policy must be calculated on the basis of the insured’s age at inception of coverage under the group policy replaced.
[P1458] Continuation of coverage or issuance of a converted policy shall be mandatory, except where:
[P1460] (1) Termination of group coverage resulted from an individual’s failure to make any required payment of premium or contribution when due; or
[P1462] (2) The terminating coverage is replaced not later than thirty-one days after termination by group coverage effective on the day following the termination of coverage:
[P1464] (a) Providing benefits identical to or benefits determined by the commissioner to be substantially equivalent to or in excess of those provided by the terminating coverage; and
[P1466] (b) The premium for which is calculated in a manner consistent with the requirements of subdivision f.
[P1468] Notwithstanding any other provision of this section, a converted policy issued to an individual who at the time of conversion is covered by another long-term care insurance policy which provides benefits on the basis of incurred expenses, may contain a provision which results in a reduction of benefits payable if the benefits provided under the additional coverage, together with the full benefits provided by the converted policy, would result in payment of more than one hundred percent of incurred expenses.
[P1469] Such provision shall only be included in the converted policy if the converted policy also provides for a premium decrease or refund which reflects the reduction in benefits payable.
[P1471] The converted policy may provide that the benefits payable under the converted policy, together with the benefits payable under the group policy from which conversion is made, shall not exceed those that would have been payable had the individual’s coverage under the group policy remained in force and effect.
[P1473] Notwithstanding any other provision of this section, any insured individual whose eligibility for group long-term care coverage is based upon their relationship to another person shall be entitled to continuation of coverage under the group policy upon termination of the qualifying relationship by death or dissolution of marriage.

[P1476] A description of the principal benefits and coverage provided in the policy;
[P1477] A statement of the principal exclusions, reductions and limitations contained in the policy; and
[P1478] (3)	A statement that the group master policy determines governing contractual
provisions.
[P1480] 7.9.4 Limitations on Prior Hospitalization or Institutionalization Requirements
[P1481] The NAIC model act also imposes limitations with respect to a requirement that an insured receive prior hospitalization or institutionalization in order to be eligible for long-term care insurance benefits. In this regard, the Act specifies that long-term care insurance policies must not condition eligibility for:
[P1482] Any long-term care insurance benefits on an insured’s prior hospitalization;
[P1483] Long-term care insurance benefits for care provided in an institutional setting on an insured’s prior receipt of a higher level of institutional care; or
[P1484] Any long-term care insurance benefits—other than waiver of premium, post-confinement, post-acute care or recuperative benefits—on a prior institutional requirement.
[P1485] Furthermore, the Act specifies certain disclosure requirements and limits applicable to post-confinement, post-acute care or recuperative benefits. With respect to disclosure, any long-term care insurance policy that contains post-confinement, post-acute-care or recuperative benefits must set out in a separate, clearly-labeled paragraph of the policy a section entitled “Limitations or Conditions on Eligibility for Benefits” in which any such limitations or conditions are detailed, including any required number of days of confinement.
[P1486] The limits imposed by the Act concerning post-confinement, post-acute care or recuperative benefits relate to:
[P1487] The maximum duration of any required institutional stay; and
[P1488] The minimum period following any required institutional stay in which admission to a facility for the same or a related condition must take place.
[P1489] According to the Act, a policy may not require a prior institutional stay longer than 30 days. In addition, the Act requires that the period within which admission to a facility for the same or a related condition must occur must not be less than 30 days.
[P1490] The language of the Act concerning prior hospitalization and institutionalization is as shown below:
[P1491] “Prior hospitalization/institutionalization”
[P1492] (1) No long-term care insurance policy may be delivered or issued for delivery in this state if the policy:
[P1493] (a) Conditions eligibility for any benefits on a prior hospitalization requirement;
[P1494] (b) Conditions eligibility for benefits provided in an institutional care setting on the receipt of a higher level of institutional care; or
[P1495] (c) Conditions eligibility for any benefits other than waiver of premium, post-confinement, post-acute care or recuperative benefits on a prior institutionalization requirement.
[P1496] (2) (a) A long-term care insurance policy containing post-confinement, post-acute care or recuperative benefits shall clearly label in a separate paragraph of the policy or certificate entitled “Limitations or Conditions on Eligibility for Benefits” such limitations or conditions, including any required number of days of confinement.
[P1497] (b) A long-term care insurance policy or rider that conditions eligibility of non-institutional benefits on the prior receipt of institutional care shall not require a prior institutional stay of more than thirty (30) days.
[P1498] (3) No long-term care insurance policy or rider that provides benefits only following institutionalization shall condition such benefits upon admission to a facility for the same or related conditions within a period of less than thirty (30) days after discharge from the institution.

[P1528] 8.0 Optional Benefits Provided by Rider
[P1529] As noted earlier, some insurers may elect to provide certain benefits as part of their basic policy or as optional benefits that may be purchased for an additional premium. Bearing in mind that some variation will inevitably exist between insurers, we will now look at long-term care insurance benefits that are normally provided as optional benefits.
[P1530] In the discussion of optional benefits, we will examine:
[P1531] Shared coverage benefits;
[P1532] Inflation coverage benefits;
[P1533] Purchase option benefits;
[P1534] Nonforfeiture benefits;
[P1535] Family care benefits;
[P1536] Restoration of benefits; and
[P1537] Return of premium benefits.
[P1538] 8.1 Shared Coverage Benefits
[P1539] Some insurers may agree to cover two insureds—usually, but not necessarily, spouses—under the same policy or may offer the two insureds separate identical policies in which each insured has a right to access benefits under either policy. When the two insureds are covered under the same policy, the provisions relative to shared coverage are basic policy provisions. Alternatively, when the two insureds are covered under separate policies the shared coverage provisions are added under an optional additional benefit rider.
[P1540] Regardless of whether the shared coverage provisions are in the basic policy or are added by rider, the same features generally apply. Those shared coverage features address:
[P1541] The policy or policies lifetime maximum;
[P1542] Operation of the waiver of premium benefit;
[P1543] Death of one of the insureds; and
[P1544] Separation or divorce of the two insureds.
[P1546] Review Question:  True or False

[P1548] True Your answer is correct. Spouses may be covered by the same insurer under the same policy, or two separate identical policies in which each insured has a right to access benefits under either policy.

[P1550] 8.1.1 Shared Maximum Benefits and Benefit Restoration
[P1551] Long-term care insurance policies normally specify a maximum benefit amount, except in the case of their providing lifetime benefits. When coverage is shared by two insureds, one of the insureds may require long-term care for an extended period and, thereby, exhaust the maximum benefits provided under the policy.
[P1552] In such a case, benefits may be restored—in whole or in part, depending on the policy or rider provision—provided neither insured has been eligible for long-term care insurance benefits under the policy or policies for a specified period. The period during which neither insured must not be eligible for long-term care insurance benefits may be as short as 6 months or as long as 2 years.
[P1553] 8.1.2 Waiver of Premium Benefit Varies Depending on Shared Benefit Design
[P1554] The Waiver of Premium benefit usually operates to waive the premium when the policy’s elimination period has been satisfied and the insured is receiving long-term care insurance benefits. In the case of shared coverage, the benefit operates differently depending on whether both insureds are covered under two policies or one policy.
[P1555] When both insureds are covered under a single long-term care insurance policy one insured’s eligibility for waiver of premium benefits will generally cause the entire premium for both insureds to be waived. In contrast, when the insureds are each covered under their own policy the eligibility of one insured for the waiver of premium benefit will cause the premium for that policy to be waived; however, the premium for the other policy would not be waived unless the other insured was also eligible for the benefit.
[P1556] 8.1.3 Death of a Shared Coverage Insured
[P1557] When one of the insureds dies, the surviving insured may continue the shared coverage. If the shared coverage was provided under two policies, any remaining benefits under the deceased's policy are transferred to the surviving insured’s policy. The surviving insured’s policy premium does not change as a result of the benefit transfer.
[P1558] When shared coverage for two insureds is provided under a single long-term care insurance policy, the premium for the surviving insured’s policy is generally increased somewhat (from the premium cost formerly attributable to that insured only) to account for the cost of administering the policy, a cost that had previously been apportioned between the two insureds. The maximum benefit under the policy is not changed.

[P1569] 8.1.4 Effect of Divorce or Separation on Single-policy Shared Coverage
[P1570] When a couple insured under a single long-term care insurance policy providing shared coverage separate or divorce, they may choose to:
[P1571] Maintain the shared long-term care insurance coverage under the same policy; or
[P1572] Exchange the shared policy for individual long-term care insurance policies.
[P1573] If the separated or divorced couple chooses to continue the shared coverage, they need do nothing; the shared coverage will simply continue. However, if they choose to exchange the shared policy for individual long-term care insurance policies certain requirements may apply. Normally, in order to qualify for an exchange to individual policies:
[P1574] Both insureds must request the exchange;
[P1575] The nonforfeiture benefit is not in effect under the policy, nor are premiums being waived under the waiver of premium benefit; and
[P1576] Neither insured is eligible for benefit payments under the policy.
[P1577] If the insureds qualify for the requested exchange, each policy issued:
[P1578] Will have one-half the lifetime maximum benefit that was applicable to the joint policy; and
[P1579] Will be deemed to have paid one half the total non-restored benefits paid under the joint policy.
[P1580] The premiums for each of the individual policies issued as an exchange will be based on each insured’s issue age and underwriting classification on the date of issue of the joint policy.

[P1659] 8.3 Long-term Care Insurance Policy Inflation Coverage
[P1660] In order for a long-term care insurance policy to be qualified under IRC §7702B, the insurer selling the policy must offer the policyowner inflation protection at the time they purchase the policy as provided under the NAIC model regulation. Although the inflation protection offered may provide greater benefits, it must be no less favorable than one of the following:
[P1661] An inflation protection benefit under which the policy’s benefit levels increase each year at a compounded rate of 5%;
[P1662] An inflation protection benefit that guarantees the insured the right to increase benefit levels periodically without providing evidence of insurability or health status; or
[P1663] A policy that covers a specified percentage of actual or reasonable charges without specifying an indemnity amount or limit.
[P1664] Furthermore, in order for the policyowner to avoid inclusion of an inflation protection benefit in a purchased policy, they must positively reject the benefit. If the insurer does not obtain a rejection of the inflation protection benefit signed by the policyowner, an inflation protection benefit providing an increase of benefit levels at a compounded rate of 5% will be included in the policy.
[P1665] Insurers are required to include a 20-year graphic comparison in their outlines of coverage of the benefit levels in a long-term care insurance policy that increases benefits with one that does not. In addition, the outline of coverage must indicate any anticipated premium increases or additional premiums to pay for the benefit increases.
[P1666] The language that appears in the NAIC model regulation with respect to the requirement to offer inflation protection is shown below:
[P1667] “Requirement to offer inflation protection”
[P1668] 1.   No insurer may offer a long-term care insurance policy unless the insurer also offers to the policyholder in addition to any other inflation protection the option to purchase a policy that provides for benefit levels to increase with benefit maximums or reasonable durations which are meaningful to account for reasonably anticipated increases in the costs of long-term care services covered by the policy. Insurers must offer to each policyholder, at the time of purchase, the option to purchase a policy with an inflation protection feature no less favorable than one of the following:
[P1669] a.   Increases benefit levels annually in a manner so that the increases are compounded annually at a rate not less than five percent;
[P1670] b.   Guarantees the insured individual the right to periodically increase benefit levels without providing evidence of insurability or health status so long as the option for the previous period has not been declined. The amount of the additional benefit shall be no less than the difference between the existing policy benefit and that benefit compounded annually at a rate of at least five percent for the period beginning with the purchase of the existing benefit and extending until the year in which the offer is made; or
[P1671] c.   Covers a specified percentage of actual or reasonable charges and does not include a maximum specified indemnity amount or limit.
[P1672] 2.   Where the policy is issued to a group, the required offer noted above shall be made to the group policyholder; except, if the policy is issued to a group otherwise defined by the Department of Insurance, other than to a continuing care retirement community, the offering shall be made to each proposed certificate holder.
[P1673] 3.   The offer noted above shall not be required of life insurance policies or riders containing accelerated long-term care benefits.

[P1684] 8.3.1 Inflation Protection May Provide Simple or Compound Benefit Increases
[P1685] Inflation protection benefits normally provide benefit increases each year—whether or not the insured is on claim—at no increase in premium at the time the benefit increase becomes effective. (Premiums for the inflation protection benefit rider, however, may be substantial.)
[P1686] Insurers normally provide inflation protection benefits that increase the policy’s benefit levels each year on a:
[P1687] Simple basis; or
[P1688] Compounded basis
[P1689] and apply to both the daily benefit and the maximum amount. The benefit level increases applied to the daily benefit may be the same or different than the increases applied to the maximum amount.
[P1690] In certain insurers, the choices available may include:
[P1691] An annual simple increase of 5% of the original benefit applied to both the daily benefit and the maximum amount;
[P1692] An annual compound increase of 5% applied to both the daily benefit and the maximum amount; and
[P1693] An annual compound increase of 5% applied to the daily benefit and an annual compound increase of 3% applied to the maximum amount.
[P1694] We can see the difference in the resulting benefit levels, assuming a long-term care insurance policy was issued with a $200 daily benefit and a $144,000 maximum amount under each of these approaches below:
[P1695] Under a 5% simple inflation protection benefit, the benefits in the first 10 policy years would be –
[P1696] Under a 5% compound inflation protection benefit applicable to the daily benefit and the maximum amount, the benefits in the first 10 policy years would be –
[P1697] Under a 5% compound inflation protection benefit applicable to the daily benefit and a 3% compound inflation protection benefit applicable to the maximum amount, the benefits in the first 10 policy years would be –
[P1698] Although we can see some difference in the benefit levels under each of these inflation protection approaches, the differences are magnified significantly at longer durations.

[P1706] 8.3.2 Purchase Option Benefit as Inflation Protection
[P1707] One of the attractive features of the inflation protection benefits we just looked at is that the annual increases in benefit levels do not require a commensurate increase in the premiums. In fact, the benefit increases do not affect the premium at all. An unattractive element of these inflation protection benefits is that the rider providing them tends to be fairly expensive.
[P1708] The guaranteed option to purchase additional benefits periodically without the need to furnish evidence of insurability also provides some protection against inflation. Under a typical guaranteed purchase option rider, the policyowner has the right to purchase additional long-term care insurance benefits on the third policy anniversary and on any subsequent third anniversary thereafter.
[P1709] The amount of additional benefits that may be purchased on each third policy anniversary is usually equal to a specified percentage of the original daily benefit amount. Accordingly, a policyowner exercising their right to purchase additional benefits may purchase additional benefits equal to 5%, 10%, or 15% of the original benefit. The maximum amount is also increased by the same percentage.
[P1710] Although the policyowner need not exercise the option right on every option date, their failure to exercise an option:
[P1711] Will cause that option to be lost forever; but
[P1712] Will not affect the availability of any future options.
[P1713] As we can see, if the policyowner exercises the right to increase the daily benefit by 15% every three years, the net result will be somewhat similar to a 5% simple inflation protection benefit.
[P1714] Under the purchase option approach to providing protection against inflation, the rider providing the benefit is much less expensive than either the simple or compound 5% inflation riders. However, unlike the 5% inflation riders the increased benefits purchased under the guaranteed purchase option involve additional premiums. Those additional premiums are based on the insured’s age on the option date and the premium rates in effect at that time. The right to purchase additional coverage under the guaranteed purchase option rider generally ceases when the insured reaches age 91.
[P1715] 8.4 Nonforfeiture Benefits
[P1716] We noted earlier that under IRC §7702B insurers are required to offer long-term care insurance policy insureds a nonforfeiture benefit. The Code section states that:
[P1717] The nonforfeiture provisionshall meet the following requirements:
[P1718] The nonforfeiture provision shall be appropriately captioned.
[P1719] The nonforfeiture provision shall provide for a benefit available in the event of a default in the payment of any premiums and the amount of the benefit may be adjusted subsequent to being initially granted only as necessary to reflect changes in claims, persistency, and interest as reflected in changes in rates for premium paying contracts approved by the appropriate State regulatory agency for the same contract form.
[P1720] The nonforfeiture provision shall provide at least one of the following:
[P1721] Reduced paid-up insurance.
[P1722] Extended term insurance.
[P1723] Shortened benefit period.
[P1724] Accordingly, insurers generally offer an optional nonforfeiture benefit that provides a paid-up policy in the event of the lapse of a long-term care insurance policy that has been in force for at least three years. The daily benefit is normally equal to the daily benefit in effect on the date of lapse. The maximum amount under the policy is usually equal to the greater of:
[P1725] 30 times the daily benefit for nursing home care in force on the date of lapse; or
[P1726] The aggregate premiums paid for the policy.
[P1727] If the policy has been in force for fewer than three years, it will lapse without further value.
[P1728] Some insurers also offer a contingent nonforfeiture benefit that applies in cases where the insured lapses a policy due to the insurer’s premium rate increase. Under this version of the nonforfeiture benefit, the insured—if premium increases equal or exceed a stated percentage of the initial premium—may elect to:
[P1729] Reduce policy benefits so that no premium increase applies; or
[P1730] Make the policy paid-up.
[P1731] Under this version of the nonforfeiture benefit, the cumulative premium increases must be at least the following percent of the initial premium for the issue ages shown:
[P1732] If the insured elects to make the policy paid-up, the daily benefit is the same as under the policy at the date of lapse, and the maximum amount under the policy is the same as it would be under the basic nonforfeiture benefit, i.e., the greater of:
[P1733] 30 times the daily benefit for nursing home care in force on the date of lapse; or
[P1734] The aggregate premiums paid for the policy.
[P1735] The 3-years-in-force requirement applicable to the basic nonforfeiture benefit does not apply to this version of the benefit.
[P1736] 8.5 Family Care Benefit
[P1737] The family care benefit enables an insured’s family members to use certain of the insured’s long-term care insurance benefits. Under the benefit, an insured may designate up to three family members as additional covered persons.
[P1738] In order for a designated family member to receive these benefits, they must meet the policy’s ADL or cognitive impairment criterion. Even though the policy may pay benefits for additional covered persons, its maximum benefit limits remain unchanged. Thus, if the long-term care insurance policy’s maximum benefit amount is $100,000 and an additional covered person uses $60,000 of benefits, the insured may only be able to access the remaining $40,000 in benefits.
[P1739] 8.6 Benefit Restoration
[P1740] An insured’s needing long-term care does not necessarily mean they will never subsequently not need such care. In such a case, an insured may be able to restore the benefits used under a restoration of benefits rider.
[P1741] Under the provisions of such a rider benefit, the insurer will restore the benefits the insured has used if he meets certain criteria. The criteria the insured must meet is that for a specified period—usually 180 days—they have not needed substantial assistance to perform 2 or more ADLs nor required substantial supervision due to a cognitive impairment. In order to ensure that the insured does not require such substantial assistance or supervision, the insurer may require a physical examination or perform an on-site assessment.

[P1786] 9.0 Income Taxation of Long-term Care Insurance Premiums & Benefits
[P1787] We noted in an earlier chapter that the principal burden of paying for long-term care services falls on the shoulders of the American taxpayer through Medicaid. As the enormous Baby Boom generation gets older and begins to reach the age at which its members are more likely to require long-term care, that tax burden for long-term care services will inevitably become greater.
[P1788] The U.S. government routinely encourages American citizens to engage in desirable behavior by offering income tax incentives to do so. Examples abound, including the tax-deductibility of traditional individual retirement account contributions and tax credits for elective deferrals by certain lower-income taxpayers. The extending of governmental incentives is evident also with respect to long-term care insurance as it attempts to move the burden of funding long-term care away from Medicaid.
[P1789] 9.1 Tax-Qualified Long-term Care Insurance Emerges
[P1790] In addition to affecting many other healthcare issues, including personal health information privacy, HIPAA defined a tax-qualified long-term care insurance policy.
[P1791] HIPAA’s defining a qualified long-term care insurance policy was an attempt to limit income tax benefits to long-term care insurance policies having specified features and benefits. Accordingly, HIPAA defines a qualified long-term care insurance policy—a definition codified in IRC §7702B—as one having the following characteristics:
[P1792] It provides insurance protection only for qualified long-term care services;
[P1793] It does not pay or reimburse expenses incurred for services reimbursable under Title XVIII of the Social Security Act;
[P1794] The contract is guaranteed renewable;
[P1795] The contract does not provide for a cash surrender value or other money that may be paid, assigned or pledged as collateral; and
[P1796] Any premium refunds—except refunds not exceeding aggregate premiums paid on the insured’s death or complete surrender of the policy—or dividends must be used to reduce future premiums or increase future benefits.
[P1797] Any premium refund received under a tax-qualified long-term care insurance policy given for a complete surrender of the contract is includible in the recipient’s gross income for tax purposes to the extent a deduction or exclusion was allowable with respect to the premium.

[P1801] 2. nursing home care  Your answer is incorrect. HIPAA defining a qualified long-term care insurance policy was not an attempt to limit nursing home care benefits to long-term care insurance policies having specified features and benefits.
[P1802] 3. income tax  Your answer is correct. HIPAA defining a qualified long-term care insurance policy was an attempt to limit income tax benefits to long-term care insurance policies having specified features and benefits.
[P1803] 9.1.1 Pre-1997 Policies Grandfathered
[P1804] Long-term care insurance policies issued before 1997 generally did not meet the criteria required to be considered tax-qualified under HIPAA. As is often the case involving such changes in the law, policies issued prior to the law’s effective date were grandfathered and, therefore, are considered “qualified” for purposes of the tax-favored treatment. Such grandfathering, however, requires that the pre-1997 policies:
[P1805] Meet the requirements for long-term care insurance policies in the state in which issued; and
[P1806] Not undergo a “material change.”
[P1807] A material change that would cause a grandfathered long-term care insurance policy to lose its favored tax status includes:
[P1808] A contract change that alters the amount or timing of an amount payable by the policyowner, insured or insurer;
[P1809] A substitution in an individual policy of one insured for another; and
[P1810] A change—other than one considered immaterial—in the terms of the contract or in the plan under which it was issued that relates to eligibility for membership in the group covered under a group insurance contract.

[P1819] 9.2 Chronically-Ill Defined
[P1820] HIPAA also defined a chronically-ill individual and specified that long-term care insurance benefits would receive favorable income tax treatment only when they were paid to provide long-term care services to an individual meeting that definition. What that means, of course, is that payment of insurance benefits for any long-term care insurance services provided to an individual who failed to meet the HIPAA definition would not receive favorable income tax treatment.
[P1821] Under HIPAA, a chronically-ill individual is defined as one who has been certified by a licensed healthcare practitioner within the previous 12 months as meeting one of the following criteria:
[P1822] The individual is unable, for at least 90 days, to perform at least two activities of daily living without substantial assistance from another individual, due to loss of functional capacity. The activities of daily living are eating, toileting, transferring, bathing, dressing and continence.
[P1823] The individual requires substantial supervision to be protected from threats to health and safety due to severe cognitive impairment.
[P1824] It is important to note that the third traditional long-term care insurance benefit trigger—the requirement for long-term care services as a medical necessity—is not included as a benefit trigger for which long-term care insurance benefits would receive favorable income tax treatment. Because of that intentional omission, long-term care insurance policies that include medical necessity as a benefit trigger or fail to meet any of the other criteria a qualified long-term care insurance policy must meet are deemed to be nonqualified long-term care insurance policies.

[P1831] 9.3 Premiums Included in Definition of Medical Care for Tax Purposes
[P1832] Within specified maximum dollar limits that are revised annually, premium payments a taxpayer makes for a qualified long-term care insurance policy are included in the definition of medical care and are eligible for tax deduction.
[P1833] For other than self-employed individuals, medical care—which also includes other expenses for the individual’s medical care and that of their spouse and dependents—is deductible by a taxpayer to the extent the total amount exceeds 7.5% of the individual’s adjusted gross income. Self-employed individuals may deduct the premiums paid for health insurance—including the premiums for qualified long-term care insurance within applicable limits—without reference to the 7.5% of adjusted gross income floor.

[P1836] 9.4 Benefits may be Tax-Free
[P1837] The favorable tax treatment of qualified long-term care insurance policies applies also to the benefits received under such a policy. Except for any dividends or premium refunds, the benefits an individual receives from a qualified long-term care insurance policy may be tax-free.
[P1838] The benefits received under a qualified long-term care insurance policy are tax-free insofar as they do not exceed the greater of:
[P1839] The costs for long-term care services actually incurred; or
[P1840] The specified inflation-adjusted per diem amount published by the federal government.
[P1841] The per diem amount published by the federal government tends to increase annually.  For purposes of this course, let’s use the amount published for 2025, $420 per day.
[P1842] For example, suppose an insured owns a qualified long-term care insurance policy that provides a daily long-term care insurance benefit of up to $450 on a reimbursement basis. If the insured’s long-term care cost in 2025 is $440 per day, the entire benefit would be tax-free irrespective of the $420 limitation because the actual cost of the care—$440 per day in this case—is greater than the $420 limitation.
[P1843] However, suppose an insured’s qualified long-term care insurance policy pays a $400 daily benefit on an indemnity basis. If the insured’s actual cost for long-term care is only $300 per day, the policy would, nonetheless, pay the daily benefit of $400.  Since the amount paid is within the per diem limitation ($420), the entire $400 daily benefit paid would be tax-free—even though only $300 of it may have been used to purchase long-term care services.
[P1844] 9.5 Nonqualified Policy Tax Status
[P1845] It is reasonable—even if possibly incorrect—to conclude that the tax benefits given to qualified long-term care insurance premiums and benefits do not apply to nonqualified policies. In fact, the Internal Revenue Service has not ruled on the tax treatment to be afforded nonqualified long-term care insurance policies issued after the qualified tax provisions became effective in 1997.
[P1846] Although it may seem that Congress’s granting of favorable income tax treatment to qualified long-term care insurance policy benefits and premiums would mean they are not available to nonqualified policies, such a suggestion is only speculation. However, before recommending or selling a nonqualified long-term care insurance policy the ethical requirement of full disclosure requires the applicant be informed the recommended policy is nonqualified.

[P1875] 10.0 Paying for Long-term Care—Alternatives
[P1876] Long-term care insurance has generally failed to produce significant sales results. Surveys involving individuals who considered purchasing long-term care insurance-- but did not do so -- have indicated that the principal reason for their refusal to buy coverage was its substantial cost. Since Medicaid, the primary funding source of long-term care, is normally available only after the individual has become impoverished, many people look for alternatives to both of those sources.
[P1877] In this chapter we will examine potential sources of long-term care funding that may be available and will look at these alternative sources.
[P1878] As we consider each of these alternatives, it is important to bear in mind that many of them have serious drawbacks.
[P1879] 10.1 Paying for Care with Accelerated Death Benefits
[P1880] At one time, life insurance was simpler—although decidedly less flexible—than it is today. Then, if a policyowner wanted to receive cash from a permanent life insurance policy during their lifetime, the options were generally limited to borrowing from the policy, using the policy as collateral for a bank loan, or surrendering the policy. When the insured died, the death benefit is payable.
[P1881] Beginning in the early 1990s—and given a push by the HIV/AIDS epidemic—some life insurers started offering their terminally-ill insureds an option to receive some or all of their policies’ death benefits while they were still alive. By providing, in many cases, a substantial death benefit payment to these still-living insureds, they might be better able to purchase needed care or use the funds to fulfill a dream. For the insured needing long-term care, accelerated death benefits might mean the difference between obtaining care in a facility of their choosing or receiving it in a less desirable facility.
[P1882] Insurers offering accelerated benefits take several different approaches to it. These differing approaches include:
[P1883] Paying the entire death benefit to the insured and retiring the contract;
[P1884] Paying some portion of the death benefit to the insured—usually 50% to 75%—and paying the balance to the designated beneficiary at the death of the insured; and
[P1885] Loaning some portion of the death benefit to the insured and paying the balance of the death benefit, less interest on the portion borrowed, to the designated beneficiary at the death of the insured.
[P1886] The variation in treatment of accelerated death benefits may also extend to the required condition of the insured to be eligible to receive them. In the case of some insurers, an insured must be considered chronically ill in order to receive accelerated death benefits. With other insurers, an insured must be terminally ill and have a life expectancy of six months or less.
[P1887] While giving a very sick insured access to a large amount of money with which to pay for needed care is certainly desirable, it is unquestionable that this option involves certain drawbacks. The most significant drawback of accelerated death benefits is that the original purpose in purchasing the life insurance—to provide income for surviving family members, for example—may still apply. So, using death benefits to provide care to a chronically ill or terminally ill insured may mean that surviving family members will not have the income needed to meet their basic monthly bills. A second potential disadvantage to accelerating death benefits is that receipt of such benefits may affect the insured’s ability to qualify for Medicaid and other social welfare programs.

[P1892] III.  chronically ill  Your answer is correct. In the case of some insurers, an insured must be considered chronically ill in order to receive accelerated death benefits.
[P1893] 10.2	Paying for Care with a Life Settlement
[P1895] Life Settlements give you the ability to raise cash by selling your life insurance policy. With a Life Settlement, you sell your life insurance policy for its present value. This option is usually only available to women age 74 and older and to men age 70 and older. The proceeds may be used for any reason, such as paying long-term care insurance premiums or paying for long-term care services directly.
[P1896] Important Considerations:
[P1897] Little or no death benefit may be left for your survivors/heirs.
[P1898] No health screening is required; you may be in good or poor health.
[P1899] There may be tax liabilities on the proceeds of the sale.
[P1900] 10.3 Paying for Care with a Viatical Settlement
[P1901] A viatical settlement is a policyowner’s sale to a third party of an existing life insurance policy under which a terminally-ill person is insured. Viatical settlements usually involve terminally-ill insureds with a life expectancy of 48 months or less.
[P1902] Although a terminally-ill insured in a viatical settlement may have a life expectancy of as long as 48 months, a viatical settlement is tax-free only if it involves an insured who meets the definition of chronically-ill or terminally-ill in the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA).
[P1903] According to HIPAA, a terminally-ill person is one with a life expectancy of 24 months or less, and a chronically-ill person is someone who:
[P1904] Is incapable of performing at least two ADLs; or
[P1905] Requires substantial supervision.
[P1906] The amount paid for an existing policy in a viatical settlement is determined through negotiation between the policyowner and the third party considering the purchase of the policy; as such, the price actually paid for a policy may be any amount to which the parties to the negotiation agree. However, the NAIC Viatical Settlements Model Act suggests the following purchase prices for existing life insurance policies under which terminally-ill individuals are insured:
[P1907] Although these are suggested amounts based on an insured’s life expectancy, a lower amount may be appropriate for lower-rated insurers to compensate for the additional financial risk to the new owner that the insurer may be financially unable to meet its death benefit commitment.
[P1908] The disadvantages of a viatical settlement are identical to the disadvantages associated with accelerated death benefits. Specifically, the original purpose behind the purchase of the life insurance may still apply, and receipt of a viatical settlement may make qualification for Medicaid and other social welfare programs more difficult.

[P1916] 10.4 Using Annuities to Pay Long-term Care Costs
[P1917] Using annuity contracts to pay long-term care costs may involve:
[P1918] Accessing an annuity’s accumulated value and avoiding surrender charges through a crisis waiver;
[P1919] A long-term care insurance rider; or
[P1920] An integrated approach using both an annuity’s accumulated value and a contingent long-term-care benefit.
[P1921] Let’s briefly look at these three approaches.
[P1922] 10.4.1 Crisis Waivers Permit Access to Accumulated Value without Charges
[P1923] One of the concerns with respect to withdrawing funds from an annuity’s accumulated value during the contract’s surrender charge period is that substantial surrender charges may apply. However, an annuity contract containing a crisis waiver permits the contract owner to access accumulated value during the surrender charge period without incurring a surrender charge.
[P1924] The waiver of surrender charges under a crisis waiver requires the contract owner to meet the criteria specified in the rider. Depending on the type of crisis waiver, the contract owner must have:
[P1925] Been admitted to a nursing home;
[P1926] Suffered a terminal illness;
[P1927] Become unemployed; or
[P1928] Become disabled.
[P1929] In addition to meeting the criteria set out in the crisis waiver, the insurer may require that the contract have been in force for a specified minimum duration or that the contract owner the younger than a specified age. Furthermore, some insurers may offer particular crisis waivers without additional premium while others charge a premium for them.
[P1930] Review Question:
[P1931] An annuity contract containing a __________ permits the contract owner to access accumulated value during the surrender charge period without incurring a surrender charge.
[P1932] I. loophole  Your answer is incorrect. An annuity contract containing a loophole does not permit the contract owner to access accumulated value during the surrender charge period without incurring a surrender charge.
[P1933] II. free withdrawal clause  Your answer is incorrect. An annuity contract containing a free withdrawal clause does not permit the contract owner to access accumulated value during the surrender charge period without incurring a surrender charge.
[P1934] III. crisis waiver  Your answer is correct. An annuity contract containing a crisis waiver permits the contract owner to access accumulated value during the surrender charge period without incurring a surrender charge.
[P1935] 10.4.2 Annuity Contracts
[P1936] An annuity is a series of regular payments over a specified and defined period of time. The funds for the annuity come from a single premium payment that the individual makes at the outset. Two types are available:
[P1937] Immediate long-term care annuity
[P1938] Deferred long-term care annuity
[P1939] 10.4.2.1	Immediate Long-Term Care Annuity
[P1941] For a single premium payment individuals make to an insurance company, they receive a specified monthly income. It is available without regard to health, so if an individual does not qualify for long-term care insurance because of age or poor health or if they are already receiving long-term care, they can still purchase an annuity. The single premium payment is converted to a monthly income stream that is guaranteed either for a specified period of time or for the life of the individual receiving the payments. The payout schedule varies based on the amount of the initial premium, your age, and gender. Generally, because of their longer life expectancy, females receive a smaller monthly payment over a longer period of time than do males of the same age. 

Important Considerations:
[P1942] The annuity amount received may not be enough to pay for long-term care expenses.
[P1943] Inflation may make the monthly income received from the annuity less than what is needed.
[P1944] The tax implications of an annuity are complicated.
[P1945] 10.4.2.2	Deferred Long-Term Care Annuity
[P1947] This type of annuity is available to individuals up to age 85. Similar to other annuities, for a single premium payment, individuals receive a stream of monthly income. The amount received depends upon health. The annuity creates two funds: one for long-term care expenses and another separate cash fund to be used however you desire. The “long-term care” fund can be accessed immediately, while access to the “cash” portion is deferred and more limited over time. The rules of the annuity define how much an individual can access on a monthly basis from the long-term care fund, and how much they can access on an annual basis from the cash fund.
[P1948] To qualify for this type of annuity, there are seven broad health criteria. However, most people will qualify even if they do not qualify for long-term care insurance.
[P1949] Important Considerations:
[P1950] If the long-term care fund is not used, it can be passed to heirs.
[P1951] The annuity may not be enough to pay for long-term care expenses.
[P1952] Inflation may make the monthly income received from the annuity less than what is needed.
[P1953] The long-term care portion of the annuity does not satisfy the requirements for a tax-qualified long-term care policy, so there is a risk of being taxed on the money from the fund that is used for your long-term care expenses.
[P1954] The tax implications of an annuity are complicated.
[P1955] In addition to crisis waivers, which provide no benefit to a contract owner other than enabling them to avoid surrender charges, long-term care insurance riders may be added to a deferred annuity contract. These riders may function in every respect just like a long-term care insurance policy.
[P1956] A concern with respect to long-term care insurance riders on annuity contracts is the need for ongoing rider premiums since deferred annuity contracts may involve either flexible premiums or no premiums at all. Although funds may be taken from the annuity’s accumulated value to pay long-term care insurance rider premiums, the normal tax treatment of such withdrawals is known as LIFO. Under LIFO tax treatment, withdrawals from a deferred annuity are considered interest first to the extent there is any gain on the contract. Insofar as the withdrawal is deemed to be interest, it is income taxable and may be subject to premature distribution penalty charges.
[P1957] However, withdrawals from a deferred annuity to pay long-term care insurance rider premiums are considered to be withdrawals of after-tax premiums, regardless of whether there is any gain on the contract. As such, the withdrawal will not result in an immediate income tax liability but will reduce the contract owner’s cost basis in the annuity.
[P1958] 10.4.3 Paying Long-term Care Costs Using Integrated Annuity/Long-term Care Benefits
[P1959] An interesting approach to paying for long-term care is through the use of an annuity integrated with a long-term care insurance benefit. Under this approach, when the contract owner becomes eligible for long-term care benefits the funds to pay for such care are initially withdrawn from the annuity’s accumulated value. When the accumulated value of the annuity is exhausted, a long-term care insurance benefit begins and continues payment for long-term care until benefits equal to twice the annuity’s accumulated value have been paid from the insurance benefit.
[P1960] For example, suppose a contract owner has an integrated annuity/long-term care contract under which the deferred annuity’s accumulated value is $200,000. The long-term care benefit would normally provide an additional $400,000 to purchase long-term-care. Under such an arrangement, the contract owner would be able to access $600,000 for purchasing long-term care services.
