[P1962] A withdrawal from a deferred annuity to pay long-term care insurance rider premiums is considered to be
[P1963] A nontaxable withdrawal of after-tax premiums, regardless of whether there is any gain in the contract. Your answer is correct. This type of withdrawal is nontaxable as an exception to the general LIFO rule.
[P1964] A nontaxable withdrawal of after-tax premiums only if there is any gain in the contract. Your answer is incorrect. This type of withdrawal is nontaxable as an exception to the general LIFO rule. The amount of gain in the contract is irrelevant.
[P1965] A taxable withdrawal if there is gain in the contract under the LIFO principle. Your answer is incorrect. This type of withdrawal is nontaxable as an exception to the general LIFO rule.
[P1966] A taxable withdrawal, regardless of whether there is any gain in the contract, under the LIFO principle. Your answer is incorrect. This type of withdrawal is nontaxable as an exception to the general LIFO rule.
[P1967] 10.5 Using Life Insurance Policies to Pay Long-term Care Costs
[P1968] A life insurance policy may provide long-term care funds through:
[P1969] An integrated life insurance/long-term care policy; or
[P1970] A long-term care insurance rider on a life insurance policy.
[P1971] 10.5.1 Paying Long-term Care Costs—Integrated Life Insurance/Long-term Care Policy
[P1972] Similar to an integrated deferred annuity/long-term care benefit, an integrated life insurance/long-term care policy involves a single premium life insurance policy and a long-term care benefit. In such a policy, a policyowner could invest $140,000 in a $200,000 single premium life insurance policy that provides a $400,000 integrated long-term care benefit.
[P1973] If the policy insured dies without using the long-term care benefit, a death benefit of $200,000 would be payable to their designated beneficiary. Alternatively, if the insured needs long-term care they may access the long-term care benefit for up to twice the policy’s death benefit. If the insured policyowner uses the entire amount of the long-term care benefit—$400,000 in this case—no further benefits of any type are available. Under this method the insured avoids the possibility of paying large long-term care insurance premiums and dying without needing long-term care.
[P1974] 10.5.2 Long-term Care Insurance Riders on Life Insurance Policies
[P1975] Long-term care insurance riders may be attached to life insurance policies and be available to pay long-term care costs without affecting the policy—not unlike any other rider attached to a life insurance policy. Rider premiums may be paid as part of the policy premiums or may be debited from the life insurance policy’s cash value. If premiums are debited from the cash value, no tax liability will be incurred under current law until the policyowner’s cost basis has been withdrawn entirely—a tax treatment known as FIFO (first in, first out). For tax purposes, FIFO assumes that assets with the oldest costs are included in the income statement's cost of goods sold (COGS).
[P1976] Such debited rider premiums do not result in immediate income tax liability even after the policyowner has withdrawn amounts from the cash value exceeding their cost basis. As in the case of withdrawals from a deferred annuity to pay premiums under a long-term care insurance rider, such excess withdrawals cause a reduction in the policyowner’s cost basis for the policy.
[P1978] 10.6	  Trusts
[P1979] A trust is when a person (the trustor) transfers something of value (the asset) to another person (the trustee). Once that takes place, the trustee manages and controls the asset for the benefit of the trustor or for a named beneficiary.
[P1980] One use of a trust is to provide flexible control of assets for the benefit of minor children. Another is to provide flexible control of assets for the benefit of an elderly or disabled person, including yourself or your spouse.
[P1981] There are generally two types of trusts drafted in Long-term Care planning:
[P1982] Charitable Remainder Trusts
[P1983] Medicaid Disability Trusts
[P1984] 10.6.1	Charitable Remainder Trust
[P1985] These trusts allow individuals to use their own assets for long-term care with the added benefit of reducing taxes. This type of trust is typically used by wealthy people with specific types of assets that they donate to a public charity at fair market value. The individual making the donation receives a tax deduction on the amount that has been gifted. The donor then receives payments from the trust that can be used to pay for long-term care. Once the donor dies, the balance of the funds in the trust go to the charity.
[P1986] Important Considerations:
[P1987] The funds available are based on the amount of the donation. These payments are only likely to be large enough to help pay for long-term care expenses a substantial amount of money is donated to the charity.
[P1988] A charitable trust may not provide enough income to pay long-term care expenses.
[P1989] The donation may affect Medicaid eligibility.
[P1990] 10.6.2	 Medicaid Disability Trust
[P1991] The purpose of a Medicaid Disability Trust is to enhance the quality of life of an individual with a disability who also qualifies for public benefits. Medicaid Disability Trusts are limited to disabled persons under age 65. With this type of trust, assets are managed by a nonprofit organization. The trust may be established by a parent, grandparent or legal guardian for the benefit of the disabled person. This is the only kind of trust that is exempt from rules regarding trusts and Medicaid eligibility. 

Important Considerations:
[P1992] If Medicaid benefits are paid on behalf of the individual, any amount remaining in the trust at the individual's death can be recovered by the state.
[P1993] There are complex tax implications.

[P2017] C.  subject to premature distribution tax penalties  Your answer is incorrect. A withdrawal from a deferred annuity to pay long-term care insurance rider premiums is not subject to premature distribution tax penalties.

[P2020] 5.   What is the function of a crisis waiver attached to an annuity contract?

[P2028] 11.0 Ethics and Suitability in Long-term Care Insurance Sales
[P2029] The availability of long-term care insurance benefits may make the difference between an individual’s ability to protect their assets for future generations or dying in poverty. It may allow a person needing care to choose a setting in which they will be most comfortable rather than being limited to one that accepts Medicaid recipients.
[P2030] While those statements are certainly true, it does not necessarily follow that purchasing long-term care insurance is the right answer for everyone. In this chapter we will examine some of the important suitability and ethical issues that apply in the sale of long-term care insurance.
[P2031] 11.1 Determining Suitability of Long-term Care Insurance
[P2032] Although the determination of long-term care insurance suitability must generally focus on the applicant for such coverage and their financial situation, suitability analysis should be somewhat broader in scope. Accordingly, long-term care insurance suitability analysis should consider the:
[P2033] Applicant;
[P2034] Long-term care insurance coverage being recommended; and
[P2035] Insurer.
[P2036] Long-term care insurance suitability analysis seeks to answer one important question: “Is the long-term care insurance policy being considered appropriate for the applicant?”
[P2037] 11.1.1 Principal Suitability Focus must be on the Applicant
[P2038] Although the suitability analysis that should precede any recommendation of a long-term care insurance policy involves elements of due diligence in requiring an evaluation of the policy and the insurer, it needs to focus initially on the applicant. Accordingly, suitability analysis for long-term care insurance should determine if the proposed policy would:
[P2039] Be harmful for the applicant; and
[P2040] Be beneficial for the applicant.
[P2041] Purchasing a long-term care insurance policy could be expected to harm the applicant if they cannot afford the premiums—either currently or in the future—and such purchase would require the applicant to forgo buying food, medicine, etc.  Several indicators can assist an agent in determining whether the applicant can afford the policy premiums. Such indicators include:
[P2042] Whether the applicant frequently has difficulty paying for utilities, food or other important needs;
[P2043] Whether the applicant's income is limited to Social Security or Supplemental Security Income (SSI);
[P2044] Whether the applicant is on Medicaid; and
[P2045] Whether the applicant could afford to keep the policy if its premium increased by 20%.
[P2046] If the applicant expects to pay policy premiums entirely from their income and such premiums would exceed 7% of that income, the applicant may not be able to afford the policy.
[P2047] A long-term care insurance policy would be beneficial for the applicant if they own significant assets and wishes to protect them. An applicant with minimal assets would probably find that required long-term care would be paid for by Medicaid.
[P2048] As a general rule, an applicant should consider purchasing long-term care insurance if they:
[P2049] Have a substantial amount of assets;
[P2050] Want to protect existing assets from being exhausted by the need to pay for long-term care services;
[P2051] Are able to pay premiums and possible premium increases without experiencing financial difficulty;
[P2052] Want to remain independent and avoid being supported by others; and
[P2053] Want to be able to choose the setting in which long-term care, if needed, is provided.
[P2054] Although there is no hard and fast rule with respect to the amount of assets that should be owned by an applicant before long-term care insurance is suitable, an applicant interested in purchasing long-term care insurance in order to protect assets and whose assets are less than $30,000 should probably consider a different method of funding long-term care. It is not only the possibility that an applicant may have too few assets for the purchase of a long-term care insurance policy to be suitable, however; an argument can be made that an applicant’s very large investment portfolio may make the purchase of a long-term care insurance policy inappropriate.
[P2055] For example, an applicant with investable assets greater than $1.5 million could probably self-fund needed long-term care. Although applicant’s with substantial investable assets—$1.5 million may be the lower limit—are not necessarily unsuitable for long-term care insurance, those assets should be considered in the suitability analysis.

[P2062] 11.1.1.1 Consider the Applicant’s Other Needs in Suitability Analysis
[P2063] Although an applicant’s financial situation—particularly income and assets—need to be considered in determining whether or not the purchase of a long-term care insurance policy is suitable, other family needs must also be considered. The principal needs that must be considered are generally survivor income needs:
[P2064] For a surviving spouse;
[P2065] For dependent children; and
[P2066] For dependent parents.
[P2067] If the applicant must provide for others—a surviving spouse and children, dependent parents, etc.—those requirements and whether they have been satisfactorily met should be taken into consideration in the suitability determination.
[P2068] 11.1.1.2 Consider the Applicant’s Family Health History and Longevity
[P2069] Some debilitating diseases and conditions appear to be more common in some families than in others. Because of the genetic element in the contracting of certain diseases or conditions, the applicant’s family history of disease should be considered in determining the likely risk for needing long-term care.
[P2070] Some diseases and conditions that appear to be genetically linked include:
[P2071] Diabetes;
[P2072] Hyperthyroidism;
[P2073] Schizophrenia;
[P2074] Lupus;
[P2075] Celiac disease;
[P2076] Multiple sclerosis;
[P2077] Parkinson’s disease;
[P2078] Stroke;
[P2079] Huntington’s chorea;
[P2080] Hemophilia;
[P2081] Cystic fibrosis;
[P2082] Alzheimer’s disease;
[P2083] Heart disease; and
[P2084] Certain forms of cancer.
[P2085] Just as certain diseases appear to have a genetic component, longevity also appears to be genetically linked. Since the likelihood of requiring long-term care increases as an individual ages, applicants whose family members lived into their 90s or older are more likely to die at an advanced age and require long-term care at some time.

[P2092] 11.1.2 Evaluating the Long-term Care Insurance Policy
[P2093] Assuming the applicant is suitable for long-term care insurance, you need to assess whether the particular long-term care insurance policy being considered is appropriate for the applicant.
[P2094] A suitable applicant that is interested principally in keeping the policy’s premium as low as possible should probably consider purchasing a long-term care insurance policy that pays benefits on a reimbursement basis rather than one paying benefits on an indemnity basis. Not only would such a policy normally be less expensive than an otherwise identical policy that paid benefits on an indemnity basis, but it would also be less likely to require premium increases.
[P2095] Similarly, an applicant wanting to be able to benefit from purchasing long-term care services at a lower price is more likely to be satisfied with a long-term care insurance policy paying benefits on a “pool of money” basis since such a policy would reward the careful purchase of such services with a longer benefit period.
[P2096] It may be important for a particular applicant that, under the policy:
[P2097] Long-term care is covered in all settings;
[P2098] Companion and homemaker services are considered covered services;
[P2099] The applicant can hire anyone, including family members, to provide personal care and homemaker services;
[P2100] Certain benefits under the policy are not subject to the elimination period;
[P2101] Receiving home care services count towards satisfying the elimination period;
[P2102] Needs to be satisfied only once during the insured’s lifetime;
[P2103] Limitations are imposed on benefits for preexisting conditions;
[P2104] A bed-holding benefit will maintain their place in a facility so the applicant can visit family, etc.; and
[P2105] Home modifications, medical equipment and caregiver training will be paid for to enable the applicant to receive care at home.

A suitable applicant that is interested principally in keeping the LTC policy's premium as low as possible should probably not consider purchasing a long-term care insurance policy that pays benefits on a yearly basis rather than one paying benefits on an indemnity basis.
[P2111] 11.1.3 Evaluating the Insurance Company Issuing the Policy
[P2112] Payment of legitimate long-term care claims under a policy could be jeopardized by an insurer’s unstable financial condition. For that reason, it is important to examine the insurer’s financial condition by considering its financial and claims-paying ratings. Agencies that rate insurance companies include:
[P2113] A.M. Best;
[P2114] Weiss;
[P2115] Moody’s; and
[P2116] Standard and Poor’s.
[P2117] In general, it is prudent—for both the applicant and the agent—to avoid placing long-term care insurance with an insurance company whose ratings by these agencies indicate its financial status or claims-paying ability is not strong. In terms of actual ratings, that means applicants should not generally be placed with companies whose A.M. Best or Weiss rating is less than B+.
[P2118] In addition to an insurer’s financial rating, the insurer’s rate increase history should be examined. Although long-term care insurance policy rate increases should be expected as the cost of obtaining long-term care rises, an insurer with a history of frequent or large rate increases at a time when other insurers maintained rates or obtained smaller rate increases should generally be avoided. Such frequent and large rate increases may indicate poor claims management or other management deficiencies that may result in future large and frequent rate increases.

[P2146] 11.3	Minimum standards for home health and community care benefits in long-term care insurance policies.
[P2148] NAIC Model Regulation provides that a long-term care insurance policy or certificate may not, if it provides benefits for home healthcare or community care services, limit or exclude benefits:
[P2150] a. By requiring that the insured or claimant would need care in a skilled nursing facility if home healthcare services were not provided;
[P2152] b. By requiring that the insured or claimant first or simultaneously receive nursing or therapeutic services, or both in a home, community, or institutional setting before home healthcare services are covered;
[P2154] c. By limiting eligible services to services provided by registered nurses or licensed practical nurses;
[P2156] d. By requiring that a nurse or therapist provide services covered by the policy that can be provided by a home health aide, or other licensed or certified home care worker acting within the scope of their licensure or certification;
[P2158] e. By requiring that the insured or claimant have an acute condition before home healthcare services are covered;
[P2160] f. By limiting benefits to services provided by Medicare-certified agencies or providers;
[P2162] g. By excluding coverage for personal care services provided by a home health aide;
[P2164] h. By requiring that the provision of home healthcare services be at a level of certification or licensure greater than that required by the eligible service; or
[P2166] i. By excluding coverage for adult day care services.

[P2218] 11.5 Ethical Concerns Often Involve Replacement and Disclosure
[P2219] Ethical concerns with respect to sales practices in the placement of long-term care insurance may involve any of the issues that seem to come to light from time to time, such as misrepresentation, lack of suitability, etc. The principal ethical concerns with respect to long-term care insurance, however, involve:
[P2220] Replacement; and
[P2221] Disclosure.
[P2222] Let’s briefly consider each of these concerns.
[P2223] 11.5.1 Replacement of Long-term Care Insurance
[P2224] We noted in an earlier chapter that if a long-term care insurance policy replaces an existing long-term care insurance policy, the NAIC model regulation mandates certain modifications to the limitations and exclusions applicable to the replacement policy. Specifically, the replacing insurer must waive any time periods that apply to preexisting conditions and probationary periods in the new policy for similar benefits to the extent those time periods were satisfied under the policy being replaced.
[P2225] There is little question but that insurers often introduce new and improved products over time. To the extent such new long-term care insurance products offer an applicant improved coverage, it may be to the applicant’s benefit to replace the existing coverage. Before recommending the replacement of an existing long-term care insurance policy with a new policy, however, the agent should be able to demonstrate that the applicant’s situation would be materially improved by it. If the applicant’s situation would not be improved, the replacement should not be made. In making such a determination, it is important to bear in mind that replacement of a long-term care insurance policy issued before 1997 would result in the loss of the policy’s grandfathered tax treatment.
[P2226] In addition, before recommending an insured exchange an existing long-term care policy for one issued by a different insurer you should determine if the existing insurer would be willing to make any desired changes to the existing policy. If the insurer would agree to such changes, replacement would generally be a less desirable alternative.
[P2227] If a replacement is recommended, you should make a complete disclosure of all material facts, including the advantages and disadvantages of the replacement policy compared with the existing policy insofar as the following are concerned:
[P2228] Finally, if a replacement is appropriate for the customer, ensure that the replacement coverage has been approved before recommending the customer terminate the existing coverage.

[P2236] 11.5.2 Required Disclosure
[P2237] Disclosing material information to an applicant is an ethical requirement insofar as it enables an applicant to make an informed decision concerning a proposed long-term care insurance recommendation. The NAIC model regulation specifies three specific disclosure forms that relate to:

[P2251] 11.8	Standards for marketing.
[P2253] Every insurer, healthcare service plan, or other entity marketing long-term care insurance coverage in this state, directly or through its producers, shall:
