[P2329] 12.0.  Medicaid Planning
[P2330] Medicaid is the U.S. health insurance program intended for individuals and families with low incomes and resources. It is jointly funded by the states and federal government, however, is managed by the states.  Among the people served by Medicaid are eligible low-income parents, children, seniors, and people with disabilities.  Medicaid is the largest source of funding for medical and health-related services for people with limited income.
[P2331] Medicaid was created on July 30, 1965 through Title XIX of the Social Security Act. Under the Act, each state administers its own Medicaid program while the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) monitors the state-run programs and establishes requirements for service delivery, quality, funding, and eligibility standards.
[P2332] Each state may have their own names for the program. Examples include "Medi-Cal" in California, "MassHealth" in Massachusetts, and "TennCare" in Tennessee. States may bundle together the administration of Medicaid with other separate programs such as the State Children's Health Insurance Program (SCHIP), so the same organization that handles Medicaid in a state may also manage those additional programs.
[P2333] State participation in Medicaid is voluntary; however, all states have participated since 1982.  In some states, Medicaid is subcontracted to private health insurance companies, while other states pay providers (i.e., doctors, clinics and hospitals) directly to ensure that individuals receive proper medical attention.
[P2334] Medicaid is an entitlement program; however, it is not funded solely at the federal level. States provide up to half of the funding for the Medicaid program.  In some states, counties also contribute funds.  The main criterion for Medicaid eligibility is limited income and financial resources, a criterion that plays no role in determining Medicare coverage.  Medicaid covers a wider range of healthcare services than Medicare.
[P2335] Although Congress and the CMS set out the main rules under which Medicaid operates, each state runs its own program. As a result, the eligibility rules differ in every state, although the framework is the same throughout the country.
[P2336] Both the federal government and most state governments have made many changes to the eligibility requirements and restrictions over the years.  One change occurred with the passage of the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005 (DRA), P.L. 109-171 .  Specifically, DRA makes significant changes to the rules pertaining to asset transfers (divestments), including the penalty calculation for divestments, annuities, the look-back period and even the countability of the equity in the homestead. As a result, DRA limits and may effectively eliminate the planning techniques for individuals seeking Medicaid eligibility.
[P2337] Medicaid law requires states to provide certain mandatory services to mandatory populations. In addition, states may receive federal matching funds for the costs of covering people and services not mandated by federal statute. Some critical services, including prescription drugs, are categorized as “optional”. About 60 percent of all Medicaid expenditures are for optional services. States also have flexibility to determine the amount, duration and scope of the services they provide under the program. For example, states must cover hospital and physician services, but they can set hospital length of stay or annual visit limits. Once a state decides to cover a service, it generally must offer the service to all Medicaid beneficiaries, regardless of eligibility group, in every region of the state. While all groups within a state are generally covered for the same set of benefits, individuals are only covered for medically necessary care.  States also have the flexibility to determine what items and services are medically necessary.
[P2338] Current law requires individuals applying for Medicaid long-term care services to divest all but a minimum level of assets ($2,000) before becoming eligible.  Countable assets include savings accounts and investments but exclude the home, one car, life insurance with a face value of less than $1,500, and certain other items.  Special rules allow a community spouse of a nursing home resident to keep a portion of the couple’s income and assets to prevent impoverishment.  If applicants transfer assets for amounts below fair market value within three years of applying for Medicaid nursing home care, they are subject to a delay in eligibility. Most elderly living in the community who are at high risk for nursing home use do not have sufficient assets, excluding home equity, to finance a nursing home stay of one year or more.  Private insurance and Medicare generally do not cover nursing home care, leaving many elderly to turn to Medicaid as the only alternative to help finance this care.
[P2339] DRA included changes that will affect the use of divestment planning for Medicaid eligibility. These rule changes include:
[P2340] applying a 5-year cumulative look-back period to all transfers (eliminating the de minimis transfer and rounding down rules);
[P2341] a new commencement date for serving out the penalty period; and
[P2342] updated Undue Hardship exception rules.
[P2343] To help prepare for planning under post-DRA rules, the discussion below assumes full implementation of DRA at the State level.
[P2344] Look-Back Period Extended to Five Years.  Under pre-DRA law, there was a three-year (36 month) look-back (from the date of application) to determine if any assets had been divested to an individual and a five-year (60 month) look-back for divestments into a trust. By contrast, the DRA provides that all transfers are subject to a five-year (60 month) look-back period. In addition to other problems raised by this new rule, it is also likely that eligibility determinations will take longer as the Medicaid caseworkers will be required to review up to five years of financial transactions rather than the pre-DRA three years.
[P2345] Commencement Date for Penalty Period.   To determine the start date of the penalty period, it is necessary to look at the date of the transfer. For post-DRA / effective date transfers, the penalty period commences on the later of the date of transfer or the date on which the applicant is otherwise Medicaid eligible.  Thus, caseworkers may have to use a hybrid calculation if an applicant has made gifts both before and after the DRA effective date. This change could result in individuals with severe physical and/or cognitive impairments being denied care services. Such an outcome will likely increase the use of the Undue Hardship exception rules.
[P2346] Calculation of Penalty Months.  The penalty period is calculated by dividing the amount of the gift by the average monthly nursing home cost (the “divisor”). This calculation results in the months of penalty, measured in a fractional amount. Under current (pre-DRA) rules in Michigan, any fractional amount is rounded down or disregarded. However, because the fractional penalty is dropped, the transfer results in only a one-month penalty. The DRA provides that States may NOT disregard any fractional penalty. Under DRA it appears that State Medicaid agencies will have to calculate penalty periods to the day or even hour!
[P2347] Undue Hardship.  This is a very important but largely untested exception to overcome imposition of divestment penalties. The rule applies when the imposition of a penalty will result in “undue hardship” to the applicant. Pre-DRA law provided that the individual States may determine the criteria for undue hardship. However, the DRA provides more specific undue hardship standards and illustrates specific elements that the State must follow in identifying undue hardship.  The Undue Hardship exception applies if the imposition of a penalty will deprive the Medicaid applicant of medical care or food, clothing, shelter or other necessities of life.
[P2348] Procedurally, the State must follow the prescribed procedure of notice that the undue hardship exception exists, a timely determination of whether the hardship exception will be granted, and a process to appeal an adverse determination. While DRA more clearly defines the process, it is likely that the same standard and process would have been required under current (pre-DRA) rules.
[P2349] Under DRA, people who have planned in advance (i.e., gifting completed more than five years in advance of need) for potential long-term care will have a better chance of being rewarded.  However, such planning could pose risks for elders and individuals with disabilities, including loss of control of their assets, and potential gift, income and capital gain tax consequences. Further, if an individual requires long-term care before the five-year look-back period ends, the donee does not have a legal obligation to refund the gift and/or may be financially unable to do so. Finally, under DRA, the donor (the applicant) will be ineligible for Medicaid.
[P2350] 12.1	Medicaid Eligibility Requirements for Long-Term Care
[P2351] To qualify for Medicaid, an individual needs to meet three categories of requirements:
[P2352] General Medicaid Eligibility Requirements
[P2353] Functional Requirements
[P2354] Financial Requirements
[P2355] A.	General Medicaid Eligibility Requirements
[P2356] Medicaid recipients must:
[P2357] Be age 65 or older or permanently disabled or blind; and
[P2358] Meet U.S. citizenship or immigration rules; and
[P2359] Be a resident of the state where they apply.
[P2360] B.	Functional Eligibility Requirements
[P2361] To receive long-term care services under Medicaid, an individual must be assessed and determined to be in need of long-term care. A medical specialist in the state evaluates care needs. This evaluation is done in conjunction with a Medicaid application but not by the same person who evaluates financial eligibility.
[P2362] As part of this assessment, the specialist determines if the individual needs nursing home care or if they are a candidate for home- and community-based services.
[P2363] The need for long-term care is generally determined by whether an individual can perform the Activities of Daily Living on their own, or whether they need assistance from another person. As discussed earlier, these activities include bathing, dressing, using the toilet, transferring (to or from bed or chair), caring for incontinence, and eating. If an individual does meet Medicaid's Functional Eligibility Criteria, they cannot receive long-term care services under Medicaid regardless of how poor they are.
[P2364] C.	Medicaid's Financial Eligibility Requirements
[P2365] States will assess both available income and available assets in determining whether an individual qualifies for the Medicaid program.
[P2366] Some of an individual’s income is considered countable income, while other income may not be counted.
[P2367] As we have said, state requirements vary. The following discussion describes the typical state rules, but your state may be different. You can find your state’s rules (and other related information) on a website maintained by the American Council on Aging.
[P2368] D.	Assets
[P2369] Some assets are considered, while other assets are excluded, and not counted. While Medicaid's assessment of income is relatively straightforward, the assessment of assets is fairly complex.
[P2370] Exempt assets include a primary residence, personal belongings, one motor vehicle, property essential to self-support, life insurance with a face value under $1,500, certain burial arrangements, and assets held in specific kinds of trusts. Unless specifically excluded, any other real or personal property that you and your spouse own is counted in the Medicaid eligibility determination.
[P2371] Assets that are jointly held by the person applying for Medicaid and other persons are generally apportioned equally among all owners.
[P2372] E.	How Will Medicaid Evaluate Assets?
[P2373] Medicaid evaluates all assets to determine whether an individual meets the state's financial criteria for eligibility. Individuals are required to provide documentation of assets during the Medicaid application process.
[P2374] F.	How Much Can an Individual Have in Assets and Still Qualify for Medicaid?
[P2375] Asset levels vary from state to state. States have the option to raise the minimum amount.  In most states, an individual can retain only about $2,000 in countable assets.  In most states, married couples can only retain about $3,000 in countable assets, if they are still living in the same household.
[P2376] If one spouse lives in an institution and the other spouse is still living in the community, Federal law allows the community spouse to keep more assets. In general, the community spouse is allowed to keep half of the married couples' combined assets, subject to both a minimum amount and a maximum amount.
[P2377] G.	What If Assets Are More Than the Allowable Limit?
[P2378] If assets exceed the amount allowed by Medicaid, the application will be denied. The state will tell the individual the amount of excess assets.
[P2379] Individuals have the right to appeal the state's determination if they feel it was incorrect or the individual can reduce assets to become eligible in the following ways:
[P2380] convert the funds to noncountable assets such burial arrangements.
[P2381] pay existing debts such as insurance and taxes.
[P2382] spend the money on medical needs and day-to-day maintenance needs of the individual and their spouse.
[P2383] Under Federal law, an individual may not reduce or transfer assets to others (for example, children) for the purpose of qualifying for Medicaid coverage of long-term care services. Doing so may result in a significant penalty period during which an individual is unable to receive Medicaid payment for long-term care services, even if their assets have been totally depleted.
[P2384] H.	What Is Considered a Transfer of Assets for Medicaid Eligibility Purposes?
[P2385] A transfer of assets is giving away property for less than it is worth or giving away so an individual can qualify for Medicaid coverage of long-term care services.
[P2386] An asset includes all income, real property, and personal property to which an individual and their spouse are entitled whether or not the individual actually receives it.
[P2387] If an individual transfers assets, Medicaid may not pay for nursing home or other long-term care services.
[P2388] I.	Are There Any Permissible Asset Transfers?
[P2389] Certain asset transfers, such as a transfer to a spouse or a disabled or blind child, are not considered disqualifying transfers.
[P2390] J.	How Far in the Past Will Medicaid Look to See if I Have Made a Transfer?
[P2391] Medicaid will look at all asset transfers made in the five-year period prior to a Medicaid application. This period is referred to as a “look back period.”
[P2392] Example: Brad Davis is an 85-year-old widower with a history of heart disease. In June 2025, he gave each of his two granddaughters $10,000 after learning he would need open heart surgery. Two months later he had a stroke and had to be admitted to a nursing home. He had enough in savings left to pay for nursing home care for five months, but then needed to apply for Medicaid in February 2026. His eligibility worker determines he meets all Medicaid requirements in March 2026, but decides his gift to his grandchildren is a disqualifying transfer of assets. He had given away assets ($20,000) for less than fair market value (he received nothing in return).
[P2393] K.	How Are Transfers of Assets Penalized in the Medicaid Eligibility Process?
[P2394] Asset transfers are typically penalized by disqualifying the applicant from becoming eligible for payment for nursing home and other long-term care services for a specified period of time.
[P2395] Transferring assets may result in disqualification, and an individual may not have any resources to pay for long-term care services.
[P2396] L.	Contributions to the Cost of Care
[P2397] Even after an individual qualifies for Medicaid coverage, they are still required to contribute to pay part of the cost of long-term care services.
[P2398] If an individual is in a nursing home, they are required to contribute most of their income to the cost of care, except for a small personal needs allowance.
[P2399] If an individual is living at home, they may be required to pay part of the cost of the home- and community-based services received.
[P2400] M.	Is There a Special Allowance for A Spouse?
[P2401] Married individuals may be allowed to provide a monthly allowance to a spouse to ensure that they have adequate income, before they are required to contribute to the cost of individual care.
[P2402] The spouse, however, is not required to contribute any of their income to the cost of care, if they are not living in the same household.
[P2403] 12.2	Medicaid's Functional Eligibility Requirements
[P2404] A.	How Does Medicaid Determine if I Am Functionally Eligible?
[P2405] A medical specialist evaluates care needs to determine if an individual meets functional eligibility criteria.
[P2406] Since there are few Federal parameters that are required to define functional eligibility, individual states define functional eligibility for their Medicaid programs. They typically consider the need for assistance with Activities of Daily Living such as bathing or eating, skilled care needs, or a combination of the two. Examples of skilled care are feeding tube maintenance, intravenous feeding, dressing changes, oxygen administration, frequent injections, and other services that require the supervision and care of a nurse or physician.
[P2407] B.	Are Functional Eligibility Requirements for Home Care the Same as for Nursing Home Care?
[P2408] Functional eligibility for home- and community-based services may be the same as, or more stringent than, the requirements for institutional care. Federal law encourages states to elect less stringent functional eligibility criteria that will serve even people who do not require nursing home level care.
[P2409] States must provide written notification of functional eligibility decisions. If authorization is denied, they must provide the reason for the denial and give individuals the opportunity to appeal the decision.
[P2410] If an individual meets a state's Functional Eligibility Criteria, they must also meet its General Eligibility Requirements, and Financial Eligibility Requirements.
[P2411] 12.3	Medicaid Eligibility Criteria: Income
[P2412] A.	What Income Counts in Determining Medicaid Eligibility?
[P2413] Income is anything received that can be used to purchase food and shelter. Income can include regularly received payments such as Social Security, veterans' benefits, pensions, salaries, wages, or interest from savings or checking accounts. It also includes payments to which an individual is entitled whether or not they actually receive them. For instance, if an individual gets $500 a month from a trust that could pay $1000, Medicaid counts $1000 as income. If an individual and their spouse are jointly paid income (such as rental income), the state divides the amount evenly, allocating half to the individual and half to the spouse.
[P2414] B.	Whose Income Is Counted?
[P2415] If an individual is in a nursing home, Medicaid counts only that individual’s income – the income of the person applying for long-term care services. Unlike the asset determination, a spouse's income is not counted. However, after the state has determined an individual is eligible for Medicaid, it will decide how much an individual has to pay toward the cost of care and how much income they can keep. If the individual is married, they may be allowed to provide a monthly allowance to a spouse to ensure that they have adequate income to live on, before they are required to contribute to the cost of their own care. A spouse's income will be counted in determining the amount of this allowance.
[P2416] If an individual is receiving long-term care services at home, the income of a spouse may or may not be counted, depending on the eligibility options their state has chosen.
[P2417] C.	How Much Income Can I Have if I Am Receiving Care in My Home?
[P2418] Income eligibility limits vary from state to state. As a rule, they are between the SSI benefit rate and the Federal poverty level.
[P2419] If an individual is receiving services under a state's home- and community-based waiver program, the income standards are sometimes more liberal. Most states will allow income as high as 300 percent of the Supplemental Security Income (SSI) income standard. If an individual lives with their spouse, states may also use rules that let them keep more each month.
[P2420] If income is over these amounts, an individual may have to pay the overage toward medical expenses. This works like an insurance deductible or co-pay.
[P2421] D.	How Much Income Can I Have if I Am in a Nursing Home?
[P2422] Unlike with assets, the amount of income is not usually an obstacle to receiving Medicaid if an individual is in a nursing home. In many states, there is no cap on the amount of income an individual can have. Once an individual has been determined eligible, however, they must pay a certain amount of monthly income toward the cost of monthly medical care.
[P2423] There are, however, some states that impose an income cap in determining Medicaid eligibility for long-term care services.
[P2424] This means if income is over a certain level, an individual is not eligible for Medicaid, even if they have no resources to pay for care. This level is adjusted annually. States can set their income cap only as high as this amount.
[P2425] E.	Can I Still Be Eligible if My Income Is Greater Than the Income Cap?
[P2426] Federal law addresses the income cap problem by allowing people in nursing homes that live in income cap states to create an income trust. These trusts are formally called "qualifying income trusts" but are more commonly referred to as Miller trusts (after a court case brought by a person with that name). These income trusts let individuals make monthly deposits of any income that exceeds a state's income cap to an income trust. As a result, individuals keep income under the applicable income cap.  Individuals are required to name the state as beneficiary of any amount remaining in the trust after they die.
[P2427] F.	Are All Assets Counted in Medicaid Eligibility Determination?
[P2428] Assets fall into two categories — those that are not counted in the Medicaid eligibility determination and those whose value is counted in the eligibility determination. Depending on the situation a given asset might be considered countable or noncountable depending upon its use and value. Most notably, your home falls into this category.
[P2429] G.	How Is Ownership Share Determined?
[P2430] The value of assets that are owned solely by an individual and their spouse are counted in their entirety when determining eligibility for Medicaid.
[P2431] If an individual owns a bank account jointly with someone other than a spouse, the entire account balance is also considered the individual’s unless the co-owners are able to prove a different proportion of ownership.
[P2432] When an individual owns an asset, other than a bank account, jointly with someone other than a spouse, the value of the asset is apportioned equally among the owners unless the owners are able to prove a different proportion of ownership.
[P2433] H.	What Types of Assets Are Not Counted?
[P2434] As a general rule, Medicaid does not count personal belongings when determining Medicaid eligibility. This includes clothing, jewelry (including your wedding and engagement rings), home furnishings, appliances, and any other personal effects. In addition, the following assets are not counted in the Medicaid eligibility determination.
[P2435] I.	What About the Value of A Home?
[P2436] A home, regardless of its value, is not counted as a resource in determining eligibility for Medicaid as long as the home is the principal place of residence.
[P2437] A home is considered to be the principal place of residence as long as the individual seeking Medicaid lives in it. If the individual goes into a nursing facility, the home is still considered to be their principal place of residence if the individual expresses intent to return to the home at some time. Even if an individual does not express intent to return to the home, the home is exempt from being counted as a resource as long as a spouse or another dependent relative is living in the home.
[P2438] Only if none of these exceptions applies will the equity value of the home become a countable resource when determining eligibility for Medicaid.
[P2439] However, while the value of a home usually will not prevent an individual from qualifying for Medicaid in general, it may prevent Medicaid from paying for any long-term care services you need. Long-term care services include inpatient nursing facility services and home- and community-based services, as well as other services provided in the home such as home health services.
[P2440] The Deficit Reduction Act added a provision to the Medicaid law under which Medicaid cannot pay for long-term care services, even if an individual is otherwise eligible for Medicaid, if equity interest in a home exceeds $560,000 (states have the option to increase this limit to as much as $840,000). These amounts will be increased based on the annual percentage increase in the Consumer Price Index.
[P2441] This provision does not apply if a spouse or a child who is under age 21 or blind or disabled, is living in the home. In addition, states can waive this provision if the state determines that applying it would impose a hardship.
[P2442] Example 1: John Jones lives by himself at home and needs home healthcare. Without this care, he will have to go to a nursing home. The equity value of his home is $600,000. He has no other assets that would make him ineligible for Medicaid. His Medicaid application is approved; however, his state limits payment of long-term care services to those with home equity of $560,000 or less. As a result, Medicaid will pay only for physician services, hospitalizations, and other services that are not defined as "long-term care services". His home healthcare will not be paid for. In addition, if he were to go to a nursing home, Medicaid would not pay for his nursing home care.
[P2443] The rule capping home equity value may be waived if an individual is able to prove hardship as defined by their state.
[P2444] J.	Bank Accounts
[P2445] The balance of bank accounts, including checking, savings, and money market accounts, that an individual and their spouse own in the month of Medicaid application is a countable asset. Any income deposited to the accounts during that month is subtracted in determining its countable value. (Income remaining in the account in the month after its receipt becomes a countable asset.)
[P2446] Individuals must provide documentation of the current balance and the state may also ask for documentation of ownership and the balance of accounts owned in the five-year period prior to application. If there are withdrawals of significant value during this look back period, an individual may be asked to provide documentation of the purpose of that withdrawal.
[P2447] K.	Securities
[P2448] The value of stocks, bonds, mutual funds, or any other financial instrument is a countable asset. The value is their equity value in the month of application. The state may also ask for documentation of securities owned in the five-year period prior to application. If the securities were sold, an individual may be asked to provide documentation of how the proceeds were spent.
[P2449] L.	Vehicles
[P2450] One vehicle, regardless of its value, is not counted if its primary use is for a household's transportation. A vehicle includes a car, truck, SUV, or any other means of transportation including boats. A vehicle does not qualify for this exemption if its primary use is pleasure.
[P2451] If an individual owns more than one vehicle, they decide which vehicle to exempt. The equity value of all vehicles, other than the one designated as the primary means of transportation, is a countable asset.
[P2452] M.	Property Essential to Self-Support
[P2453] Property that is essential to trade or business and is currently being used by and/or providing income to an individual and their spouse is noncountable. For example, a farm or a boat used by a commercial fisherman is considered property essential to self-support.
[P2454] N.	Life Insurance
[P2455] If the face value (or policy amount) of all life insurance policies that an individual owns is $1,500 or less, then the cash surrender value of the life insurance is not counted in the Medicaid eligibility determination. The cash surrender value is the amount that could be obtained from the insurance if it were cashed in prior to death or maturity. This exemption also applies to a spouse.
[P2456] The face value of burial insurance or term life insurance without a cash surrender value is not counted when determining the total face value of life insurance.
[P2457] If the face value of all life insurance policies that an individual or their spouse own, exceeds $1,500, the cash surrender value becomes a countable asset.
[P2458] O.	Burial Arrangements
[P2459] Medicaid does not count burial space, burial funds meeting certain conditions, and irrevocable burial contracts in the Medicaid eligibility determination. These exclusions apply both to an individual and their spouse. Specifically:
[P2460] Burial space is a noncountable asset. Burial space includes the burial plot, gravesite, casket or any other burial repository, vault, headstone, and arrangements for opening and closing of the grave.
[P2461] Burial funds up to $1,500 each for you and your spouse are not countable for Medicaid eligibility purposes. Such funds may include burial contracts, savings or checking accounts designated for burial, and other revocable burial arrangements.
[P2462] Prepaid burial contracts are not countable as long as they are irrevocable. There is no regulatory cap on the amount that can be placed in the contract; however, some states' laws independently cap the amount that can be placed in such contracts.
[P2463] Medicaid applicants whose assets are above Medicaid limits often spend down their assets by converting them to these excludable burial arrangements. Doing so is allowable and is not considered a disqualifying transfer of assets.
[P2464] P.	Trusts
[P2465] There are three types of trusts that are not countable for Medicaid eligibility purposes:
[P2466] These are trusts that were established for the benefit of those who were under 65 and disabled when they were established as well as trusts that are composed solely of the income of someone who is in a medical institution. These are called special needs trusts, pooled trusts, and qualifying income (or Miller) trusts. They must meet certain Medicaid requirements to be exempt.
[P2467] The available principal of all other trusts is a countable asset.
[P2468] In the case of an irrevocable trust, any portion of the trust principal, or income (such as interest income) from the trust principal, that is not available to you and from which payment cannot be made to you is considered a disqualifying transfer of assets . The date of the transfer is the date the trust was established or, if later, the date on which payments from the trust was foreclosed.
[P2469] Q.	Annuities
[P2470] When an annuity can be converted to a lump sum, the lump sum amount, less any penalties for the conversion, is considered a countable asset.
[P2471] In addition, if an individual or their spouse purchased an annuity on or after February 8, 2006, and applied for Medicaid payment of nursing home or other long-term care services, the full value of the annuity will be considered a disqualifying transfer of assets unless the state is named as a remainder beneficiary of the annuity.
[P2472] Further, if an individual or someone on their behalf purchased an annuity after February 8, 2006, and they applied for Medicaid payment for nursing home or other long-term care services, the full value of the annuity will be considered a disqualifying transfer of assets, unless the following requirements are met:
[P2473] The annuity is an employee pension, Roth IRA, or account or trust established in accordance with section 408 of the Internal Revenue code; or
[P2474] The annuity:
[P2475] is irrevocable and nonassignable;
[P2476] is actuarially sound compared to the beneficiary's life expectancy as determined by standards established by the Social Security Administration [offsite];
[P2477] provides for payments in equal amounts during the term of the annuity; and
[P2478] does not defer payment or provide for a balloon payment.
[P2479] These additional requirements do not apply to an annuity purchased by a spouse.
[P2480] R.	Retirement Funds Other Than Annuities
[P2481] Retirement funds are work-related plans for providing income when employment ends. These include pension or retirement plans from an employer, individual retirement accounts (IRAs), and plans for the self-employed, sometimes called Keogh plans.
[P2482] A retirement fund is a countable asset if a retiree is able to withdraw a lump sum from the plan. As a rule, such funds are accessible only before the fund begins to generate income payments. The countable amount is the lump sum less any penalties for early withdrawal.
[P2483] S.	Other Assets
[P2484] A number of other assets that are excluded for eligibility in the Supplemental Security Income (SSI) program are also excluded for Medicaid eligibility purposes. These are assets that are not commonly available to individuals, and they are described at the Social Security Administration website.
[P2485] Any other real or personal property that an individual or their spouse own is counted in the Medicaid eligibility determination.
[P2486] T.	Are There Exceptions to the $2,000 Asset Limit?
[P2487] States have the option to allow individuals to have more than $2,000 in assets.
[P2488] They may further liberalize the standard for individuals who own long-term care insurance and reside in states participating in the Long-Term Care Partnership Program. These states have added provisions to their Medicaid rules that give people financial incentives to purchase private long-term care insurance that meets the requirements of their state's program. These incentives include both an increase in the amount of assets a Medicaid applicant can have and an exemption from estate recovery of those assets.
[P2489] Example: Sarah Evans lives in a state which participates in the Long-Term Care Partnership Program. Several years ago she purchased a long-term care insurance policy that provided $100,000 in benefits. She has been in a nursing home for a couple of years and has used up most of her insurance benefits. She has $100,000 in savings, which normally would be significantly higher than the Medicaid eligibility limits. However, since she owns long-term care insurance and lives in a Partnership state, she meets Medicaid asset eligibility levels. She would be able to keep as much as $102,000 (the benefit amount of her insurance plus the $2,000 Medicaid eligibility limit).
[P2490] U.	How Does Medicaid Determine How Much My Spouse Can Keep in Assets?
[P2491] If an individual is married to someone who is living in the community (called the community spouse), the assets owned by the individual and their spouse are counted in the Medicaid eligibility determination. Individuals are allowed to keep $2,000, but their spouse can keep much more to ensure that they have enough money for future needs. This amount is referred to as the spousal resource allowance.
[P2492] It is based on the total amount of countable assets owned by either an individual or both the individual and a spouse as of the date permanently institutionalized (not the date of Medicaid application). The home, one vehicle, personal household belongings, and burial accounts are all exempt (or noncountable) assets when determining total countable asset value. Some states also use rules for establishing a spousal allowance for their home- and community-based services.
[P2493] Federal law dictates both the maximum and minimum amounts that a spouse can keep. States may adopt these or other standards as long as their standards do not go above the maximum or below the minimum specified by the Federal law.
[P2494] By way of example, in 2025, the maximum amount your spouse can keep is one half of combined total assets, not to exceed $157,920. Some states use lesser amounts; this is the maximum.
[P2495] For example, if a couple has $300,000 in assets, the spousal allowance would be $157,920. If the couple had $140,000 in assets, the spousal allowance would be $70,000.
[P2496] The minimum amount a spouse can keep (2025) is $31,584 even if that amount is greater than one-half the couple’s assets.
[P2497] For example, if a couple had $40,000 in assets, the spousal allowance would be $31,584 in 2025. If a couple had $14,000 in assets, the spousal allowance would be $14,000.
[P2498] These amounts are adjusted each January based on changes in the Consumer Price Index.
[P2499] If an individual thinks the spousal resource allowance is inadequate to meet a spouse's future needs, a request may be made to adjustment to this allowance. The request for a hearing may only be made after a determination of Medicaid eligibility — either an approval or denial — has been made.
[P2500] V.	How Does Medicaid Decide to Increase the Spousal Allowance?
[P2501] The state will take the following steps to decide if the asset allowance should be increased:
[P2502] Determine how much income could be generated by the existing asset allowance;
[P2503] Determine if the interest income, in combination with other income available to a spouse, brings a spouse's income up to the minimum monthly maintenance needs allowance;
[P2504] If the generated interest income does not bring a spouse's income up to the minimum standard, the state will allow an individual to allocate some or all of their income to their spouse;
[P2505] If a spouse's income is still less than the minimum amount, the fair hearing officer may increase the asset allowance so that interest income generated from the assets may bring a spouse's income up to the minimum amount.
[P2506] W.	Transfer of Assets Rules
[P2507] The Medicaid transfer of assets rules apply to anyone applying for Medicaid coverage for long-term care services, including care provided in a nursing home, intermediate care facility for the mentally disabled, or any other medical institution as well as home- and community-based care provided under a state's waiver for persons who would need to be in a nursing home if they did not receive the home care services. States may also apply the transfer of assets rules to other noninstitutionalized persons for long-term care services provided in the home such as home healthcare.
[P2508] These rules apply to any asset transfers made either by an individual or their spouse.
[P2509] X.	What Is Considered a Nonpermissible Transfer of Assets?
[P2510] As a general rule, giving away assets without receiving something of essentially equal value in return is considered a transfer of assets for less than fair market value unless it is considered a permissible transfer.
[P2511] In addition, if an individual takes action to avoid the receipt of an asset to which they are entitled, that may be considered a transfer of assets for less than fair market value. Some examples of such transfers are irrevocably waiving a right to pension income, waiving the right to receive an inheritance, or not accessing an injury settlement to which an individual is entitled.
[P2512] Other examples of nonpermissible transfers are:
[P2513] Elimination of a joint ownership share. If an individual, or someone acting on their behalf, takes action to reduce or eliminate ownership share or control of a jointly held asset, the action is considered a transfer of assets.
[P2514] Trusts. Payments from both revocable and irrevocable trusts that are made are allowable. Any other payments are considered to be transferred assets. In the case of an irrevocable trust, any portion of the trust principal or income from the trust principal that is not available to you and from which payment cannot be made to you is considered a disqualifying transfer of assets. The date of the transfer is the date the trust was established or, if later, the date on which payments from the trust was foreclosed.
[P2515] These rules do not apply to special needs trusts, pooled trusts, or qualifying income trusts as defined for Medicaid eligibility purposes, all of which are noncountable assets.
[P2516] Annuities. If an annuity is purchased and an application for Medicaid payment of nursing home or other long-term care services is made, the full value of the annuity will be considered a disqualifying transfer of assets unless the state is named as a remainder beneficiary of the annuity, and unless the requirements named above are met. Further, if an annuity is purchased and an individual applies for Medicaid payment for nursing home or other long-term care services, the full value of the annuity will be considered a disqualifying transfer of assets, unless the requirements named above are met.
[P2517] 1. The annuity is an employee pension, Roth IRA, or account or trust established in accordance with section 408 of the Internal Revenue code; or
[P2518] 2. The annuity:
[P2519] is irrevocable and nonassignable;
[P2520] is actuarially sound compared to the beneficiary's life expectancy as determined by standards established by the Social Security Administration [offsite];
[P2521] provides for payments in equal amounts during the term of the annuity; and
[P2522] does not defer payment or provide for a balloon payment.
[P2523] Promissory notes, loans, and mortgages. The value of the outstanding balance on a loan, mortgage, or promissory note as of the date of your application for Medicaid is considered a disqualifying transfer of assets unless it:
[P2524] is actuarially sound compared to the beneficiary's life expectancy as determined by standards established by the Social Security Administration [offsite];
[P2525] provides for payments to be made in equal amounts during the term of the loan with no deferral or balloon payments made; and
[P2526] prohibits cancellation of the balance upon the death of the lender.
[P2527] Life estates. Life estates in another person's home are considered a disqualifying transfer of assets unless the purchaser lives in that home for at least one year after the purchase date.
[P2528] Y.	How Does Medicaid View a Transfer of Assets?
[P2529] As discussed, Medicaid rules do not allow an individual to reduce assets to the Medicaid limit by giving them away for less than fair market value before they apply for benefits.   In evaluating an asset transfer, states consider whose assets were transferred, to whom they were transferred, when the asset was transferred, and the purpose of the transfer.
[P2530] If the transfer is determined to be disqualifying, the state establishes a disqualification or penalty period during which you may not receive Medicaid payment for long-term care services. The length of the penalty period and the start date of the penalty period depend on when the transfer took place, the amount of the transfer, and the average private cost of nursing home care in the state where you live.
[P2531] Z.	If I Transfer Assets, How Long Will I Be Disqualified from Coverage?
[P2532] States establish the length of the period of ineligibility (the penalty period) by dividing the total value of assets transferred by the average monthly cost of private nursing home payment in the state.
[P2533] Example: Brad Davis gave each of his two granddaughters $10,000 two months before he had a stroke and had to be admitted to a nursing home. He had enough in savings left to pay for nursing home care for five months, but then needed to apply for Medicaid in February 2025. His eligibility worker determines he is eligible for Medicaid in March 2025, but decides his gift to his grandchildren is a disqualifying transfer of assets.
[P2534] In determining the length of Brad's penalty period, his eligibility worker divides the amount transferred ($20,000) by the private cost of nursing home care ($5,000 in his state). The penalty period is four months.
[P2535] When Does the Penalty Period Begin?
[P2536] The penalty period begins on the date on which an individual is eligible for Medicaid, and is receiving institutional care that Medicaid would pay for were it not for the imposition of the penalty.
[P2537] Example: Brad Davis gave $20,000 to his granddaughters in June 2025. His penalty period begins in March 2025, the month he is otherwise eligible for Medicaid. It will last for four months until the end of June 2025. During this time he must find resources to pay for his nursing home care privately.
[P2538] AA.	More about Permissible Asset Transfers to Family Members
[P2539] A number of transfers may be made permissibly at any point in time prior to the Medicaid application without adversely affecting your Medicaid eligibility. As a general rule, any transfer of assets is permissible when made to your spouse or on behalf of your spouse. Specifically, the following transfers are permissible:
[P2540] The home or any other assets you owned were transferred:
[P2541] to a spouse or to another solely for the benefit of the spouse;
[P2542] from a spouse to another solely for the benefit of the spouse;
[P2543] to a blind or disabled child or to a trust created solely for the benefit of that child.
[P2544] An individual may also transfer a home to:
[P2545] A child who is under the age of 21;
[P2546] A sibling, provided they jointly owned the home and lived there for at least one year before an individual’s admission to the medical institution;
[P2547] A child who is not blind or disabled or under 21 who lived in the home for at least two years before admission to the medical institutional and provided care that allowed the individual to continue to live at home rather than in an institution.
[P2548] Example: Hannah Adams was diagnosed with Alzheimer's in March 2025. As the disease progressed, she thought it would be wise to remove her name from all her assets, including her home, and transfer them to her son, Jake, who had been blind since birth. She completed the transfers in August 2026 and applied for Medicaid home- and community-based care in November 2026. The transfers were made during the five-year look back period, but since they were made to her blind child, they were not considered a disqualifying transfer of assets.
[P2549] BB.	Other Permissible Asset Transfers
[P2550] A transfer may also be considered permissible if an individual can show that:
[P2551] They intended to dispose of the asset at fair market value or for other valuable consideration;
[P2552] The asset was transferred for a purpose other than to qualify for Medicaid; or
[P2553] The transferred asset was returned.
[P2554] CC.	How Much Money Will Medicaid Let Me Keep for Personal Needs?
[P2555] Medicaid allows an individual to keep a small amount of money for monthly personal needs, such as haircuts, in a nursing home (Personal Needs Allowance, or PNA). This amount must be at least $30, but states can allow larger amounts up to $200.
[P2556] If an individual is receiving home- and community-based services, the state must take into account food and shelter costs in addition to any personal needs when it sets this amount. The allowed amount varies from state to state but is usually a percentage of the Supplemental Security Income (SSI) standard.
[P2557] DD.	How Much Does Medicaid Allow for Other Expenses?
[P2558] Medicaid makes allowances in certain instances for medical expenses and health insurance premiums, and for home maintenance when an individual is expected to be able to leave a nursing home within six months.
[P2559] The medical expense allowance lets you keep money for medical expenses not paid for by third parties. These include health insurance premiums such as Medicare and other necessary medical or remedial care expenses that are not paid by Medicaid.
[P2560] The home maintenance allowance lets an individual keep money for maintenance of their home when their physician certifies they are able to return home within six months. States are not required to give you this allowance. Those states that do give you an allowance decide the amount that is allowed.
[P2561] EE.	How Does Medicaid Decide How Much Money My Spouse Can Keep?
[P2562] The income allowance for a spouse is based on a formula in Federal law. This amount cannot be more than a set amount per month unless you are subject to a court order in a greater amount for the support of your spouse.
[P2563] In determining the allowance, the following amounts are totaled:
[P2564] Standard maintenance amount; and
[P2565] Allowance for shelter expenses.
[P2566] Shelter expenses include rent, mortgage, taxes, insurance, condominium maintenance fees, and utilities.
[P2567] The total of the standard maintenance amount and shelter expenses is called the minimum monthly maintenance needs allowance and is compared to a spouse's gross income. If a spouse's income is less than this amount, the difference becomes the spousal allowance. If a spouse's income is greater than this amount, there is no allowance.
[P2568] Her husband can give her $1,376 of his income each month for her needs. If his income is less than this amount, all of his income will be available to her.
[P2569] States may use this same formula if an individual is receiving home- and community-based services or they may choose to let individuals set aside another amount based on what they think a spouse needs for food, shelter, and other day-to-day needs. The maximum amount is adjusted each January to reflect changes in the Consumer Price Index, and the standard maintenance amount and shelter allowance are adjusted each July to reflect changes in the Federal poverty level.
[P2570] FF.	Does Medicaid Make an Allowance for Family Members Living in My Home?
[P2571] Medicaid makes an allowance for family members living in the home with a spouse. Family members include minor children as well as children, parents, or siblings you are allowed to claim as dependents for income tax purposes.
[P2572] The family allowance is one-third the amount by which the standard maintenance needs allowance of at least $1,650 exceeds the family member's gross monthly income.
[P2573] Amy's dad can give her $450 each month for her needs in addition to the $1,376 he gives to her mother. If his income is less than the combined amounts, all his income will be available to her and her mother.
[P2574] States may use this same formula if an individual is receiving home- and community-based services or they may choose to let an individual set aside another amount that is based on what they think a family needs for food, shelter, and other day-to-day needs.
[P2575] After determining which of these allowances apply, the state notifies an individual of the amounts it has allowed for deductions as well as how much the individual must pay each month toward the cost of care. This amount is adjusted whenever income, expenses, or circumstances change.
[P2576] 12.4	Medicaid Estate Recovery
[P2577] A.	What Is Medicaid Estate Recovery?
[P2578] When a person who has been on Medicaid dies, states are required, under Federal law, to recover from that person's estate, up to the total amount spent by Medicaid on that person's behalf when they were alive.
[P2579] Who Is Subject to Estate Recovery?
[P2580] States must recover from the estates of permanently institutionalized people of any age as well as from the estates of individuals age 55 or older on whose behalf the state paid Medicaid benefits.
[P2581] What Parts of My Estate Are Potentially Subject to Estate Recovery?
[P2582] States are required to recover from all probated estates, and they can recover from any property that is in the estate, including the home. States may also recover from assets that pass to heirs outside of probate, such as annuities and trusts.
[P2583] Are Any Estates Exempt from Estate Recovery?
[P2584] Yes, certain estates are exempt. The most notable exemption is that estates that pass to a surviving spouse are exempt from recovery, as long as the spouse is alive.
[P2585] States, however, may recover from the spouse's estate after their death.
[P2586] There are a few other exemptions as well, such as when estate recovery would cause undue hardship on the heirs to the estate.
[P2587] E.	Will Medicaid Put a Lien on My Home?
[P2588] Maybe. States are allowed to put a lien on your home when you start receiving long-term care services under Medicaid, but they are not required to. Liens are used by states to ensure that any equity that you have in your home remains available to recovery. However, Federal law also puts restrictions on when a state can place a lien on your home. For instance, Medicaid cannot put a lien on your home if your spouse lives there.
[P2589] F.	When Will My State Tell Me about Its Estate Recovery Program?
[P2590] States are required to notify you when you apply for Medicaid that your estate may be subject to estate recovery. They must also notify your estate when they begin the recovery process.
[P2591] G.	What Is the Process for Estate Recovery?
[P2592] After a Medicaid recipient dies, estate recovery usually begins with a letter sent to a surviving family member and/or the estate executor informing them of the state's claim on the recipient's estate.
[P2593] 13.0.  Medicare
[P2594] Although their names are similar, Medicaid and Medicare are very different programs. Medicare is an entitlement program funded entirely at the federal level.  Its primary focus is on the older population.
[P2595] As discussed earlier, Medicare is a health insurance program for:
[P2596] people age 65 or older,
[P2597] people under age 65 with certain disabilities, and
[P2598] people of all ages with End-Stage Renal Disease (permanent kidney failure requiring dialysis or a kidney transplant).
[P2599] The Medicare Prescription Drug, Improvement, and Modernization Act of 2003 (the Medicare Modernization Act or the Act) was passed by Congress on December 8, 2003.  The legislation provided a prescription drug benefit for Medicare beneficiaries, a temporary prescription drug coverage program with drug discount cards, a new Medicare managed care program and reimbursement and coverage changes to both Medicare Part A and Part B.  Many believe that the provisions of the Medicare Modernization Act relating to the prescription drug benefit and the private fee for service coverage were the most significant changes to the Medicare program since its inception.
[P2600] According to the Administrator of the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid (CMS), the Act’s primary focus was on prevention and personalized care.
[P2601] The major changes to Medicare coverage as a result of the Act were changes in Covered Benefits.  Specifically:
[P2602] The Act added an initial preventive physical examination if performed within the first six months of Part B coverage. The examination benefit includes an EKG but excludes other diagnostic tests. (Section 611) (Trans. No. 417, Dec. 22, 2004)
[P2603] The Act provided coverage for cardiovascular screening blood tests performed once every two years. (Section 612) (Trans. No. 408, Dec. 17, 2004)
[P2604] The Act added diabetes-screening tests for Medicare beneficiaries who have one or more of the risk factors specifically listed. Medicare will pay for no more than two tests per year. (Section 613) (Trans. No. 409, Dec. 21, 2004)
[P2605] The Act expanded coverage for chiropractor services to include diagnostic and other services that the chiropractor is legally authorized to perform in the State in which they are licensed. The modification will be implemented with a two year demonstration projects in four sites—two urban and two rural. B. National and Local Coverage Determinations
[P2606] National Coverage Decisions (NCDs) are defined in the Medicare Modernization Act as a determination by the Secretary whether a particular claim or services is covered on a national basis. The Act requires the Secretary to make public the factors it uses to make coverage decisions and to develop guidance. The Secretary is required to make a decision on requests for NCDs within six months if no technology assessment or deliberation by the Medicare Coverage Advisory Committee is required or within nine months if an outside assessment or deliberation is needed. The Secretary must publish the proposed decision with a thirty-day public comment period. The Secretary must then make a final decision within sixty days of the end of the comment period.
[P2607] The Act requires the Secretary to develop a plan for coverage decisions to be consistent on a national basis and for deciding whether an LCD should be adopted nationally.
[P2608] Lastly, the Act authorized CMS to expand its cost coverage of clinical trials by paying for routine costs in certain Investigational Device Exemption Category A trials. The Act did not affect coverage for category B devices and the category A device itself remains uncovered.
[P2609] In 2010, two pieces of legislation were enacted.  The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (PPACA) was signed into law on March 23, 2010 and The Healthcare and Education Reconciliation Act of 2010 (HCERA) was signed into law March 30, 2010. This legislation included several provisions related to the Medicare program. Among other things, the legislation:
[P2610] Gradually phased in coverage in the Medicare Part D coverage gap (the law on March 23, 2010, and The Healthcare rate in the gap from 100 percent of total drug costs in 2010 to 25 percent in 2020; the coverage gap was reduced to zero starting in 2025 by the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022.
[P2611] Provided a one-time $250 rebate for Part D enrollees with any spending in the coverage gap in 2010. (Section 3315, as superseded by Section 1101(a) of HCERA)
[P2612] Established a Medicare coverage discount program to provide a 50 percent discount on brand-name drugs to Part D enrollees with spending in the coverage gap. Drug manufactures are required to provide a 50 percent discount off negotiated prices on brand-name drugs and biologics covered under Part D plans for Part D enrollees with spending in the coverage gap. (Section 3301, as modified by Section 1101 of HCERA)
[P2613] Phased in a reduction in coinsurance for generic drugs in the coverage gap, and a reduction in coinsurance for brand-name drugs in the gap, and reduced the beneficiary coinsurance rate for both brands and generics from 100 percent in 2010 to 25 percent in 2020, until enrollees qualify for catastrophic coverage. Reduced the catastrophic coverage threshold between 2014 and 2019 to provide additional support for those with relatively high drug costs. (Section 3301, as modified by Section 1101 of HCERA)
[P2614] Authorized Medicare coverage of personalized prevention plan services, including an annual comprehensive health risk assessment. Required the Secretary to publish guidelines for the health risk assessment.
[P2615] Reimbursed providers 100 percent of the physician fee schedule amount with no adjustment for deductible or coinsurance for personalized prevention plan services when these services are provided in an outpatient setting. (Section 4103, as modified by Section 10402)
[P2616] Eliminated cost-sharing, including coinsurance and deductibles, for prevention benefits that are rated A or B by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF). Authorized the Secretary of HHS to modify coverage of Medicare-covered preventive services to conform to the USPSTF recommendations. (Sections 4104-4105)
[P2617] Expanded coverage to individuals who have been exposed to environmental health hazards from living in an area subject to an emergency declaration made as of June 17, 2009, and have developed certain health conditions as a result, effective upon enactment. (Section 10323)
[P2618] Modified the income-related monthly Part B premium, by freezing the income thresholds for the income-related Part B premium at 2010 levels ($85,000/individual, $170,000/couple) through 2019, beginning in 2011. (Section 3402); as of 2025, the thresholds are $106,000 for an individual and $212,000 for a married couple filing their taxes jointly.

[P2621] 14.0 Long-term Care Partnership Program
[P2622] Public funds—principally Medicaid funds—expended to provide long-term care services are substantial and likely to increase significantly in the years ahead as members of the Baby Boom generation begin to enter their retirement years. For many years efforts have been made to staunch the flow of these funds. One of the most important efforts is known as the Partnership for Long-term Care.
[P2623] 14.1 Partnership for Long-term Care Began in 1980s
[P2624] In the 1980s the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation—the nation’s largest philanthropy devoted exclusively to American healthcare—funded an initiative that would initially culminate in a demonstration project in 1987 known as the Partnership for Long-term Care. The goal of the project was to re-direct the burden of funding long-term care away from Medicaid and onto the shoulders of insurers by encouraging more people to purchase long-term care insurance coverage.
[P2625] Under the Partnership for Long-term Care program, the states were brought together with private insurers in order to create a program—aimed generally at individuals with moderate levels of income and assets—that would apply special Medicaid eligibility rules for participants enabling them to participate in Medicaid funding for long-term care costs without requiring they become impoverished.
[P2626] In order to participate in the Partnership program, individuals were required to purchase long-term care insurance meeting specific coverage requirements. By requiring the purchase of long-term care insurance by individuals who might not otherwise purchase it, designers of the program hoped to enable the states to avoid some of the costs for long-term care services.
[P2627] Review Question:

[P2632] 14.1.1 Three Partnership Models Emerge
[P2633] Four states implemented Partnership for Long-term Care programs in the early 1990s. Those states—California, Connecticut, Indiana and New York—initially selected two different Partnership models. A third model has since been added, and Partnership programs may involve a:
[P2634] Dollar-for-dollar model;
[P2635] Total Asset Protection model; and/or
[P2636] Hybrid model.
[P2637] Let’s briefly examine each of these Partnership models.
[P2638] 14.1.1.1 The Dollar-for-Dollar Partnership Model
[P2639] The dollar-for-dollar Partnership model protects a long-term care recipient’s assets up to an amount equal to the amount of long-term care insurance coverage purchased. So, if an individual purchased $250,000 of long-term care insurance benefits, $250,000 of their assets would be protected from Medicaid’s spend-down requirement.
[P2640] For example, under this model a program participant who had exhausted private long-term care insurance benefits but continued to require long-term care, would be able to access Medicaid for funding the care even though they still had $250,000 in assets. The states choosing this model at the time the Program was initiated were:
[P2641] California;
[P2642] Connecticut; and
[P2643] Indiana.

[P2649] 14.1.1.2 The Total Asset Protection Partnership Model
[P2650] The total asset protection Partnership model shields all the program participant’s assets from Medicaid’s spend-down requirement. However, in order to participate in this expanded program model, a participant is required to purchase a long-term care insurance policy providing a specified amount of benefits.
[P2651] Although the actual minimum benefits required for participation in the total asset protection model are defined by the individual states, the only state that opted for the total asset protection model—New York—initially required that Partnership long-term care insurance policies provide:
[P2652] Nursing home coverage for 3 years; and
[P2653] Home healthcare coverage for 6 years.
[P2654] 14.1.1.3 A Hybrid Partnership Model Introduced
[P2655] Late in the decade of the 1990s, a third Partnership model was begun that offers program participants the choice of protecting:
[P2656] A specified dollar amount of assets equal to the total long-term care insurance benefits purchased; or
[P2657] All assets.
[P2658] This model, referred to as a hybrid Partnership model was offered by Indiana beginning in 1998 and gives program participants the option of protecting some or all their assets. New York subsequently added a dollar-for-dollar option to its total asset protection program.

[P2665] 14.2 Results Experienced in Initial Partnership Programs
[P2666] Not surprisingly, the states involved in the Partnership programs and the federal government collected data concerning various aspects of the demonstration project. Among the data collected are the following:
[P2667] The demographics of participants in the Programs;
[P2668] The long-term care policies purchased under the Programs; and
[P2669] The policy benefits accessed by Program participants.
[P2670] The data reported in this section are taken from the Government Accountability Office briefing to Congressional staff dated September 9, 2005.
[P2671] 14.2.1 Initial Partnership Program Participant Demographics
[P2672] Demographic data concerning initial participants in the Partnership for Long-term Care programs indicated that partnership policyowners at the time of their policy purchase had the following characteristics:
[P2673] The average age ranged from 58 in Connecticut to 63 in New York;
[P2674] Female participants led male participants with 56% (Connecticut) to 59% (California and New York) being women;
[P2675] The majority of purchasers—70% (California) to 78% (Indiana)—were married; and
[P2676] The overwhelming majority of participants—92% (Connecticut) to 95% (New York) were first-time purchasers of long-term care insurance.
[P2677] The majority of Program participants in California, Connecticut and Indiana reported having total assets in excess of $350,000 at the time of purchase. (New York does not collect asset data on Program participants.) Approximately one-half of Program participants in the three states reported average monthly household incomes in excess of $5,000.

[P2684] 14.2.2 Partnership Policy Benefits Accessed
[P2685] As you learned earlier in this course, insurance carriers have sold about 10 million long-term care insurance policies.  Of the roughly 7 million of these policies that remain current, the industry sold about 4 million through individual agents and slightly more than 2 million through employers or groups.  These policies specifically cover the costs of long-term care services (2025 figures) that can include nursing home care (median cost of $111,325 per year for a semi-private room), assisted living facilities ($58,794 per year), and home healthcare ($34 per hour for a certified aide). Over the course of one year, long-term care insurance policies paid $4 billion in claims on behalf of disabled policyholders, a small fraction of the over $200 billion in national long-term care spending at that time.
[P2686] The overwhelming majority of Partnership policies purchased provide comprehensive—at home and nursing home—care.  Most states also require that such policies be tax qualified, provide specific consumer protections, and include inflation protection.
[P2687] 14.3 Legislative Action Imposes then Lifts Moratorium on Partnership Program
[P2688] In the Omnibus Budget Reconciliation Act (OBRA) of 1993, the federal government enacted restrictions on the Partnership program by imposing a moratorium on program initiation in any other states; however, the four states in which a Partnership program had already been established were permitted to continue their programs. Congressional concern leading to the moratorium was that the use of Medicaid funds to pay for long-term care for individuals with substantial assets was inappropriate.
[P2689] Following a subsequent examination of the Partnership program and its benefits by the Government Accountability Office and a reevaluation of the program, the federal government lifted the moratorium on Partnership programs under the provisions of the Deficit Reduction Act (DRA).
[P2691] 14.3.1  The Deficit Reduction Act of 2005
[P2692] The DRA set forth requirements that must be met in order for a State plan amendment (SPA) to meet the definition of a Qualified Partnership. These include the following:
[P2693] The LTC insurance policy must meet several conditions. These conditions include meeting the requirements of specific portions of the National Association of Insurance Commissioners’ (NAIC) LTC Insurance Model Regulations and Model Act.
[P2694] The Qualified Partnership SPA must provide that the State Insurance Commissioner, or other appropriate State authority, certify to the State Medicaid agency that the policy meets the specified requirements of the NAIC Model Regulations and Model Act. The State Medicaid agency may also accept certification from the same authority that the policy meets the Internal Revenue Code definition of a qualified LTC insurance policy, and that it includes the requisite inflation protections. If the State Medicaid agency accepts the certification of the Commissioner or other authority, it is not required to independently verify that policies meet these requirements. Changes in a Partnership policy after it is issued will not affect the applicability of the disregard of resources as long as the policy continues to meet all of the requirements referenced above.
[P2695] If an individual has an existing LTC insurance policy that does not qualify as a Partnership policy due to the issue date of the policy, and that policy is exchanged for another, the State Insurance Commissioner or other State authority must determine the issue date for the policy that is received in exchange. To be a qualified Partnership policy, the issue date must not be earlier than the effective date of the Qualified Partnership SPA.
[P2696] The State Medicaid agency must provide information and technical assistance to the State insurance department regarding the Partnership and the relationship of LTC insurance policies to Medicaid. This information must be incorporated into the training of individuals who will sell LTC insurance policies in the State.
[P2697] 3. The State insurance department must provide assurance to the State Medicaid agency that anyone who sells a policy under the Partnership receives training and demonstrates an understanding of Partnership policies and their relationship to public and private coverage of LTC.
[P2698] The issuer of the policy must provide reports to the Secretary, in accordance with regulations to be developed by the Secretary, which include notice of when benefits are paid under the policy, the amount of those benefits, notice of termination of the policy, and any other information the Secretary determines is appropriate.
[P2699] The State may not impose any requirement affecting the terms or benefits of a Partnership policy unless it imposes the same requirements on all LTC insurance policies.
[P2700] A SPA that provides for a Qualified State LTC Insurance Partnership under the amended section 191 7(b)(1 )(C) of the Act may be effective for policies issued on or after a date specified in the SPA, but not earlier than the first day of the first calendar quarter in which the SPA is submitted.
[P2701] The DRA requires the Secretary to develop standards regarding the portability of Partnership policies by January 1, 2007. These standards will address reciprocal treatment of policies among Partnership States. The Secretary is also required to develop regulations regarding reporting requirements for issuers of Partnership policies and related data sets. It is not necessary for States to wait for these standards and rules to be promulgated before submitting a Partnership SPA. A State may submit a Partnership SPA at any time after the effective date of the DRA.

[P2703] The policy must cover a person who was a resident of the Qualified Partnership State when coverage first became effective. If a policy is exchanged for another, the residency rule applies to the issuance of the original policy.
