[P2890] 14.4  State Partnership Programs
[P2892] As a result of the lifting of the Partnership moratorium, states became again free to establish such programs. Although not all states have instituted Long-term Care Partnership programs, many have.  Although we discussed all partnership models earlier, note that the DRA specifies that all new LTC Partnership programs use the dollar-for-dollar methodology.  See Appendix A for specific legislation relating to the program in states in which you do business.
[P2893] Creation and implementation of a Partnership program is a complex undertaking by States, as is evidenced, by the continuing legislative efforts to track the sale of these products to consumers.  According to the Robert J. Wood Foundation, the successful implementation of Partnership program will require the input and effort of a variety of stakeholders—state policy-makers, private industry and consumers.
[P2894] Partnership efforts, involve many facets of state government including the Medicaid agency, Governor’s office, state budget office, state unit on aging, state legislature, and the Office of Insurance. For states with enabling legislation prior to the DRA, then modifications to that legislation may be needed to conform to the requirements of the DRA.
[P2895] Lastly, to create a successful balance between coverage and costs, states must make every effort to ensure that consumers are well informed about what they are purchasing, the level of benefits to be provided, and what is protected.
[P2897] A Case Study:  Ethel
[P2898] In a case study crafted by the George Brown Warren School of Social Work for the State of Missouri, the following is an example of an average purchaser of long-term care insurance through the partnership program. 

Ethel is a 50-year-old woman who purchases a partnership program in year 1 with an annual premium of $1,474 and three years of policy protection. Twenty years later, she has a stroke and requires in-home services to provide long-term care. At the time of her stroke, she has $100,000 in assets. The estimated monthly cost of long-term care that year is $1,724 or $20,688 per year. For the next 36 months, she is provided coverage through her LTC partnership policy. At the end of the 36 months, she is eligible to protect a total of $62,064 of her assets based on the value of her LTC partnership policy. For the next 22 months, she uses her assets to pay for her long-term care. At this time, she has spent down her assets to $62,064 and is now eligible for Medicaid Insurance. The total estimated savings in Missouri was $66,098 for this individual. However, this one individual spent a total of $71,838 on premiums and out-of-pocket expenses combined, to save a total of $62,064 in assets.
[P2905] NOTE:  To determine the overall savings to Missouri we used the following formula from the table above:  D+E-C=F.  This formula accounts for the Policy Coverage, Out-of-Pocket Expense and Tax Deduction amount give this individual.
[P2907] While Ethel actually spent more on her long-term care, including insurance and care costs, the state of Missouri actually saved money on her long-term care needs thanks to Medicaid’s financial eligibility requirements, as well as Ethel’s carefully accrued lifetime savings. This case study illustrates the potential impact of a partnership program on Missouri’s state budget from one individual case, which brings into question the economic impact of these partnership programs on the four pilot states. For partnership programs to be deemed a success, not only should they result in a change in the demographics of the purchasers, as mentioned previously, but they should also result in significant cost-savings to the states in which they have been implemented. A review of the data gathered in each of the four pilot states may shed some light on the true economic impact of the long-term care insurance partnership programs and whether they are fulfilling their desired goal.
[P2909] 14.4.1  Impact of Partnership Programs on Medicaid Spending
[P2910] According to the American Association of Retired Persons (AARP), whether the partnership programs will help save the Medicaid program money is a major policy question.  Proponents argue that, by deferring the use of Medicaid for those who otherwise would spend down their assets and qualify for benefits, people who purchase partnership policies will reduce Medicaid’s spending on LTC.
[P2911] Others argue that partnership programs will qualify people for Medicaid who otherwise would never have used the program because their own assets would have paid for their LTC costs.  An additional argument is that if Medicaid is intended to be a safety net for people with few assets and limited incomes, partnership programs could deplete Medicaid resources by qualifying people for benefits who can, and should, finance their own services. Partnership policies have the potential to save Medicaid dollars if they are purchased by people who would not have bought other (nonpartnership) policies. If, instead, these policies replace LTCI policies that do not include Medicaid asset protection, then they may result in higher Medicaid spending. So far, the data are inconclusive because few purchasers have begun to use benefits.
[P2912] 14.4.2  Issues and Concerns
[P2914] AARP advises that with the likely expansion of LTCI partnership programs into additional states, consumer education is critical. The addition of a partnership option in a growing number of states will add a layer of complexity to the already-difficult process of deciding whether to buy LTCI and, if so, which policy to purchase.  While partnership programs allow purchasers to protect a certain level of assets if they deplete their insurance benefits and qualify for Medicaid, many consumers do not understand that Medicaid eligibility is not automatic. To qualify for Medicaid, individuals must meet the state’s income and functional eligibility criteria, which may change by the time they apply for Medicaid.
[P2915] 14.4.3  Consumer and Agent Education
[P2916] Consumer and insurance agent education are vital components of any Partnership program.  The role of the insurance agents is to ensure that consumers understand their options as well as the terms and conditions of any given policy. Foremost, insurance agents must guarantee that consumers understand the criteria that will allow them to become eligible for both private LTC coverage and, if necessary, Medicaid.  The NAIC requires delivery of a Shopper’s Guide to consumers for this purpose.
[P2917] Consumers generally do not understand one agent designation over another, or to know whether a designation indicates expertise on the part of the agent. While insurance companies provide extensive information about their products to agents, it is often related to marketing and sales rather than detailed information about how a policy works.
[P2918] The advice agents give consumers can have long-lasting effects. For instance, agents sometimes don’t offer inflation protection or don’t recommend its purchase because of the added premium cost. Yet this protection is critical for consumers who aren’t expected to use their benefits for years to come. Adding inflation protection does add cost to the premium, but affordability needs to be balanced across all the elements of an LTCI policy. Consumers must understand at the point of sale, for instance, that lack of inflation protection will gradually reduce the value of their benefit and will result in steadily increasing out-of-pocket costs for them at the point that they begin to use benefits.
[P2919] An agent may encourage the purchase of a policy that is at the limit of a consumer’s affordability without taking into account future life changes such as the death of one spouse, which can reduce the income of the living spouse and result in an unaffordable premium. Consumers might spend thousands of dollars of limited income to pay for an LTCI policy that they could lose shortly before they need to claim those benefits. From the perspective of public policy, a worst-case scenario may be when a consumer receives a tax benefit for purchasing an LTCI policy, lapses that policy, and then turns to public benefits for help with the cost of long-term care. In those cases, taxpayers have paid twice: once for the tax subsidy and again for the care.
[P2920] Some agents represent a single company and are limited to selling that company’s products. Those agents may have a quota to meet or be expected to sell one of the company’s products over another. Other agents represent several companies and can sell many different products. However, commissions may be a factor in the product the agent will encourage a consumer to buy, particularly when the company is paying large commissions or bonuses to gain market share. Besides selling for excessive commissions, an agent might submit an application to a company that specializes in accepting substandard business (accepting health conditions, for example, that other companies won’t cover), exposing purchasers to almost certain premium increases later if premiums are not high enough to cover the additional risk.
[P2921] The NAIC adopted a provision intended to improve agent training. It requires companies selling LTCI to use only agents who have completed eight hours of training specific to LTCI. A qualifying course may not include training related to marketing or a specific company’s products. Like other NAIC provisions, however, it applies only in states that voluntarily adopt this measure.
[P2922] Consumers may also be able to take advantage of information and counseling through the federally funded State Health Insurance assistance Programs (SHIP), but only if they know one of these programs exists in their state and how to reach it. California law requires companies to notify consumers of the availability of the SHIP and provide its toll-free number on the outline of coverage. Many of the SHIPs can help people one-on-one to evaluate their suitability for the product they are considering and help them understand what the policy covers and how the benefits work.

[P2971] 14.4.4  Reciprocity Between States
[P2972] Under the DRA, states may provide asset disregards (and related estate recovery offsets) for Medicaid applicants who receive benefits under qualified long-term care insurance policies (Partnership policies) that were purchased in the same state.  This notice sets standards for states that choose to enter into a reciprocity agreement under section 6021(b) of the DRA, under which they agree to provide the same disregards and offsets for qualified Partnership policies that a Medicaid applicant purchased in another State that participates in the reciprocity agreement.  Let’s take a look at those Reciprocity Standards developed under the DRA:
[P2973] A.	Reciprocity Standards in the Provision of a Medicaid Asset Disregard For Eligibility Determination and Estate Recovery
[P2974] DRA Partnership States that have not elected to be exempt from the reciprocity standards described below, and Original Partnership States that have elected to adopt such reciprocity standards, are referred to here as "Participating States.”  Each Participating State agrees as follows:
[P2975] Any individual who has purchased a Partnership policy in any Participating State; who has received benefits under the policy; and who applies for Medicaid in a Participating State other than the one in which the policy was issued, will receive an asset disregard in an amount equal (dollar for dollar) to the benefits received under the policy;
[P2976] The asset disregard procedure and calculation will be the same for every individual with a Partnership policy that applies for Medicaid in the Participating State, without regard to whether the policy was purchased in another State, or the date the policy was purchased;
[P2977] An amount equal to the benefits received under the Partnership policy will be exempt from Medicaid estate recovery provisions; and,
[P2978] If a person moves from the State in which their Partnership policy was issued; later applies for Medicaid in another Participating State; and is determined to be eligible using a Partnership asset disregard, the Partnership asset disregard will not be revoked upon eligibility redetermination should the State subsequently decide to become exempt from the reciprocity agreement.
[P2979] Let’s take a closer look at the provisions of the reciprocity standards.
[P2980] B.	Other State Medicaid Eligibility Provisions Not Affected
[P2981] These reciprocity standards only apply to the asset disregard described in Section II, above.  Individuals who have received benefits under a Partnership policy, and qualify for an asset disregard, must meet all other Medicaid eligibility requirements in the State in which they are applying for Medicaid coverage.  These may include requirements that relate to the Partnership policy, but only if those requirements do not affect the asset disregard.
[P2982] Example:
[P2983] Some Partnership States may require Medicaid applicants holding Partnership policies to exhaust all of the benefits under the policy before becoming eligible for Medicaid.  Other Partnership States may allow applicants to apply for Medicaid coverage (and receive dollar for dollar asset disregard) even if residual benefits remain in the policy.)
[P2984] C.	Deemed Participation of States With Partnership Programs Established Under the DRA
[P2985] As required by the statute, all DRA Partnership States will be deemed to be participating in the reciprocity agreement unless they elect to be exempt from the reciprocity standards by notifying the Secretary, in writing, of their election.  All States with State Plan Amendments (SPA) effective dates prior to January 1, 2009, will be deemed to be participating in the reciprocity standards unless, prior to the effective date of these standards, the State elects exemption from the standards through a new SPA.  States with State Plan Amendment effective dates after January 1, 2009 will also be deemed to be participating in the reciprocity standards unless they elect exemption through a SPA.
[P2986] D.		Participation by States Operating a Partnership Under the Authority of a State Plan Amendment Approved Prior to May 14, 1993
[P2987] States with State Plan Amendments approved prior to May 14, 1993 may elect to adopt these reciprocity standards, and participate with those States operating a Partnership under the authority of the DRA.  To do so, those States must submit a new SPA to that effect.  Such States must agree to accept all of the reciprocity standards with respect to all other Participating States.
[P2988] E. 		Effect of Reciprocity Exemption
[P2989] In order for a Medicaid applicant to be eligible for the asset disregard, both the State in which the individual is applying, and the State in which the Partnership policy was purchased, must currently be participating in the reciprocity standards.  Accordingly, a State that elects an exemption from the reciprocity standards will not provide an asset disregard for Medicaid applicants who originally purchased Partnership policies in other, participating, Partnership States.  Similarly, persons who originally purchased Partnership policies in a State that elected exemption from the reciprocity standards will not be eligible for asset disregards in other Partnership States.  Once a State elects exemption from the standards, the exemption applies regardless of when a Medicaid applicant originally purchased a Partnership policy in another State (i.e., even if the Medicaid applicant purchased the policy prior to the date on which a State elected exemption from the reciprocity standards).
[P2990] F. 	Notice of Exemption by Currently Participating States
[P2991] States that are currently participating in the reciprocity agreement agree that they will provide written notice to the Secretary at least 60 days prior to the effective date of electing an exemption from the reciprocity standards.  The 60- day notification period makes it possible for the Department to notify other Participating States that, as of the effective date of withdrawal, asset disregards should no longer be made available to Medicaid applicants who originally purchased their policies in the State electing an exemption.
[P2992] G. 		Withdrawal of Reciprocity Exemption
[P2993] A State that has elected exemption from the Partnership reciprocity standards may also withdraw its election at any point.  A State may do so by submitting a new SPA.  Once a State withdraws its election, the State agrees that reciprocity will be applied to all people holding Partnership policies regardless of when the policy was originally purchased.
[P2994] H.		Change in Participation Status
[P2995] States that wish to change their participation status should submit a new state plan amendment.

[P3019] 15.0 Working With Clients
[P3020] Now that we’ve talked about what long-term care is, who provides it, how it is paid for, and long-term care insurance (including partnership policies), let’s take a moment to discuss some issues relating to your relationship with long-term care insurance clients. We’ll do this in two sections:
[P3021] Issues relating to working with seniors; and
[P3022] Issues relating to ethics and suitability applicable to all clients.
[P3023] Let’s start first with seniors.
[P3024] 15.1 Working With Seniors
[P3025] 15.1.1 Avoiding Elder Financial Abuse
[P3026] Your long-term care clients may be smart people at the top of their careers or they may be older seniors who are frightened about what is happening to their brothers, sisters, and friends.
[P3027] Most states are concerned about the potential for abuse that grows out of the need to work with elderly people who may be past their better days. If you don’t handle the relationship right, you could get into trouble. This section gives some information about penalties the states imposes on improper dealings with seniors.
[P3028] The flip side of this is that, if you do handle it right, you can render an important service to your senior clients. This section covers this as well.
[P3029] 15.1.2 Embezzlement
[P3030] Embezzlement is conversion to your own use of money or other personal property from a client.
[P3031] The penalty for this depends on how much you convert and varies from state to state. At the bottom end of the range are fines and restitution, together with a misdemeanor record. At the high end are fines in the tens of thousands of dollars and jail time of 10 or 20 years. Restitution may also be required.
[P3032] These penalties apply regardless of who the victim is, but they may be enhanced if the victim is age 60 or over or a “vulnerable adult.”
[P3033] 15.1.3 Cheating “Vulnerable Adults”
[P3034] In many states, similar penalties apply to anyone who uses fraud, deceit, misrepresentation, coercion, or unjust enrichment to obtain a vulnerable adult’s money or property knowing that the individual is a vulnerable adult (or having reason to know).
[P3035] A “vulnerable adult” is an individual age 18 or over who, because of age, developmental disability, mental illness, or physical disability requires supervision or personal care or lacks the personal and social skills required to live independently.
[P3036] Vulnerability Comes Gradually
[P3037] These penalties come as a result of increased financial abuse of the elderly. Financial abuse can occur in many ways and is definitely not restricted to the long-term care insurance sale setting. It is something of which you should definitely be aware.
[P3038] People often become vulnerable in gradual ways, particularly as a result of dementia, hearing loss, and visual impairment.
[P3039] 15.1.4 Clients Are Worried About Aging
[P3040] While it’s clear that not everyone who purchases long-term care insurance will be what we might call elderly, many potential buyers will be in their late fifties or in their sixties, a time in their lives when they worry about how they will fare as they age.
[P3041] Aging is often a difficult subject for people to manage. They begin to feel their mortality more and may well feel it with a large degree of discomfort. The long-term care policy sales process should not serve to increase that discomfort.
[P3042] 15.1.5 Make the Process Instructive
[P3043] The long-term care sales process should not be one in which a consumer feels intimidated or coerced into making a purchase. Clients should not be frightened into buying a policy. Make the process instructive.
[P3044] Let the client know that the purchase of a long-term care policy provides security: there will be cash available to pay for long-term care services that might arise. Owning a policy offers your client some measure of freedom to choose where and when they will receive care, the kind of care to be received, and how much of it there will be.
[P3045] 15.1.6 Have a Family Member or Friend Participate
[P3046] Working with seniors requires you to be aware of your client. Be a good listener. Like all of us, seniors need a sense of independence, but this desire for independence could exceed their capacity. You should notice if questions become repetitive or disconnected from the answers you provide.
[P3047] It is often a good idea to make a long-term care insurance sales presentation in the presence of a third party—a child, another family member, a friend, or even a trusted colleague from work— especially when the sale is to older people or to individuals who live alone.
[P3048] 15.1.7 Helping a Client Make an Important Decision
[P3049] Always avoid any kind of behavior that might be considered even the slightest bit abusive. This is not only self-protection for you. Knowing the capacity of your client to make important financial decisions is important in crafting a plan that will best meet their needs.
[P3050] Now, let’s look at the ethics and suitability issues in long-term care insurance sales.
[P3051] 15.2 Suitability and Ethics in Long-Term Care Insurance Sales
[P3052] Long-term care insurance benefits can make the difference between being able to maintain a life-long standard of living and dying with nothing. It may allow a person needing care to choose a setting in which they will be most comfortable rather than being limited to one that accepts Medicaid recipients.
[P3053] While those statements are certainly true, it does not necessarily follow that purchasing long-term care insurance is the right thing for everyone to do. Let’s take another look at some of the important suitability and ethical issues that apply in the sale of long-term care insurance.
[P3054] 15.2.1 Principal Suitability Focus must be on the Client
[P3055] Before making a recommendation, you need to consider the client, the available policies, and the insurer. Start with the client. Your suitability analysis for long-term care insurance should determine if the proposed policy would:
[P3056] be harmful for the client; or
[P3057] be beneficial for the client.
[P3059] Is the Purchase Harmful?
[P3060] Purchasing a long-term care insurance policy could be harmful if your client cannot afford the premiums—either currently or in the future. Such a purchase could require the client to forgo food, medicine, etc. The following indicators will tell you that the client cannot afford premiums:
[P3061] The client has difficulty paying for utilities, food or other important needs;
[P3062] The client’s income is limited to Social Security or Supplemental Security Income (SSI);
[P3063] The client is on Medicaid (in which case the individual would be considered uninsurable); and
[P3064] The client could not afford to keep the policy if its premium increased by 20%.
[P3065] If the client expects to pay policy premiums entirely from their income, premiums should not exceed 7% of that income.
[P3067] Is the Purchase Beneficial?
[P3068] A long-term care insurance policy can be beneficial for your client if they own significant assets and wishes to protect them. An individual with minimal assets would probably qualify for Medicaid.
[P3069] As a general rule, an individual should consider purchasing long-term care insurance if they:
[P3070] has substantial assets;
[P3071] wants to protect those assets from being exhausted by the need to pay for long-term care;
[P3072] is able to pay premiums and possible premium increases without experiencing financial difficulty;
[P3073] wants to remain independent and avoid being supported by others; and
[P3074] wants to be able to choose the setting in which long-term care, if needed, is provided.
[P3076] We just said that a client may be a candidate for long-term care insurance if they have substantial assets. What do we mean by “substantial assets?” Frankly, this is a judgment call that depends on client wishes, resources available to live on, and the desire or need to pass something on to heirs. It can be said, though, that $30,000 is not substantial. If you client has less than $30,000 to protect, forget long-term care insurance.
[P3077] Just as it is possible to have too little to be a good candidate for long-term care insurance, it is possible to have too much. A client who has a large investment portfolio might be well advised simply to self-insure. Making this determination requires finding out more about the individual’s assets. Are they stable, conservative, income producing assets or has this prospect invested everything they own in space widget futures.
[P3079] 15.2.2 Consider the Client’s Other Needs in Suitability Analysis
[P3080] Although your client’s financial situation needs to be considered in determining suitability, other family needs must also be considered. Your client may be responsible for supporting:
[P3081] a surviving spouse;
[P3082] dependent children; and
[P3083] dependent parents.
[P3084] If your client must provide for others, don’t forget them. Make sure that your long-term care recommendation doesn’t take away from the support that your client wants to provide for their family. Remember, a big part of suitability is making sure a client’s goals are met.
[P3085] 15.2.3 Consider the Client’s Family Health History and Longevity
[P3086] Your client’s family history of disease should be considered in determining the likely risk for needing long-term care. It’s also important to keep in mind that lifestyle can have a significant impact on an individual’s long-term health. Lifestyle choices: eating well, getting enough sleep, moderation in alcohol consumption, exercising, and so on, can offset genetic disposition to some extent. Some diseases and conditions that appear to be genetically linked include:
[P3087] Just as certain diseases appear to have a genetic component, longevity also appears to be genetically linked. Since the likelihood of requiring long-term care increases as an individual ages, clients whose family members lived into their 90s or beyond are more likely to die at an advanced age and are more likely to need long-term care at some time.
[P3089] 15.2.4 Suitability Analysis
[P3090] In making your suitability analysis for a client, you must use the suitability standards developed by the insurer and should consider the:
[P3091] client’s financial information, including the client’s ability to pay for the coverage currently and in the event of the premium increase, as well as assets;
[P3092] client’s goals or needs with respect to long-term care;
[P3093] advantages and disadvantages of using insurance to meet the client’s identified goals or needs; and
[P3094] values, benefits and costs of the client’s existing insurance compared to the values, benefits and costs of the recommended purchase or replacement.
[P3095] Suitability Analysis—Documentation
[P3096] You are required to make reasonable efforts to obtain the necessary information from the client. This includes giving the “Long-term Care Insurance Personal Worksheet” to the client.
[P3097] You must return a completed personal worksheet to the insurer before your client is considered for coverage (except in the case of sales of employer group long-term care insurance to employees). The information you receive from your clients is private. Sale or dissemination of this information outside your company or agency is prohibited.
[P3098] 15.2.5 Evaluating the Long-Term Care Insurance Policy
[P3099] Once you determine that long-term care insurance is suitable for your client, you still need to assess which policy is most appropriate.
[P3100] A client who is most interested in low premiums should probably look for a policy that pays on a reimbursement basis. Indemnity policies are more expensive and are more likely to have premium increases than reimbursement policies.
[P3101] Make sure you understand client needs and whether a policy covers them. It may be important to your client that:
[P3102] Long-term care is covered in all settings;
[P3103] Companion and homemaker services are considered covered services;
[P3104] The client can hire anyone, including family members, to provide personal care and homemaker services;
[P3105] Certain benefits under the policy are not subject to the elimination period;
[P3106] Receiving home care services counts towards satisfying the elimination period;
[P3107] The elimination period needs to be satisfied only once;
[P3108] Limitations are not imposed on benefits for pre-existing conditions;
[P3109] A bed-holding benefit will maintain their place in a facility so the client can visit family, etc.; and
[P3110] Home modifications, medical equipment and caregiver training will be paid for to enable the client to receive care at home.
[P3111] 15.2.6 Evaluating the Insurance Company Issuing the Policy
[P3112] Payment of legitimate long-term care claims under a policy could be jeopardized by an insurer’s unstable financial condition. For that reason, it is important to know the insurer’s financial condition. Agencies that rate insurance companies include:
[P3113] A.M. Best;
[P3114] Weiss;
[P3115] Moody’s; and
[P3116] Standard and Poor’s.
[P3117] Avoid placing long-term care insurance business with an insurance company whose financial status or claims-paying ability is not strong. In terms of actual ratings, stick to companies rated by A.M. Best or Weiss B+ or greater (greater is better).
[P3118] In addition to financial strength, you should know the insurer’s history of rate increases. You can’t expect that rates will never go up; the costs of long-term care services are going up. But you can avoid insurers with a history of frequent or large rate increases during times when other insurers didn’t.
[P3119] 15.2.7 Ethical Concerns Often Involve Replacement and Disclosure
[P3120] Long-term care sales have many of the same ethical concerns that apply to other insurance sales, such as misrepresentation, lack of suitability, etc. In addition to the suitability issues, just discussed, this course will focus on:
[P3121] replacement; and
[P3122] disclosure.
[P3123] Let’s briefly consider each of these concerns.
[P3124] Replacement of Long-Term Care Insurance
[P3125] Before you recommend that your client replace and existing long-term care insurance policy, you must be able to show that the new policy will materially improve your client’s situation. If you can’t, the replacement should not be made.
[P3126] If you are proposing to replace a policy issued before 1997, remember that this will result in the loss of the policy’s grandfathered tax treatment. Replacing the old policy with a new tax qualified policy might be appropriate, but you have to consider benefits that might be lost.
[P3127] In addition, before recommending an insured exchange an existing long-term care policy for one issued by a different insurer, you should determine if the existing insurer would be willing to make any desired changes to the existing policy. If the insurer would agree to such changes, replacement would generally be a less desirable alternative. These changes, of course, would not involve contractual provision but benefit limits and riders that might have been added to the policy at the time of application.
[P3128] Client Must Know Both Advantages and Disadvantage of the Replacement
[P3129] If you are recommending a replacement, you must make a complete disclosure of all material facts, including the advantages and disadvantages of the replacement policy compared with the existing policy insofar as the following are concerned:
[P3132] If you decide replacement is appropriate for your client, never terminate the old policy until the new coverage is approved.
[P3134] Waivers of Time Limits in Replacement Policy
[P3135] If you are replacing a long-term care insurance policy, don’t let your client lose credit for any time limits or other requirements satisfied under the old policy. Policies are modified, for example, to waive time periods that apply to pre-existing conditions. Other probationary periods can also be waived to the extent those time periods were satisfied under the policy being replaced.
[P3136] There is little question that insurers often introduce new and improved products over time. To the extent such new long-term care insurance products offer a client improved coverage, it may be to the client’s benefit to replace the existing coverage.
[P3138] Required Disclosures
[P3139] Disclosing material information to a client is an ethical requirement (replacement or not). It is essential to help a client to make an informed decision about your long-term care insurance recommendation. Most states specify three specific disclosure forms that relate to:
[P3140] Long-term Care Insurance Personal Worksheet;
[P3141] Things You Should Know Before You Buy Long-term Care Insurance; and
[P3142] Potential Rate Increase Disclosure Form.
[P3143] Insurance policies are complicated contracts that may be misunderstood by consumers. State regulations require that insurers prominently disclose certain information to their long-term care insurance customers. Those disclosures may be required in the form of:
[P3144] a statement in a separate section of the policy;
[P3145] an insured’s signed acceptance;
[P3146] an explanation in an outline of coverage; or
[P3147] a combination of these disclosure forms.
[P3148] Renewability Disclosure
[P3149] Individual long-term care insurance policies are required to be guaranteed renewable. Every individual long-term care insurance policy must contain a renewability provision that:
[P3150] is appropriately captioned;
[P3151] appears on the first page of the policy;
[P3152] clearly states that the coverage is guaranteed renewable; and
[P3153] includes a statement that premium rates may change.
[P3154] Disclosures for After-Issue Riders and Endorsements
[P3155] The following disclosures must be made about additions of riders or endorsements to a policy made after the policy was issued—for example, at reinstatement or renewal (unless the customer requested them):
[P3156] Customers must sign before any rider or endorsement may eliminate benefits or coverage;
[P3157] Customers must sign before any rider or endorsement may increase benefits or coverage if it also increases the premium (unless the increase is required by law); and
[P3158] If a separate additional premium is required for any additional benefits added by endorsement or rider, the additional premium charge must be indicated in the policy, rider or endorsement.
[P3159] Disclosure for Usual and Customary Benefit Payments
[P3160] A long-term insurance policy paying benefits on a “usual and customary,” “reasonable and customary,” or other similar basis must include a definition of the term and an explanation in the outline of coverage.
[P3161] Disclosure of Pre-Existing Conditions Limitations
[P3162] If a long-term care insurance policy or certificate contains a limitation on benefits because of pre-existing conditions, the policy or certificate must include a separate paragraph in which a statement of such limitations appears. The separate paragraph in the policy must be labeled as “Pre-existing Condition Limitations.”
[P3163] Disclosure of Tax-Qualified Status
[P3164] A tax-qualified long-term care insurance contract must include a disclosure statement in the policy and in the outline of coverage stating that the policy is a qualified long-term care insurance contract under §7702B(b) of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986.
[P3165] Disclosure that Premiums Could Increase
[P3166] The circumstances under which insurers may increase long-term care insurance policy premiums are a mystery to many clients. For that reason, insurers must provide a disclosure of their rate-changing practices to clients for long-term care insurance.
[P3167] The required disclosure must be made to the client at the time of application or enrollment, unless the method of application does not allow for delivery at that time. In such cases, disclosure must be given to the client no later than at the time of delivery of the policy or certificate.
[P3168] Contents of the Future-Premiums Disclosure
[P3169] The following disclosures must be made:
[P3170] A statement that the policy may be subject to rate increases in the future;
[P3171] An explanation of potential future premium rate revisions and the options available to the owner in the event of such a revision;
[P3172] The premium rate that will be in effect for the client until a rate increase is requested;
[P3173] The disclosure must contain a general explanation for applying premium rate adjustments that includes:
[P3174] A description of when any premium rate adjustment would be effective—on the policy anniversary or next billing date, for example; and
[P3175] A statement of the insured’s right to a revised premium rate schedule if the premium is changed; and
[P3176] Finally, the client must be given information about premium rate increases implemented by the insurer over the prior 10-year period that identifies the:
[P3177] Policy forms on which premiums have been increased,
[P3178] Calendar years during which the policy form was available for purchase, and
[P3179] Amount or percentage of each increase.
[P3181] 15.2.8 The Client Must Sign an Acknowledgement
[P3182] An applicant for coverage is required to sign an acknowledgment that the insurer made the required disclosures concerning the:
[P3183] possibility of rate increases in the future; and
[P3184] insurer’s rate increase history over the prior 10 years.
[P3185] The acknowledgment must be signed at the time of application for the coverage. However, if the method of application prohibits the client’s signed acknowledgment at the time of application, the client must sign no later than at the time of delivery of the policy or certificate.
[P3186] 15.2.9 Notice of Upcoming Rate Increases
[P3187] Insurers must provide notice of an upcoming premium rate increase to all policyowners and certificate holders at least 45 days before implementing the premium increase. The notice must include:
[P3188] A statement that the policy may still be subject to future rate increases;
[P3189] Another explanation of potential future premium rate revisions and the options available to the owner in the event of such a revision;
[P3190] The new premium rate that will be in effect for the client until a future rate increase is requested;
[P3191] A description of when any premium rate adjustment would be effective; and
[P3192] A statement of the insured’s right to a revised premium rate schedule if the premium is changed.
[P3193] 15.2.10 Standards for Marketing Long-Term Care Insurance
[P3194] The following standards apply to the marketing of long-term care insurance. You or the insurer must:
[P3195] Ensure that any comparison of policies will be fair and accurate;
[P3196] Ensure that excessive insurance is not sold or issued;
[P3197] Prominently display on the first page of the outline of coverage and the policy a statement indicating the policy may not cover all costs associated with long-term care;
[P3198] Provide copies of the disclosure forms to the client;
[P3199] Make every reasonable effort to determine whether a client already has accident and sickness or long-term care insurance and the types and amounts of any such insurance. In the case of qualified long-term care insurance contracts, however, no inquiry as to whether a client or enrollee has accident and sickness insurance is required;
[P3200] Provide written notice to the prospective policyholder or certificate holder at the time of solicitation that a senior insurance counseling program approved by the commissioner is available and the name, address, and telephone number of the program;
[P3201] Use the terms “noncancellable” or “level premium” only when the policy or certificate conforms with the definitions of such terms included in the regulations; and
[P3202] Provide an explanation of contingent benefit upon lapse.
[P3204] 15.2.11 Prohibited Practices
[P3205] In addition to these marketing requirements, certain acts and practices are specifically prohibited in connection with the marketing of long-term care insurance. You may not:
[P3206] Knowingly make of a misleading representation or incomplete comparison of any insurance policies or insurers for the purpose of inducing a person to lapse, forfeit, surrender, terminate, retain, pledge, assign, borrow on or convert any insurance policy or to take out a policy of insurance with another insurer;
[P3207] Employ any method of marketing having the effect of or tending to induce the purchase of insurance through force, fright, threat, or undue pressure to purchase or recommend the purchase of insurance;
[P3208] Use a marketing method that fails to disclose that a purpose of the marketing is solicitation of insurance and that contact will be made by an insurance agent or insurance company; or
[P3209] Misrepresent a material fact in selling or offering to sell a policy.
[P3211] 16.0	Conclusion
[P3213] It is clear to virtually everyone who might be potentially affected—individuals, families, their communities, their state and local government bodies and the federal government—that it is possible that our country will experience a health care crisis related to the need of our aging, long-lived population for long-term care. The only way to address this is through proactive planning. This planning and the available resources that have been developed to support planning goals have to be brought to the attention of individuals, along with the idea that it is important for them to engage, also proactively, in developing a contingency plan for how to deal with their own potential need for long-term care. Long-term care insurance, while it is under-utilized today to help individuals manage the cost of long-term care, can play an important role in the planning that individuals and families undertake. For this to be true, however, requires agents who sell long-term care insurance in Indiana to be knowledgeable about a broad array of long-term care planning issues and resources, which includes, of course, knowledge about Indiana long-term care insurance policies. Because insurance agents are the ones primarily responsible for bringing long-term care insurance planning to the attention of consumers, and are even more important in the role of explaining what long-term care insurance is and how it works, the need for insurance agents  to develop their expertise is ongoing.
[P3215] The need for long-term care is often difficult to talk about. Not only does is involve an individual’s mortality (as with life insurance), but it also involves a loss of capacity, which many fear more than death. In addition, the resources to pay for long-term care, ranging from personal savings, to government programs, to various types of insurance are quite complicated.
[P3217] Here are a few of the things we covered in this course and how you can apply them in the field:
[P3219] Long-Term Care Services and Providers: We talked about the different ways that people with physical or mental impairments can receive care. When discussing care options with your clients, pay particular attention to the level of care they will receive and the costs of that care;
[P3221] Sources of Long-Term Care Funds: Don’t focus just on long-term care insurance. It is not always the answer. Be savvy about all the alternatives for financing long-term care insurance. Explain the income tax treatment of tax-qualified long-term care policy premiums and benefits;
[P3223] Long-Term Care Insurance: Don’t ignore long-term care insurance. Understand what it can do for your clients and what it can’t do. You should describe the basic provisions and optional benefits in long-term care insurance policies;
[P3225] Indiana Medicaid: You should be able to discuss the criteria that must be met before benefits are payable under Medicare and Medicaid for long-term care services; and
[P3227] Medicaid Planning and the Partnership Program: Let clients know that qualifying for Medicaid could entail spending down everything they have. Explain how a partnership policy could protect them from this sad possibility. Discuss the general outline of the Long-term Care Partnership programs available in many states.
[P3229] Your clients may be of all ages but with LTCI, many are seniors. Pay attention to your clients and take special pains if your clients are older. Understand their needs and educate them about long-term care. And get the client’s family involved if necessary.
[P3231] Good luck working with long-term care insurance.
[P3233] And thank you for studying with RegEd!
